<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on the Book of Revelation, Chapter 3. Having previously addressed the pride and spiritual blindness of the "lukewarm" bishop of Laodicea, Rupert now interprets Christ's remedy: the application of the "eye-salve" of humility and the transformative power of divine discipline.</meta>

<page-num>cxi</page-num>
<header>On Revelation, Chapter 3</header>

### And anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see.

<margin>Eye-salve is humility. Luke 10.</margin>
The eye-salve <term>collyrium: a medicinal ointment used in antiquity for treating eye infections</term> by which the defects of the eyes are cleansed, signifies the sweetness of humility. This humility assists the "little ones," so that those mysteries which are hidden from the wise and the prudent may be revealed to them. <note>original: "sapientibus & prudentibus abscondita sunt"; a reference to Christ’s prayer in Matthew 11:25 and Luke 10:21.</note> Therefore, "anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see"—that is, purify your heart with true humility, so that you may see your own poverty and recognize the true riches of God’s goodness.

### Those whom I love, I rebuke and chasten.

It is as if he says: The things I speak to you in rebuke and correction, receive them as the grace and goodwill of a lover. For it is not the habit of Wisdom to allow the child she loves to be youthfully puffed up and vanish into vanity; rather, she both loves and chastens. She strikes the unrestrained child, and the same one she once nursed as an infant, she now beats and strikes with a rod when he becomes too talkative and reckless. Thus, while I chasten you—while I prick you as if with nails driven deep—I truly love you all the more.

### Be zealous, therefore, and repent.

"Be zealous" <note>original: "Aemulare"</note>—that is, by loving him who loves and chastens you, imitate him with a good fervor of the soul. You who were lukewarm, grow hot through this zeal; and because you have been ungrateful to your lover until now by not returning his love, repent. Until now, he has struck down the "haughty eyebrow" <note>original: "superciliū"; a Latin idiom for pride or arrogance.</note> of the one who seems wealthy and rich, who vainly imagines himself to abound in good works. Now, he asks quite amiably of this man, or of any such wealthy person, that he share the glory of his works with God, or with the Son of God, who grants all things. This is so that he may glory in God, or cause God to be glorified in him, and so that he may glorify the Holy One in all his works.
<margin>1 Corinthians 1.</margin>

### Behold, he says, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will enter to him and dine with him.

The meaning is this: that which I have said to you so far in rebuke is like someone standing at a rich man's door and knocking, so that, being admitted as a guest, he may dine with him on the treasures stored within. If he is admitted, the "feast of charity" <note>original: "conuiuiū charitatis"</note> is celebrated, because charity cannot exist between fewer than two people. Thus...

<summary>Rupert explains that Christ’s rebukes are acts of love intended to foster humility, which he likens to a medicinal eye-salve that allows the soul to see its own poverty. He concludes by interpreting Christ’s "knocking at the door" as an invitation to a communal feast of love between the believer and God.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 3:20-21. Rupert is finishing his explanation of the "knocking at the door" and beginning his interpretation of the "throne" promised to the victor, linking Christ's victory to his humility.</meta>

<page-num>cxii</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book II</header>

For what do you say—that you are rich? You boast in a good conscience; but look, I stand and knock at the door of your heart. Admit me, and have me as a participant or companion of your glory, so that you do not boast alone, but with me. Indeed, boast not in yourself, but in me, through whom you have been made rich. If in this way you or anyone else hearing my voice opens the door to me, and carries out all good things by referring them to the glory of God, I will enter in to him, and in his heart, as if in the house of a friend, I will have confidence. And now indeed I will dine—that is, I will take delight with him in the good things of his conscience—and he himself in the future shall enjoy my good things with me.

**To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne, just as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on His throne.**

<margin>One must be humbled in all things</margin>
At this level, to "overcome" means to drive far away all the levity of boasting and vain glory through the maturity of wisdom. It means that even when a person appears great to others, they remain small in their own eyes, according to what that same Wisdom says:

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 3</margin>
The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God. <note>original: "Quanto magnus es, humilia te in omnibus & coram deo inuenies gratiam." Quoted from Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 3:18.</note> For humility, whose company Wisdom has never lacked, is accustomed to fly toward heaven.

<margin>To sit on my throne</margin>
Therefore he says: "To him who overcomes, I will grant to sit with me on my throne"—not so that he might be made equal to divinity <term>divinitati: the state of being God</term>, but so that he might be joined to eternity. "Just as I also overcame," he says. How did he who speaks these things—Christ—overcome, except through the inestimable greatness of his humility and charity?

<margin>Philippians 2</margin>
For since he was in the form of God, he did not wish to boast in that form alone, but (pay close attention) he wished for humans—who had become inglorious through the sin of the first man—to become fellow participants in his glory. Therefore, "he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant"; therefore "he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, even death on a cross." <note>original: "semetipsum exinaniuit... factus obediens vsque ad mortem"; a reference to the famous "Christ Hymn" in Philippians 2:6-8.</note> This is the supreme victory of humility and wisdom, which destroyed the pride and foolishness of the first man. <margin>The first voice like the sound of a trumpet</margin>
This first voice is his—the same as the one heard earlier, which said: "Write what you see." Therefore, he did not simply say, "and the voice which I heard," but "the *first* voice which I heard." Prophets understood their own visions.

...just as heaven, like a visible structure, is joined together with doors, bolts, and bars. Therefore, what follows is immediately understood in its proper sense: *I was in the spirit* <note>original: "fui in spiritu"</note>. It is as if he were saying, "I immediately understood through a spiritual sense those things which were being shown to me through images," so that we might not doubt that what the voice said pertains to the intellect: *and I will show you what must take place soon after these things.* For it is not as some heretics have claimed—that prophetic visions of this kind occurred in such a way that the prophets themselves did not understand what realities or meanings their visions contained. Consequently, there was no need for him to say here, "and I will show you what you have seen, and what things are, and what must take place after these," in the same way he had said earlier: *Write, therefore, what you have seen, and what things are, and what must take place after these.* For those things which he had seen, and those which then existed, he already knew; because he had seen the past while walking with the Lord until His end, and he was then seeing the present state of the Church. However, he did not yet know the future. Therefore, the voice rightly instructs him only concerning future things: *I will show you,* it says, *what must take place soon after these things.* Nevertheless, those things he had seen, even those that had passed, he saw as many and deeply mystical images—not so much for his own instruction as for ours.

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 4:3. Having previously discussed the one sitting on the throne and the stones symbolizing judgment (jasper and sardius), Rupert now turns to the rainbow surrounding the throne, interpreting it as the balance of God's mercy alongside His judgment.</meta>

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>On Revelation Chapter 4</header>

[He] does not repel faith from His grace. Wherefore he immediately adds:

> **And there was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald in appearance.**

<margin>The rainbow is a sign of propitiation <note>original: "propitiatio"; refers to the act of regaining God's favor or making atonement</note>. Genesis 9.</margin>
The rainbow is indeed a sign of propitiation, as the Lord said to Noah: *I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my covenant which I have made with you.* Therefore, the "rainbow around the throne" is the mercy prepared for all those seeking it at the coming of the Redeemer—a mercy which runs ahead of judgment throughout the circuit of the world with the great proclamation of Gospel preaching.

<margin>There is no judgment of God without mercy. Matthew 25.</margin>
Nevertheless, just as that judgment by water <note>The Great Flood</note> was not without mercy (which saved eight souls in the ark), so that judgment by fire <note>The Final Judgment at the end of time</note> will not be without mercy for those who, because of the six works of mercy they performed, will be placed at the right hand, while the King says: *For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat,* etc. So too, this coming of mercy of which we now speak did not proceed without judgment.

<margin>John 13. <note>The text cites John 13, but the quote "Now is the judgment of the world" is found in John 12:31</note> John 9.</margin>
For when mercy was being most greatly built up through the passion of Christ, He said: *Now is the judgment of the world.* But even before the moment of that same passion, He says in a certain place: *For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see might see, and those who see might become blind.* Since, therefore, mercy running together with judgment saved eight souls there <note>in the time of Noah</note>, by which the world was restored—and since mercy is necessary in the future judgment—why is mercy described in this way now (when He says He has come for judgment) by saying: *And there was a rainbow around the throne*, which, as has been said, is a sign of propitiation? Clearly, it is because of the greatness or multitude of mercy in which He now comes. For He so judged, and so performed the judgment of the world, that in that very act of judging, this merciful and faithful <term>High Priest (pontifex)</term> might, with His whole purpose, grant repentance and the remission of sins through His own blood. Thus, by rising again, He might lead back our nature—which was decaying and dried up like hay because of sin—to an unfading state of glory.

<margin>The emerald is of extreme greenness.</margin>
Hence, when he had said, *and there was a rainbow around the throne,* he added: *Like an emerald in appearance.* For the emerald is of such extreme greenness that [it surpasses] green herbs, foliage, and gems...

<summary>Rupert interprets the rainbow around God's throne as a symbol of the covenant of mercy established with Noah and fulfilled through Christ. He argues that God’s judgment is never separated from His mercy, comparing the salvation of Noah's family to the salvation offered through Christ’s passion.</summary>
<keywords>Rainbow, Covenant of Noah, Mercy vs Judgment, Emerald, Passion of Christ, High Priest, Salvation, Gospel preaching</keywords>

...and it stains all the air around it with its reflected greenness. Therefore, the rainbow is like an emerald in appearance because this mercy will reform our old age <note>original: "senium"; refers to the decay of the mortal condition or the "old man" of sin</note> into the solid beauty of eternal greenness <note>In medieval theology, "viriditas" (greenness) symbolized spiritual vitality, freshness, and the life-giving power of God</note>.

<margin>The twenty-four seats of the elders. Wisdom 3. 1 Corinthians 6.</margin>
> **And around the throne were twenty-four seats, and upon the thrones sat twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, and on their heads were golden crowns.**

Just as we understand the kingdom of God in the "throne," so in the "seats" we understand the judicial power of the saints, because it is written: *The saints shall judge nations.* <note>Wisdom 3:8</note> But why are the elders sitting in the seats shown to be twenty-four in number? On this, there is a diverse exposition among the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers," early influential theologians like Jerome and Augustine</note>. For some (of whom the blessed Jerome is one and the best known) wish the twenty-four books of the Old Law <note>The Hebrew Bible, which was traditionally counted as 24 books in the Jewish and early Christian tradition</note> to be understood as symbolized here by these same twenty-four elders. Several others understand the Church—which was generated through the twin Testaments from the patriarchs and apostles—in these same elders; or perhaps those who fulfill the perfection of work (which is symbolized by the number six <note>Six was considered a "perfect" number in medieval numerology because it is the sum of its divisors (1+2+3)</note>) through the clear preaching of the Gospel: for four times six makes twenty-four. We, however, while approving both this sense and that one as not useless, will nevertheless attempt to bring forth something certain concerning the majesty of the Scriptures.

<margin>Allegory concerning the kingdom of David and Saul. 1 Samuel 15. 2 Samuel 22 <note>Rupert cites these as 1 and 2 Kings following the Vulgate numbering</note></margin>
That throne set in heaven, which (as has already been said) we understand as the kingdom of God, and around which these seats were placed, began to be set from the time when David—the father of Christ according to the flesh—obtained the kingdom of the Israelite people. For he reigned over the people of God as a "type" <note>A "type" is a historical person or event that foreshadows a future reality in Christian theology</note> of that same Christ, his future son. And just as it was destined that, with the kingdom of sin destroyed, that King of Justice—strong of hand and desirable—would reign, so it happened that, with the kingdom of Saul cast aside (whom God rejected because of pride), David reigned like a very tender "worm of the wood," <note>original: "vermiculus"; David describes himself as a worm in Psalm 22:6, a passage traditionally read as a prophecy of Christ's humility</note> humble in his own eyes, so that in the right order of heavenly condescension, the father king would sit before his son over the people of God. For, so that we may not doubt it is so—namely, that of that father and this son...

<summary>Rupert interprets the twenty-four elders of Revelation as symbols of either the books of the Old Testament or the combined authority of the Patriarchs and Apostles. He further connects the establishment of God's throne to the historical transition from the prideful King Saul to the humble King David.</summary>

# On Revelation Chapter 4

<margin>Luke 1.</margin>
<margin>The twenty-four elders are the twelve judges and the twelve apostles. Judges 3.</margin>
...that there may be one seat <note>original: "sedes"; here used interchangeably with "throne"</note>, Gospel authority meets us, when the Archangel Gabriel says to Mary: *And the Lord God will give to him the throne of David his father, and he will reign in the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end.* <note>Luke 1:32-33</note> If therefore we look upon that throne placed in heaven in a broadened sense—in which David sat, and after him this son of his—it immediately appears what the twenty-four seats in its circuit are, or who the twenty-four elders are, and how they are in its circuit. For after the Son to whom the Lord God gave the throne of David his father, twelve apostles succeeded; and before that father [David], those who first presided over the people of God by God’s election were twelve judges. The first was Othniel, son of Kenaz, brother of Caleb; the second Ehud <note>original: "Aioth"</note>, son of Gera, son of Jemini; the third Shamgar, son of Anath; the fourth Barak, son of Abinoam of Kedesh-Naphtali; the fifth Gideon, son of Joash; the sixth Jair the Gileadite; the seventh Jephthah the Gileadite; the eighth Ibzan <note>original: "Abessan"</note> of Bethlehem; the ninth Elon <note>original: "Ahialon"</note> the Zebulunite; the tenth Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite; the eleventh Samson; the twelfth Samuel.

<margin>Matthew 19.</margin>
These, preceding that throne—the throne or kingdom of David—in time, sit around the throne placed in heaven as if from the front side. But the other judges, namely the twelve apostles, to whom it was said: *You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel* <note>Matthew 19:28</note>, succeeding the Son of David in time, sit around 그 throne as if from the rear side. Therefore, there are twenty-four seats in the circuit of the throne, and twenty-four elders upon the thrones.

<margin>Why they are called "elders."</margin>
<margin>Judges 2.</margin>
And they are rightly called "elders" <note>original: "seniores"</note>, because namely through the maturity of their faith they restrained the people of God who were behaving with youthful lawlessness <note>Rupert contrasts the "senior" maturity of the leaders with the "youthful" (iuueniliter) impulses of the sinful populace</note>. For of those earlier ones it is written: *And the Lord raised up judges, who would deliver them from the hands of the plunderers, but they would not listen to them, fornicating with strange gods and adoring them.* And thereafter: *And when the Lord raised up judges, in their days His mercy was moved, and He heard the groans of the afflicted, and delivered them from the slaughter of the plunderers. But after the judge was dead, they returned, and did much worse things than they had done.* <note>Judges 2:16-19</note>

<summary>Rupert of Deutz identifies the twenty-four elders of Revelation as the twelve Old Testament Judges and the twelve New Testament Apostles. He argues they surround Christ’s throne (the "Throne of David") in a chronological circle—the Judges in front and the Apostles behind.</summary>

### And there were seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven spirits of God.

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
<margin>John 16</margin>
<margin>Acts 2</margin>
Before the throne are the seven spirits of God. These illuminate the often-mentioned kingdom of God, which is the church of God. There indeed—that is, in that heavenly glory—they illuminate in such a way that the inhabitants see the brightness of God *face to face*. Here, however, where the church still journeys in part as a pilgrim, they illuminate her so that she does not yet see perfectly, but as if *through a mirror and in a riddle* <note>original: "per speculum & in aenigmate"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12, meaning our current understanding of divine things is indirect and obscured</note>. Yet they illuminate enough so that she may know the truth of God and avoid errors, according to the promise of Him who said: *When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth* <note>John 16:13</note>. From the time when He who spoke these words during His passion rose again and ascended into heaven, the splendor of those lamps has shone more broadly across the world. Moreover, these seven lamps shine from a single lampstand <note>original: "candelabro"</note>; these seven spirits come from one and the same Christ. Their light appeared upon His disciples in the form of tongues of fire on the fiftieth day <note>The feast of Pentecost; see Acts 2</note> after His resurrection. The first lamp is the spirit of wisdom. The second is the spirit of understanding, and then the other spirits follow in order, just as they are described by the prophet as resting upon a single flower <note>This refers to Isaiah 11:1–2, where the "Spirit of the Lord" rests upon a "shoot" or "flower" from the stem of Jesse. In medieval art and theology, this "flower" is Christ.</note>. In this passage of Revelation they are called lamps, according to the description of another prophet, shining upon a single lampstand <note>Zechariah 4:2</note>.

## And in the sight of the throne there was as it were a sea of glass, like crystal.

<margin>
The sea is the baptism of Christ.
Exodus 12.
1 Corinthians 10.
</margin>
Why is there a sea in the sight of the throne? Clearly for this reason: so that whoever wishes to ascend to that seat of God and enter into that kingdom of God may do so, provided they cross this sea and are illuminated by the brilliant light of the aforementioned lamps. For the baptism of Christ is called a "sea," namely because of its well-known resemblance to the Red Sea. Through that sea, the people of God were liberated from Egyptian slavery and passed across after the lamb was sacrificed, while Pharaoh was drowned along with his chariots, his horses, and his horsemen.

<summary>Rupert explains that the seven lamps of Revelation represent the Holy Spirit's sevenfold gifts which illuminate the Church, and identifies the "sea of glass" as Christian baptism, prefigured by the Exodus.</summary>

Divinity now shines in that body like the sun in glass; mortality has perished in that body, just as the mobility or flow of water vanishes when it becomes crystal. Furthermore, we hope that we ourselves shall be raised and transformed into his likeness—that is, we shall be <term>impassible</term> <note>From the Latin "impassibilis," meaning "unable to suffer," "unchanging," or "incapable of being harmed by external forces."</note>. There will therefore be a sea of glass indeed, but one like crystal.

<margin>The four living creatures are the four evangelists.</margin>
These living creatures have long been well-known to the Holy Church by face and by name, as they represent the figures of the four evangelists. <note>Matthew (man/angel), Mark (lion), Luke (ox), and John (eagle).</note> However, according to the literal order of the text, we must first ask how these creatures are said to be both "in the midst of the throne" and "around the throne," <note>Revelation 4:6</note> since the twenty-four elders—who are certainly more numerous—are said above to be "around" and not also "in the midst" of the throne. To find this more certainly, 

<margin>Ezekiel 1</margin>
one must first know that according to Ezekiel, these living creatures are both four and one. For so he spoke in his first vision: *from the midst of them came the likeness of four living creatures...* <note>original: "ex medio eorum similitudo quatuor animalium"</note> and so on. He says in another vision: 

<margin>Ezekiel 10</margin>
*This is the living creature that I had seen by the river Chebar.* <note>original: "Ipsum est animal quod videram iuxta fluuium Chobar."</note> And when the Cherubim moved, the wheels went along with them. And afterward: *This is the living creature that I saw under the God of Israel, by the river Chebar. And I understood that they were Cherubim; each one had four faces, and each one four wings, and the likeness of a human hand was under their wings; and the likeness of their faces were the same faces I had seen by the river Chebar.* He himself also reveals a little how there are four living creatures and yet one living creature, when he says: *Each one had four faces, and each one had four wings.* <note>Ezekiel 1:6</note> Therefore, we say first that the 

<margin>The four creatures, or the four faces of the one, are the four <term>sacraments</term> of Christ. <note>Here, "sacraments" refers to the "mysteries" or "sacred events" of Christ's life, rather than the ritual sacraments of the Church.</note></margin>
one living creature is Christ. The four creatures, however, or the four faces of the one, are the four principal <term>sacraments</term> of Christ, which it is not permitted for a Christian to be ignorant of: the first of which is the **Incarnation**; the second, the **Passion**; the third, the **Resurrection**; and the fourth, the **Ascension**. Indeed, a Christian is not allowed to fail to recognize these faces or be ignorant of these mysteries; rather, one ought to look back upon them in daily confession, just as the Apostolic tradition has set them before us in the Creed. <note>The "symbolo" refers to the Apostles' Creed, the foundational statement of Christian belief.</note> For it begins: *I believe in God the Father Almighty, Creator of heaven and earth, and in Jesus Christ His only Son...*

<margin>The Gospels and the five books of Moses.</margin>

<margin>John has one order for the four animals; Ezekiel has another.</margin>

For in the Gospel, Christ is first a **man** by nature; then a **calf** through his passion <note>The calf or ox represents sacrifice, referring to Christ’s death on the cross.</note>; then a **lion** through his resurrection; and finally a **flying eagle** through his ascension. 

Regarding the Evangelists, according to the style of the discourse written by each, one is said to have the face of a man, another of a lion, another of a calf, and another of a flying eagle; and this is worthily proclaimed in both the Johannine and the prophetic visions of these animals. 

<margin>Luke as the calf.</margin>
Regarding **Luke** and **John**, everyone is of one opinion: namely, that Luke is rightly symbolized by the face of the **calf**, and John by the face of the **flying eagle**. However, regarding **Matthew** and **Mark**, there are differing opinions. For some—among whom the blessed **Jerome** is the first and most prominent—Matthew is represented by the **man** and Mark by the **lion**. For others—among whom the blessed **Augustine** is the greatest or best known—Matthew is seen in the **lion**, and Mark, by those who look closely, in the **man**. 

<margin>Luke 1, Luke 3. The genealogy of Christ according to Luke through adoptive lines.</margin>
For Luke, both at the beginning and the end of his discourse, is occupied with the temple or the priesthood. In his work, the faithful narrative relates how the "Holy of Holies" <note>The "anointed" one.</note> was anointed—that is, how he was conceived by the Holy Spirit—and likewise at the Jordan, where the Holy Spirit descended upon that same true priest in the form of a dove. This Evangelist, designating him as a priest for the expiation <term>Expiation: The act of making amends or reparation for guilt or sin; atonement.</term> of sins, does not recount his lineage by descending, but by ascending. And in ascending, he passes through Abraham and reaches God, to whom we, having been cleansed and expiated, are reconciled through the priesthood of the same Christ. Hence, he arranged both the beginning and the end of that same genealogy, which he carried out <note>original: "gessit"</note>, through adoptive fathers or sons...

While usually translated simply as "a king," the author emphasizes the literal Latin "man-king" to support his argument.</note> It does not say only "to a king," but to a "king-man."

<margin>In what way the leaders of the churches are likened to these four living creatures.</margin>

# On Revelation Chapter 4
### Page cxxxv

<margin>
Matthew, Peter.
Other saints full of eyes.
</margin>
Matthew comes from the tax collector’s booth, where Jesus saw him sitting; <note>Matthew 9:9</note> and by writing the Gospel—or the "book of the generation of Christ"—he approaches that throne to offer glory, honor, and blessing, alongside the other living creatures, to the One sitting on the throne, who lives forever and ever. He is "full of eyes behind" because, with a humble conscience, he looks back upon who or what he once was; <note>As a tax collector, Matthew would have looked back on his life of worldly gain with repentance.</note> he is "full of eyes in front" because, with simple thanksgiving, he recognizes what he has received and what he has become. In this way, the other saints are also God’s living creatures: they are full of eyes in front and behind, knowing where they came from or how they were made, and where they are going, or for what purpose they were created. They also possess this vision by practicing repentance for past evils and maintaining caution regarding future ones.

Six wings represent the perfect truth of Holy Scripture.

In the one Christ, this must first be considered in this way: that each of those things previously mentioned—namely the incarnation, the passion, the resurrection, and the ascension—each of these, I say, has "six wings." This is because the ancient divinity—the Word, the eternal and everlasting Godhead who created all things in six days—worked fully and truly in each of these events within the "new man." <note>original: "novo hoĩe [homine]" — This refers to the humanity assumed by Christ, the "Second Adam."</note> For in Him, whether He is being incarnated and born, or while He suffers, or as He rises and ascends into heaven, the true and perfect divinity dwells. Likewise, these individual events possess six wings in such a way that the perfection of the scriptures concerning them loftily escapes every thought "exalting itself against the knowledge of God." <note>2 Corinthians 10:5</note> This truth does not fear being held or ensnared by the deceptive little arguments of "vain philosophy." For it does not crawl upon the ground, but holding onto heaven through perfect truth, it looks down upon the earth. The number of six wings suggests to us the perfection of that truth through its own mathematical perfection. For this number <note>The number six</note> is the first of the "perfect numbers," because it is the first that is composed of its own parts. For it has a middle part, which is three; a second part, which is two; and a third part, which is one. <note>In medieval arithmetic, a "perfect number" is one where the sum of its divisors equals the number itself: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.</note> These three, namely...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book III
#### Page xxxvi

...two, and one complete six. <note>original: "duo, & vnum ſex perficiunt." The author is likely continuing a numerical argument from the previous page regarding the perfection of the number six in relation to the four mysteries of Christ.</note> <margin>Six wings, likewise six works of mercy. Matthew 25.</margin> Therefore, each of them has six wings; that is, the truth of salvific doctrine is perfect in each one. But also for everyone else—even those who do not hold the office of teaching or the study of Scripture—it is necessary to have six wings so that they might be able to fly away from distress and flee from the wrath to come. These wings are the **six works of mercy**, which the One sitting upon the throne enumerates to those standing at His right hand: *I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you covered me; I was sick, and you visited me; I was in prison, and you came to me.* <note>Matthew 25:35-36. These were standard categories of Christian charity in medieval theology.</note> It follows:

<margin>The active life is in the "circuit," the contemplative life is "within." Luke 10.</margin> **And around and within they are full of eyes.**
By "around," the **active life** is rightly understood; by "within," the **contemplative life**. For he who is devoted to the works of the active life "goes around" many things, as the Lord testifies when He says: *Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things.* <note>Luke 10:41. Martha was the traditional model for the "active life" of service.</note> But he who holds to the contemplative life, meditating on the law of the Lord, is "within"; he rests within, and like Mary, he sits "within" at the feet of the Lord. <note>Mary of Bethany was the model for the "contemplative life" of prayer and study.</note> Therefore, these living creatures are full of eyes both "around and within" because the preachers of the Gospel (or any leaders of the church, if they lead lawfully) are cautious and provident both in their external actions and in their internal contemplation.

**And they had no rest day and night, saying: Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come.**
From the moment the throne was placed in heaven and the Lord sat upon it—that is, from the time when the kingdom of sin was destroyed and the kingdom of justice was established through the passion of Christ, and the Lord reigned in His Church—these living creatures have no rest (meaning they have no idleness). They cry out to the "Thrice Holy" <note>original: "ter sanctum"</note> Lord, <margin>Faith in the Holy Trinity.</margin> preaching the Holy Trinity to the whole world through the doctrine of the Gospel. Those four principal mysteries <term>sacramenta: here meaning sacred mysteries or milestones</term>—namely the incarnation, the passion, the resurrection, and the ascension—principally preach the glory or the knowledge of this Holy Trinity in Christ. This did not happen before. For no one preached this name...

...revealed in public proclamation. The **first animal**, or first face, which is the **Incarnation of Christ**, proclaims this blessed Trinity in this way: <margin>In the Incarnation. # Rupert’s Commentary, Book 4
## Page 138

<margin>
The confidence 
of martyrs 
against

...[ad]versity, by preaching the faith of the holy and indivisible Trinity, which is to say three times: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty." <note>original: "Sanctus, sanctus, sanctus dominus deus omnipotens." And when the persecutors have grown weary of killing and cease to do so, he *is to come* to judge the cause of the killing, and then not a hair of the martyrs' heads shall perish.

upon the throne, who lives forever and ever. Behold, this is that same wonder by which the Psalmist, long ago astonished in spirit, said: "O Lord our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth." <note>original: "Domine dominus noster, quam admirabile est nomen tuum in vniuersa terra." Psalm 8:1.</note> And immediately revealing what he wondered at, he said: "because your magnificence is raised above the heavens." <margin>The four faces of Christ from Psalm 8.</margin> In this verse, he proclaimed the fourth face of those living creatures—namely, the Ascension of the Lord—by anticipation. For afterward, he briefly noted the four faces in order, saying: "what is man that you are mindful of him, or the son of man that you visit him?" <note>Psalm 8:4.</note>

For this is the **first face**, the **face of a man**: namely, the incarnation of the Word of God, by which he was made flesh and became the son of man. 

"You have made him a little lower than the angels." <note>Psalm 8:5.</note> This is the **second face**, the **face of the calf** <note>The calf or ox traditionally symbolizes sacrifice and the Passion of Christ.</note>: namely, the passion of the same Lord, in which he was made lower than the angels so that he might suffer and die—since the holy angels are neither mortal nor capable of suffering. Hence, when he led his struggle in agony, an angel from heaven appeared to him to strengthen him, as a greater [strengthening] a lesser—that is, the one who cannot suffer <term>impassibilis</term> strengthening the one suffering, and the immortal strengthening the one dying. <note>This refers to Christ's Agony in the Garden of Gethsemane (Luke 22:43), where Rupert interprets the angel's presence as a temporary reversal of status because Christ chose to become mortal.</note>

"You have crowned him with glory and honor." <note>Psalm 8:5.</note> This is the **third face**, the **face of the lion**: namely, the resurrection of the same Lord, in which, having despoiled hell because of his suffering of death, he was crowned as victor with the glory of immortality and the honor of incorruption. 

"And you have set him over the works of your hands." <note>Psalm 8:6.</note> This is the **fourth face**, the **face of the flying eagle**: namely, the ascension of the same Lord, by which that flesh ascended to the place from which the divinity had descended to take on flesh, and now he sits at the right hand of God. Having said these things, on account of the greatness of these matters, he repeats at the end—marvelling and exclaiming—the very thing he had said at the beginning: "O Lord our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth." How these things, above all the works of the Lord, created wonder in him who foresaw them in the spirit before they happened...

<summary>Rupert explains how Psalm 8 serves as a prophecy of the "four faces" of Christ’s life: his Incarnation (man), Passion (calf), Resurrection (lion), and Ascension (eagle). He highlights the theological mystery of Christ becoming lower than the angels during his suffering to achieve a glorious resurrection.</summary>
<keywords>Psalm 8, Four Living Creatures, Incarnation, Passion of Christ, Resurrection, Ascension, Christology, Angelology</keywords>

# 140 Commentary of Rupert, Book 3

...thus throughout all the earth, these things—above all other works of the Lord God <note>original: "domini dei"</note>—both when they happened and ever since they were done, are most to be wondered at, with the Apostles preaching them, and the four living creatures of those same faces—that is, the Evangelists—both preaching and writing them. "When," he says, "those living creatures gave glory and honor and blessing to the one sitting upon the throne, who lives forever and ever." <note>A paraphrase of Revelation 4:9.</note> And to him who sits upon the throne, we give glory with gracious words, and we give honor with dutiful deeds.

<margin>Giving glory and honor to God.</margin> We glorify him when we worthily and laudably preach his goodness; we honor him when, by living holily, we prepare our hearts and bodies as vessels of honor and clean dwellings for his Holy Spirit. But to glorify and honor God in this way is not something we have from ourselves, but from his gift, just as the Apostle says: 

<margin>2 Corinthians 4.</margin> "We have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the excellence of the power of God may be in us, and not from us." <note>2 Corinthians 4:7.</note> 

<margin>2 Corinthians 3.</margin> Likewise: "Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God." <note>2 Corinthians 3:5.</note> 

We add therefore the third, namely giving 

<margin>Giving blessing.</margin> blessing—that is, the giving of thanks—to him who has made us fit so that we might be able to glorify him by our deeds, and we say with the same Apostle in the same epistle thus: 

<margin>2 Corinthians 1.</margin> "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation." <note>2 Corinthians 1:3-4.</note> 

Thus did these living creatures, having the first fruits of glory and honor. They glorified God by preaching with the word of wisdom and knowledge and with an eloquent mouth; they honored God by doing not their own will but God’s, and by crucifying their flesh for the honor of God, along with its vices and lusts. 

<margin>Galatians 5.</margin> They blessed God by attributing everything they could say for his glory and everything they could do for his honor not to themselves but to him, who, by sending the Holy Spirit from heaven, so taught these simple and uneducated men <note>original: "idiotas." In a medieval context, this refers to those without formal rhetorical training, specifically the Apostles as "laymen."</note> that they knew how and were able to speak for his glory; and he so animated those who were previously weak that they were able not only to live for his honor, but even to die for it. These three things they gave to him sitting upon the throne, living for ever...

<summary>Rupert explains that the "glory, honor, and blessing" offered by the four living creatures represent the preaching and holy lives of the Evangelists. He emphasizes that these virtues are gifts from God rather than human achievements, citing Paul’s epistles to show that even the Apostles’ ability to suffer and die for the faith came from the Holy Spirit.</summary>

# On Revelation Chapter 4

...forever and ever <note>original: "secula seculorum"</note>, drawing from this a great refreshment for their poverty and a great restoration of holy hope. For while they are glorifying, honoring, and blessing God—even as they suffer persecution and are killed—they leave behind Him who sits upon the throne, who lives forever and ever. Because He survives and lives eternally, He is able to care for them after their deaths and to require an account for their blood. When those living creatures offered these things, he says, the twenty-four elders fell down before the one sitting on the throne and worshipped Him who lives forever and ever.

<margin>
The reason why God is most rightly worshipped.
</margin>
The primary cause of the whole matter, for which He who sits and lives is worthy of our worship, is the grace and mercy which He worked for us in Christ or through Christ. For being worshipped merely for temporal goods is not so pleasing to Him; this was how the "carnal Israel" <note>Rupert uses this term to describe those who followed the law literally but lacked spiritual insight.</note> used to worship Him. When it was said to them, "I will give you a land flowing with milk and honey," <margin>Exodus 13, Deuteronomy 6</margin> and other such sayings, they understood or attended to nothing but earthly promises. But the holy and perfect fathers, such as Moses and all those who possessed the Spirit of God, worshipped God because of this future grace of Christ. Therefore, in their worship or in the sacrificing of animals, they were prefiguring these "faces" <note>The four faces of the living creatures: man, lion, ox, and eagle.</note> of which we speak, as has been said above.

<margin>
The worship of the twenty-four elders.
</margin>
When, therefore, those living creatures gave <note>The OCR reads "carent," likely a mistake for "darent" (gave) or "canerent" (sang) based on Revelation 4:9.</note> glory, honor, and blessing, the twenty-four elders fell down and worshipped. This is because wherever those aforementioned <term>sacraments</term> <note>In this context, "sacraments" refers to the sacred mysteries of Christ's life and the symbols in the vision.</note> are celebrated in Christ and preached to the world by the messengers of the Gospel, from that moment—as it is written—in His name <margin>Philippians 2</margin> every knee is bent, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. Among all these, those who labored most for His kingdom are prominent. As mentioned before, these include the twelve <margin>Judges 3, Matthew 19</margin> <term>judges</term> <note>original: "iudices"</note> of Israel from the Old Testament before the reign of David, and in the New Testament—with Christ now reigning upon the throne of David—the twelve apostles who will judge the twelve tribes of Israel. 

<margin>
Why they cast their crowns before the throne.
</margin>
Worshipping, he says, they cast their crowns before the throne. Those who have labored in the kingdom or for the kingdom of God do so worthily in the sight of the one reigning and sitting—

<summary>Rupert explains that the twenty-four elders represent the union of the Old and New Testaments (twelve judges and twelve apostles) who worship God for His eternal grace rather than earthly rewards. Their act of casting down crowns signifies that all honor for their labors belongs to Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Book 4 of the Revelation of St. John. It specifically addresses the scene where the twenty-four elders cast their crowns before the throne of God, exploring the relationship between human merit and divine grace.</meta>

<page-num>142</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 3</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

...were crowned. But these elders, considering that they achieved their crowns not by their own merits, but by the grace of a preceding and following mercy <note>original: "gratia peruenientis & subsequentis misericordiæ"</note>—and weighing carefully that He for whom and through whom all things exist, who had brought many sons into glory, the author of their salvation, was made perfect through suffering—do they not hold their own dignity in small regard, and attribute all that they have earned to Him with humble reverence? 

Therefore, they cast their crowns before the throne—that is, whatever virtue or dignity they possess, they offer it to God with thanksgiving, saying: "You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things, and by Your will they existed and were created." Let the dignity of any of the saints or the righteous be compared; let the dignities or merits of the elders be compared to the dignity, work, or merit of this Ancient of Days <note>original: "antiqui dierum"; a title for God from the Book of Daniel 7:9</note>—what are their dignities or merits? For He created all things, and by His will they existed and were created—that is, by no one's counsel or merit, but by His will alone they existed and were created. 

<margin>The double creation of man.</margin>
He said, "You created all things," and again, "they existed and were created." He did not repeat the word "creation" redundantly, but intended two creations of the rational creature to be understood. Of these, the latter is indeed the more useful: that by which we are recreated in Christ through the Holy Spirit, of which the Psalmist says:

<margin>Psalm 104</margin>
<margin>Genesis 1</margin>
"Send forth Your Spirit and they shall be created" <note>original: "Emittes spiritū tuū & creabuntur"; Psalm 104:30</note>. The former creation, however, is that found in Genesis: "And God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them." Concerning this creation by which we are recreated through the Holy Spirit, of which the Apostle <note>Medieval authors often refer to St. Paul simply as "the Apostle."</note> also says: 

<margin>Ephesians 2</margin>
"For we are His workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them" <note>Ephesians 2:10</note>. Regarding this creation, I say, it was first said: "for You created all things"—that is, all people, or all kinds of creatures—just as we find in the Apostle:

<margin>Colossians 1</margin>
"For it pleased Him that in Him all fullness should dwell, and through Him all things be reconciled" <note>Colossians 1:19-20</note>. Furthermore, regarding the earlier creation, he added: "and by Your will they existed and were created." It was not enough to have said "they existed" unless he had added "and they were created."

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the elders casting their crowns as an act of humility, acknowledging that their salvation comes through grace rather than merit. He explains the "double creation" of humanity: our original physical creation in Genesis and our spiritual re-creation through Christ.</summary>

namely, the door opened in heaven, the voice heard like the voice of a speaking trumpet, the rainbow around the throne, and the elders sitting upon twenty-four seats, the burning lamps before the throne—which are themselves seven in number—and in the sight of the throne something like a sea of glass, and in the midst of the throne and around it, four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. "And I saw," he said, "in the right hand of the one sitting upon the throne, a book." This one book is Holy Scripture: scripture, I say, all divinely inspired; which is called and is one book for this reason: because it was written by one Spirit, and it is the treasury or sanctuary of the one Word of God. This book, in Isaiah, is also unreadable <note>original: "irreferabilis"; meaning it cannot be unrolled or explained.</note> to both the one who knows letters and the one who does not. For the entire sequence of both the Old and New Testaments warns that penance must be done for sins, the heavenly kingdom must be sought, and infernal weeping must be avoided as a warning. <meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 5. On the previous page, the author identified the "sealed book" held by God as the entirety of Holy Scripture. <margin>A book is better than riches</margin>
He possesses powers on the right and on the left: in the right hand this book, the fiery law <note>original: "legem igneam"; a reference to Deuteronomy 33:2, where the law is described as coming from God's right hand in fire. Medieval theologians saw this as the light and heat of the Holy Spirit.</note>; in the left, riches and glory. Just as the right hand is better than the left, so much more blessed a good is this book—the fiery law—than riches and glory. For what are riches in this context, and what is glory, if not earthly riches and worldly glory? Therefore, riches and glory are rightly placed in his left hand, because any such good (temporal wealth and status) is of the kind that is not given to the chosen ones <note>original: "electis"; the "elect" or those predestined for salvation.</note> alone; indeed, it is more often lacking for them, and given more slowly to the chosen than to the wicked. But the fiery law, that is, this book, is the good and the consolation of the chosen alone. And this is the part that remains forever, as the Lord testifies in the Gospel when he says:
<margin>Luke 10</margin>
"Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her." And indeed, some (such as David and Solomon) received much from both sides: from the right hand, the book; from the left, riches and glory. For along with their knowledge of the law, they also possessed the wealth and the glory of a temporal kingdom. Both of these were gifts from the One sitting on the throne. But it is beneficial for every soul to whom these are given to hold what is given from the right hand with delight, but to keep what is held in the left hand beneath them, managing it with generous distribution, saying: "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me."
<margin>Song of Solomon 2</margin>
This is to say: Temporal goods are under my control and disposal; but that part which remains when those things pass away—the best part, which is the Word of God—to read or hear the law and to commit its understanding to memory: this is my greatest delight. The text says, "written within and without, sealed with seven seals." The book is written within and without because, without a doubt, Holy Scripture must be read for its historical or literal content <note>original: "historiali siue literali tenore"; the "outer" meaning of the text as a sequence of events.</note> and understood for its spiritual sense <note>original: "spirituali sensu"; the "inner" meaning or hidden theological truth.</note>.
<margin>The seven seals are the seven mysteries of Christ.</margin>
It is also sealed with seven seals in such a way that it contains within itself the entire fullness of the mysteries of Christ. Unless He had come and fulfilled these, no one would understand them; any person wishing to loosen these most firm seals would labor in vain, because whatever they struggled to say by way of explanation would not be consistent. Finally, those to whom Christ did not come <note>This likely refers to those who lived before the Incarnation or those who reject Christ, for whom the "seals" of the Old Testament remain closed.</note>...

<margin>2 Corinthians 3</margin>
...or those who have not received Christ, even until now they handle the book as something closed and sealed; indeed, they do not even see that it is sealed, because a veil is placed over their heart <note>original: "velamen positum est supra cor eorum"; a reference to St. Paul’s description of those who read the Old Testament without recognizing Christ.</note>. And whatever things they eagerly desire to speak as if they were explaining them, these words are not transformative. Moreover, it is well said that it is "sealed with seven seals," because there are clearly seven mysteries of Christ around which the holy Scripture of the Law and the Prophets revolves: namely, the **Incarnation**, the **Passion**, the **Resurrection**, the **Ascension**, the **giving of the Holy Spirit the Comforter** <note>original: "spiritus sancti paracleti"; from the Greek 'parakletos', meaning one called to one's side, an advocate or helper.</note>, the **calling of the nations**, and the **second coming of Christ for judgment**. We shall speak of each of these in their proper places, by His gift. Indeed, holy Scripture is sealed with these mysteries in such a way that whoever does not receive them is in no way strong enough to understand its truth.

# And I heard a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice: "Who is worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof?"

<margin>The expectation of the ancients regarding the coming of Christ. Hebrews 11.</margin>
This "strong angel," proclaiming thus with a loud voice, signifies the breathless expectation and the great desire of the ancient saints. Regarding them, the Lord says in the Gospel: "Many prophets and righteous men have desired to see the things that you see, and have not seen them." And the Apostle, in the Letter to the Hebrews, having enumerated the fathers, says: "All these died according to faith, not having received the promises, but beholding them and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers upon the earth." And further on: "And all these," he says, "found to be approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, God providing something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us." Surely that expectation—that greeting and confession from afar—was the great cry of a great desire, such as was fitting to be signified here in this vision by the "loud voice of the strong angel" powerfully proclaiming.

<margin>On the Incarnation. Isaiah 7 and 9.</margin>
For example: those of whom he [the Apostle] last spoke, who were all "approved by the testimony of faith" yet did not receive the promises. They used to read what was written in one of their books regarding the Incarnation of the Son of God: *Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel.* And thereafter: *A child is born to us, a son is given...*

<summary>Rupert explains that the "seven seals" of the biblical book represent the seven core mysteries of Christ's life and mission. He interprets the "strong angel" of Revelation 5 as a symbol for the intense longing of Old Testament prophets who foresaw Christ from a distance but died before his arrival.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Revelation chapter 5, focusing on the inability of any created being to fulfill the prophecies of the Old Testament (the "sealed book") until the arrival of Christ. <page-num>158</page-num>
<header>158 Commentary of Rupert, Book 4</header>

...the fullness of the [Scri]ptures revolves around these seven mysteries. And those desiring and sighing to see their fulfillment said: *Who is worthy to open the book and loosen its seals?* They looked about in their minds at all the seed of Israel; they saw those daily being born and dying, they considered the living and remembered the dead, and absolutely no one was so great or appeared to be such that he could loosen these seven seals—that is, no one in whom or through whom these many and great mysteries might be fulfilled. This is what follows:

> **And no one in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth, was able to open the book, nor to look upon it.**

<margin>What it means to "open the book."</margin>
There were angels in heaven; there were some righteous men living on earth; and there were those "under the earth"—namely, among those in the underworld <note>original: "apud inferos"; here Rupert refers to the "Limbo of the Fathers," a place where medieval theologians believed the righteous of the Old Testament waited for Christ.</note>, yet in a certain state of rest—patriarchs and prophets, as well as many dead kings and righteous people. Yet none of them could or had been able to "open the book"—that is, to fulfill the aforementioned mysteries of the Scriptures—nor even "to look upon it"—that is, not even to hope for themselves that they could carry out such a great and divine task as the business of the salvation of the world. There follows:

> **And I wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the book, nor to see it.**

It was not enough for the blessed John to have heard the loud voice of the strong angel powerfully proclaiming, "Who is worthy to open the book and loosen its seals?"—by which voice or proclamation the great longing of the ancient saints was signified—unless the "anointing" <margin>1 John 2</margin> (of which John himself speaks elsewhere: *and his anointing teaches you about all things* <note>original: "unctio eius docet vos de omnibus"; a reference to 1 John 2:27.</note>) also anointed his mind. This was so that in that very state of ecstasy, he might weep because of the sweetness of the things he had seen, and through his weeping, he might experience how sorrowful the longing of those saints had been.

"I wept therefore," he says, "much." **And one of the elders said to me: "Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so as to open the book, and to loo[sen]...**"

<summary>Rupert explains that no figure from the Old Testament, whether living, dead, or angelic, was capable of fulfilling the divine plan of salvation represented by the sealed book. He highlights John’s weeping as a reflection of the collective longing of all ancient saints for the coming of Christ, the "Lion of Judah."</summary>

# On the Fifth Chapter of the Apocalypse

<note>original: "In Apocalypseos Cap.v"</note>

K iij <note>A printer's "signature" used to keep the pages in the correct order.</note>

...truly open its seven seals.

This speech from one of the elders not only consoles the weeping man <note>referring to the Apostle John, who was weeping because no one was found worthy</note> but also makes the witness observant and teachable, so that he might better understand the things and images he sees. John is forewarned and brought to remember past events in this very state of spiritual ecstasy by these words: *Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has triumphed.* The Elder calls him a "Lion," even though John was just about to see him as a "Lamb." For it follows: *And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a lamb standing as if it had been slain.* Why is this? Clearly, it is because he who was a lamb in his passion through his gentleness and patience—and like a lamb silent before its shearer, he did not open his mouth—that same person, once his passion was completed, soon ascended to take his prey like a lion's cub. 
<margin>Isaiah 53</margin>
He despoiled the underworld <note>original: "infernum"; here referring to Christ's "Harrowing of Hell" where he was believed to have rescued the souls of the righteous</note> and, resting in the tomb and lying down like a lion or a lioness, he crushed the very death of the body—both in himself and in us—on the third day with a great roar and a great earthquake. But that lion will roar much louder then, when he comes to judge, with a mighty storm thundering around him, making all the dead wake up as if they were merely sleeping. Therefore it says: *Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah.* This means he is a man who, according to the 
<margin>Genesis 49</margin>
prophetic truth which the patriarch Jacob foretold, was born of the tribe of Judah. By his own strength, he conquered the prince of the opposing strength <note>referring to the devil</note>. He is so great and of such a kind that he was and is worthy to open the book and to loosen its seven seals. 

But why did the Elder say "from the tribe of Judah, the root of David," when he could have said "from the tribe of Judah, from the lineage of David"? For Christ is from the seed of David just as he is from the tribe of Judah. Why, then, did he not say "of the lineage" or "of the seed of David" in the same way he mentioned the tribe of Judah? Clearly, it is because such a phrasing would not have touched upon the reality or the cause of *how* he is a lion, or *how* he was able to conquer. For while Christ is from the tribe of Judah and the seed of David, it is not from that human source that he is God, 
<margin>Christ is the root of David according to his divinity</margin>
nor is it from there that he conquered death or was able to rise again. Rather, it is from that human source that he is a man, and from there that he was able to die or be slain like a lamb.

<summary>This page explains why Christ is described as both a "Lion" (representing his power and resurrection) and a "Lamb" (representing his sacrifice). It explores the theological distinction between Christ's humanity as a descendant of David and his divinity as the "Root" from which David himself comes.</summary>

<keywords>Lion of Judah, Lamb of God, Root of David, Resurrection, Harrowing of Hell, Jacob’s Prophecy, Passion of Christ, Divinity vs Humanity</keywords>

### Commentary of Rupert, Book III

<margin>
The vineyard from the vine, which is Christ.
Isaiah 5
Jeremiah 2
Hosea 5
</margin>
...could be. Therefore, it was said more magnificently, as it ought to have been said: *the root of David*. Indeed, it is magnificent and wonderful that he is the root of the very stock from which he descended. For if you look at the flesh of Christ <note>referring to his human nature</note>, he is not the root of David in that way, since the vine does not carry the root, but the root carries the vine. Therefore, he is called the "root of David" according to his divinity, because just as a root supports the vine or the branch, so Christ, according to his divinity, supports David, the father of his fleshly lineage. Why else was David and that entire nation in the prophetic scriptures accustomed to being called "the vineyard of the Lord," if not because through faith they clung to the Christ who was to come, who says, *I am the vine*? Finally, just as the apostles are the branches, so David is a branch of this vine; nor can anyone from the old or new times belong to the Lord's vineyard, unless they cling or have clung to this vine through faith.

It follows:

<margin>
Christ is both a lamb and a lion.
Genesis 49
Exodus 12
</margin>
> And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures and of the elders, a lamb standing as if it had been slain, having seven horns and seven eyes.

Christ is one and the same person: he is a lamb by dying innocently, and he was also made a lion by bravely overcoming death. Both images are founded upon the authority of the ancient scriptures. For the same one whom the patriarch Jacob foretold as a lion or a lion's cub <note>original: "catulum leonis"</note>, Moses represented through a lamb in Egypt. How does this lamb stand in the midst of the throne and the four living creatures and the elders, except because, as is said elsewhere, he is *King of kings and Lord of lords*? Indeed, the author expresses the power and wisdom by which he dominates and commands by saying: *having seven horns and seven eyes.* For the sevenfold Spirit <note>the "septiformis spiritus" refers to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord</note> resting in Christ or upon Christ—which was compared above to seven lamps—is here compared to seven horns because of his preeminence in power and strength, and to seven eyes because of the illumination of grace or wisdom.

<margin>
Job 12
</margin>
Hence Job speaks: *With him is strength and wisdom.* Likewise: *With him is wisdom and strength.* Therefore, *I saw a lamb standing in the midst of the throne, and of the four living creatures, and of the elders*—that is, Christ, the Holy of Holies, reigning and...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz explains Christ's dual nature: as God, he is the "Root" supporting David, and as the "Lamb," he possesses the sevenfold Spirit representing perfect power (horns) and wisdom (eyes).</summary>

### On the Apocalypse, Chapter 5

...ruling in the midst of all the saints, with seven horns and seven eyes—that is, the seven spirits—of which he possesses the full fullness in himself, strengthening and illuminating all those who, through faith, are gathered around him. It is also added, "as if slain." What does "as if slain" mean, if not that he was once killed, but is now alive? For he, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him <margin>Romans 6</margin>. Nevertheless, the marks of his death—the places of the nails in his hands and feet, and the place of the spear in his side, which he showed and offered to be touched by his disciples after his resurrection—are preserved in everlasting memory. These marks are for himself a matter of glory, for us a source of grace, and for his enemies a cruel conscience <note>meaning a source of guilt or conviction</note>, so that they may see and be put to shame, according to that prophetic word: *They shall look upon him whom they have pierced.*
<margin>
Zechariah 12
Deuteronomy 33
Proverbs 3
</margin>

> And he came and took the book out of the right hand of him who sat upon the throne.

Since (as has already been said above) the fiery law <note>original: "ignea lex," a reference to Deuteronomy 33:2</note> is in the right hand of the one sitting on the throne, which is this book, while in his left hand are riches and glory, it is very important to note this: when Christ came into this world through the mystery of the incarnation <term>incarnation: the Christian belief that God took on human flesh in Jesus</term>, he took nothing of riches or glory from the left hand, but only the book, or the fiery law, from the right hand.
<margin>Christ was a despiser of riches as an example for us.</margin>
Providing a good example to all his disciples and those who believe in him, he wanted and sought nothing of riches or glory in this world—this poor and needy man. Indeed, when these things were offered to him (as we read in the Gospel <margin>John 6</margin>), because those whom he had satisfied with five loaves and two fish were about to come and seize him to make him king over them, knowing this, he fled. He deigned only to meditate on the law of the Lord day and night; he deigned only to receive the book from the right hand, intending to open it and loose its seven seals. Indeed, those who follow his example to the best of their ability and receive this book are followed by the labors and adversities of the world. But regarding this, it is also written: *He shall be filled with reproaches* <margin>Lamentations 3</margin>, which means that to endure reproaches for the sake of justice will be sweet to him.

> And when he had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell down before...

# On Revelation Chapter 5

...who adore the Father may also adore the Son; they adore God and the man Jesus Christ. Each holds a harp—instruments, namely, of unceasing praise. These are not man-made instruments, but faithful hearts and bodies sounding praise with the pick <note>The original term is *plectro*, the tool used to pluck a stringed instrument.</note> of God's tongue. For harps, where strings are stretched upon wood, are rightly compared to bodies mortified <note>Put to death or disciplined.</note> for Christ’s sake. They also have bowls <note>The text uses *phialas*, often translated as vials or shallow bowls used in offerings.</note>—vessels, namely, with wide-open mouths—that is, hearts that are not narrow, but expanded through charity.

<margin>Bowls full of incense</margin>
Such bowls are full of incense, which, he says, are the prayers of the saints. Truly, the very width of the bowls' mouths is created by the ample charity of their hearts, so that the prayers of the saints might be honored with the name of incense.

<margin>Psalm 140</margin>
From this comes that saying in the Psalm: *Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.* <note>original: "Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo." Hebrews 9
</margin>

# Rupert’s Commentary, Book 4

"Are you worthy to take and open the book?" <note>original: *dignus es accipere & aperire librum?*</note> For He suffered and died once, and in this way He opened the book once—that is, He fulfilled the scriptures. Therefore, when they say to Him who had already opened it (that is, had already fulfilled it), "You are worthy to take it," it is the same as if they were saying: "You are worthy and powerful to open the meaning to those who read, and to grant an understanding of the scriptures." For He, through His own dignity, achieved both the former and the latter. By dying, He fulfilled the scriptures; by rising, He gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles, which opened their senses to understand the scriptures. He loosened the seals of the book—that is, He showed that the mysteries of the scriptures had been loosened and made intelligible.

Whence comes this dignity of yours, O Lord? "Because you were slain," they say, "and have redeemed us to God in your blood." If you had not been slain, the book could by no means have been opened. For this reason, when Peter was drawing his sword <note>The Latin *evaginanti gladium* refers to Peter unsheathing his sword in the Garden of Gethsemane.</note> because he preferred to kill men rather than have you, the true Lamb of God, be killed by men, you said:

<margin>Matt. 26</margin>
"Return your sword to its place. Can I not ask my Father, and He will provide me now with more than twelve legions of angels? How then shall the scriptures be fulfilled? For it must happen this way." <note>original: *conuerte gladium tuum in locum suum. Num possum rogare patrem meum... Quomodo ergo implebuntur scripturae?*</note>

Since, therefore, you were slain, in that very act you opened the book and fulfilled the truth of the scriptures. "You were slain and have redeemed us to God in your blood." It should be noted that such a song is not found in the two testimonies that follow—those of the multitude of angels and of every creature. This is because the angels (who did not perish) and the other rational creatures are not the ones spoken of here; rather, it is only the Church of men, understood here through the **twenty-four elders** and the **four living creatures**, which has been <term>redeemed</term> <note>Redemption (from *redemptio*) literally means "buying back," referring here to the price of Christ's blood.</note> in the blood of Christ.

For this reason, these [the elders and creatures] say: "Because you were slain and have redeemed us." The angels, however, say only this: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain," and they do not add, "and you have redeemed us." Furthermore, all other creatures which are in heaven, on the earth, under the earth, and in the sea, say none of these things. Instead, they only bless, in their own way, the One sitting upon the throne by whom they were made, and the Lamb through whom they were made. Therefore, it is humans alone who are the first, before the angels and before every creature, in this [song]...

<summary>Rupert explains that Christ’s death "opened" the scriptures by fulfilling prophecy and that only humanity can sing of "redemption" since angels never fell from grace. He emphasizes that spiritual understanding is a gift from the risen Christ through the Holy Spirit.</summary>

### On Revelation, Chapter 5

...they bear witness, saying: "Because you were slain and have redeemed us." To whom have you redeemed us? "To God," they say. From where have you redeemed us? "From every tribe, and tongue, and people, and nation." Truly, you have gathered us from a great dispersion; you have united us from a great discord. For this is why people differ so much from one another: because they belong to many clashing tribes, diverse languages, dissimilar peoples, and different nations. Furthermore, they disagree so much because, captured by the devil, they are held entangled in the various snares of error. But you redeemed us for God to make us children of God: so that, as it is written in the Gospel, you might gather into one the children of God who were scattered.

<margin>John 11.
Exodus 12.
The symbolic lamb.</margin>
The lamb that was slain in Egypt as a figure <note>In medieval theology, a "figure" or "type" is an Old Testament event that foreshadows a New Testament truth.</note> of you redeemed that people in its blood from only one nation. Specifically, its blood was taken from the threshold and placed on the lintel and both doorposts of the houses where it was eaten, preventing the striker <note>The "striker" refers to the Angel of Death in the Exodus narrative.</note> from entering and striking. And when the firstborn of the Egyptians were killed, those who were previously held by them were not only released but even compelled to leave. And with the Red Sea divided, they indeed passed through safely, while the Egyptians pursuing them with their chariots and horses perished in the midst of the waves.

<margin>Redemption through the true lamb.</margin>
In such a way did that lamb then redeem that people; or rather, you, O Lord and Ruler, O Lamb, redeemed them through the sacrifice of that lamb in a symbolic redemption. But now, you yourself have redeemed us to God in your own blood, so that your blood, poured out for us, taken from the sacrament of your baptism, is impressed upon our foreheads with the sign of the cross. Likewise, taken from the sacred altar, it is placed upon both doorposts of our houses <note>Rupert is metaphorically comparing the doorposts of the Hebrew homes to the "mouths" of the human heart and body which receive the Eucharist.</note> when it is received by the mouth of both heart and body.

Once this is done, the striker—the devil—is not permitted to enter; instead, the firstborn—that is, original sin <note>Rupert draws a parallel between the death of the Egyptian firstborn and the destruction of original sin in the believer.</note>—is destroyed within us, and all the actual sins that were against us and pursued us are swallowed up in the waters of baptism.

<margin>Kingdom and priests.</margin>
Thus you have redeemed us, freeing us from evil spirits and gathering us from the nations, and you have made us a kingdom and priests for our God—

<summary>Rupert explains how Christ's sacrifice fulfills and surpasses the symbolic sacrifice of the Passover lamb in Egypt, moving from a single nation's liberation to a universal redemption through baptism and the Eucharist.</summary>

### In Chapter 5 of Revelation

[earth] <note>original: "ram"; completing "terram" from the previous page</note>, upon the earth of the living, from which those apostate spirits <note>The fallen angels who followed Lucifer.</note> were cast out because of their pride. It should be noted that they transitioned from the first person to the third person when, having first said, **"and you have made us a kingdom and priests to our God,"** they then add, **"and they shall reign upon the earth."** This is a very devout transition, avoiding even the vocal sound of anything resembling vain glory. For although they could have truly said, "and we shall reign upon the earth," it pleased them to speak more humbly: **"and they shall reign upon the earth."** Therefore, let **"you have made us a kingdom for our God"** be the praise of all confessing together, while **"and they shall reign upon the earth"** is spoken by individuals bowing themselves in humble reverence. 

Nor should it be overlooked that it does not say, "and they shall reign *in* the earth," but **"they shall reign *over* the earth."** <note>The author distinguishes between living "in" the physical world and having spiritual authority "over" earthly desires.</note> For the saints are indeed on the earth by their physical condition, because their spirits are in earthly bodies, but in their life and conduct they are *above* the earth, and they hold dominion over their earthly and corruptible members. Even now, as long as their bodies are mortal, they rule them with labor and care; but in the future, they shall reign over them in peace and security.

Therefore, because the angels were both created in Him and reconciled to humans through His blood, and because their number is replenished from humanity through Him, they are rightly present around the throne and the living creatures and the elders to testify. Their testimony is heard with a loud voice—that is, with great affection—saying: **"Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, etc."** <note>Revelation 5:12.</note> Because they are angels who did not perish, they do not say, "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain and has redeemed *us*," in the way the humans said a little before: **"Since you were slain and have redeemed us to God in [your] blood."**

<summary>Rupert explains that the "thousands of thousands" of angels praise the Lamb because Christ is their Creator and the one who restores their ranks by redeeming humans to fill the void left by the fallen angels. He notes a subtle distinction in the text: angels praise the Lamb's worthiness but do not claim to be redeemed by His blood as humans do.</summary>

Let him also receive **blessing**, as he is worthy; let all his saints bless him, attributing what they are not to themselves but to him, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
