### Commentary of Rupert, Book 4
l.

...and glory, and power forever and ever. <note>Revelation 5:13</note>
Those creatures to whom the passion of Christ brought the benefit of peace and glory—namely, both the host of angels and of men—have placed the title of that same death of Christ in their testimony. The former, namely men, say to the Lamb: "You are worthy, Lord, for you were slain and have redeemed us." <note>original: "dignus es domine quoniam occisus es, & redemisti nos"; Revelation 5:9. Rupert notes that humans include the personal "redeemed us."</note> The latter, namely the angels, who were not redeemed because they had not perished <note>Rupert follows the common medieval theology that since angels did not "fall" in the same way humanity did, they do not require "redemption," though they are restored to full number by the addition of the elect.</note>, say only this: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain." <note>Revelation 5:12</note>

<margin>Psalm 148</margin>
Furthermore, the other creatures—those in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and those in the sea: the sun, moon, and stars, the waters above the heavens, and all others whom the Psalmist stirs to praise the Lord—provide the third testimony in this place. This is so that the word concerning the **dignity of the Lamb** may stand. 
<margin>How other creatures praise God and the Lamb.</margin>
These creatures make no mention of their own redemption (as the living creatures and the twenty-four elders do), nor do they even mention the slaying of the Lamb (as all the angels do); instead, they say only: "To the one sitting on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing," etc. <note>Revelation 5:13. Rupert distinguishes between rational beings (men/angels) who understand Christ's death and the non-rational creation which simply reflects the Creator's glory.</note> For the Lamb was not slain for the redemption of such creatures, nor for any restoration of them. Simply because they were created, they sing together to the Creator—not indeed by a rational or vocal confession, but by the natural presentation of their state. 

And because the redemption of men and the restoration of the angelic orders was accomplished through the slaying of the Lamb alone—for only the person of the Son suffered—whereas the nature or substance of all creatures was established by the Father speaking through the Word (that is, through the same Son), it is right that both men and angels proclaim the slaying of the Lamb in that aforementioned confession. These [non-rational] creatures, however, praise both the one sitting on the throne (the Father) and the Lamb (the Son of the Father). The first thing in their praise is **blessing**. Why is this? Namely, because among these there are certain creatures that exist not only by his command in nature, but also subsist by his blessing in the posterity of their succession—specifically every living and moving creature which the waters brought forth after their kind, and every winged bird according to its kind. 
<margin>Genesis 1</margin>
For it is written: "And God saw that it was good..."

"Amen" is interpreted as "truly" or "faithfully." Therefore, to say Amen is to confirm a true testimony. Here the four living creatures <note>The "four animals" or "living creatures" are traditionally interpreted by theologians like Rupert as the four Evangelists: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John</note> speak and act; that is, the four Gospels confirm that every creature asserts or testifies—each in its own way—that blessing, and honor, and glory, and power belong to the Lamb just as much as to the one sitting on the throne, and to the Son, Jesus Christ, just as much as to God the Father. The end or the fulfillment of all testimonies is adoration persevering into eternity. The twenty-four elders—that is, all the churches or the prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note> and judges of the churches—lead this adoration worthily, just as they previously performed the duty of bearing witness.

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 4

(As has already been stated above) the four living creatures represent the four greatest <term>mysteries<note>original: "sacramenta." In this medieval context, the word refers more broadly to "sacred mysteries" or pivotal events in the life of Christ rather than the ritual sacraments of the Church.</note></term> of Christ, which no Christian should be permitted to be ignorant of: namely, the incarnation, the passion, the resurrection, and the ascension. Secondarily, however, they represent those who wrote the four Gospels. Thus, one—or the first—of the four living creatures is the incarnation of Christ. We hear the voices of this incarnation as often as that same incarnation is preached to us in the church. Moreover, a voice is heard like the sound of thunder because, clearly, the fullness of the virginal birth loves to be preached openly to the whole world, rather than as a shameful vanity whispering in corners. 
<margin><unclear>Christ</unclear></margin>
Thus, it is rightly compared to the thundering heavens, according to that word of David: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>Psalm 19:1. Rupert uses the Davidic authorship of the Psalms to validate the heavenly nature of the Gospel preaching.</note>
<gloss>[This refers to] Christ, who is described by his purity and whiteness.</gloss>
**And I saw, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering that he might conquer.**

<margin>
This horse 
and its 
rider are 
Christ, God 
and man.
</margin>
*And I saw*, which is to say, I understood. And indeed, everyone who "comes"—that is, whoever faithfully believes—understands the mystery of Christ’s incarnation to be like a horse. One understands the one sitting upon it to be not only man, nor only God, but simultaneously man and God dwelling in man; man joined to God, or God to man, in a unity of person. For just as we call a horse and the man sitting upon it a single "horseman," so we confess this man and the dwelling God to be one Christ. Yet, God is much more closely joined to this man than a man is to the horse he sits upon; for a man may dismount from a horse, but the God who assumed him never departs from that man. Only once did the dead flesh lie in the tomb, but the divinity never departed from the soul. The flesh rose again when the soul was taken back up with the power of the divinity, and thereafter both flesh and soul remain with the Word as one indivisible Christ. Therefore, we understand the white horse and the one sitting upon it as the one Christ. We also understand this horse to be that beast of burden mentioned in the parable of the man who fell among thieves. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:30-37), where the Samaritan's animal was traditionally interpreted by medieval theologians as Christ’s humanity bearing our sins.</note>

**And another horse went out, a red one; and to him who sat upon it, it was given that he should take peace from the earth.** 

The red horse of the city of the devil—the city of Babylon—is a bloodthirsty people, and its rider and driver is the devil. We read indeed in Zechariah of the Lord’s "rosy horse" <note>original: "equum domini roseum"; see Zechariah 1:8</note>. But that horse is no other than the one seen above as a white horse. For that one is white by its own purity, and rosy by its own blood; which is why it is said in the Song of Songs: "My beloved is white and ruddy" <note>Song of Solomon 5:10; original: "Dilectus meus candidus & rubicundus"</note>. This horse, however, is red <term>rufus|red/rust-colored</term> with the blood of others—the blood of the saints which it has shed. This horse "went out" during the aforementioned Passion of the Lord, having long ago shed all righteous blood, from the blood of Abel the just to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah <note>Matthew 23:35</note>; and then it went out to fill up the measure of its murders, joining together the Gentiles and Pontius Pilate to kill the Lord. For the devil was sitting upon it. And "it was given to him to take peace from the earth," so that he might take peace away from the earthly generation subject to him, causing them to kill one another. This was "given" to him—that is, permitted—as he persuaded the Jews (whose rider he was and whom he was driving) to demand that the seditious Barabbas be released to them, while asking that Jesus be crucified. By doing this, he took peace from the earth—that is, he consumed it. For from that time on, there was never peace for that nation; by a just judgment, those who had destroyed the Prince of Peace inherited the seditions of Barabbas, whom they had asked to be released. And therefore, "to take peace from the earth" was given to him.

<margin>

<note>Matthew 27</note>
</margin>

Do we not understand this red horse to be the custom of those who persecute the church of God? From it [the north] were the <unclear>seven</unclear> emperors of the Gentiles until Constantine the Great, who was baptized by the blessed Sylvester. <note>This refers to the medieval tradition that Pope Sylvester I baptized Constantine, ending the era of Roman persecution.</note>

<summary>Rupert explains the second seal's red horse as the devil-driven "city of Babylon," contrasting Christ's "rosy" horse (colored by his own sacrifice) with the devil's "red" horse (colored by the blood of martyrs). He links the loss of peace to the Jewish rejection of Christ in favor of the rebel Barabbas.</summary>

### That they should kill one another.

How true this is, anyone sees and marvels at more fully who reads of that destruction of Jerusalem, as wonderful as it was wretched, carried out under Titus and Vespasian <note>Rupert refers to the Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD, a pivotal event for medieval interpreters of the Apocalypse</note>. We will need to remember this destruction again when we come to the explanation of the sixth seal.

### And there was given to him a great sword.

<margin>A great sword signifies a long persecution.</margin>
<margin><unclear>here also is the sum [of what] had been done by the ancestors</unclear></margin>
By the "great sword," a great and long-lasting persecution is understood. This sword of persecution is permitted to be wielded by that malignant rider <note>the rider of the red horse, often identified as the Devil or a personification of war</note> from the time of Christ down to his final chosen ones—drawing it, as it were, from the head of the Great Body <note>Christ</note> down to its very feet. However, more must be said about this in its proper place, where Babylon the harlot is shown to be drunk with the blood of the saints.

### And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third living creature saying: "Come and see."

<margin>The third seal is the resurrection of Christ.</margin>
<margin>John 20</margin>
On the day that Christ Jesus rose from the dead and, standing in the midst of his disciples, said to them, "Peace be with you; receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven" <note>John 20:21–23</note>—it was then that the Lamb opened the third seal of the book. He did this because he fulfilled the great proclamations of the Scriptures that were written concerning him. 
<margin>Genesis 49</margin>
For example: "Judah is a lion’s whelp: from the prey, my son, you are gone up; resting, you couched as a lion, and as a lioness; who shall rouse him up?" <note>Genesis 49:9; original: "Catulus leonis Iuda ad praedam fili mi ascendisti..."</note>
<margin>Hosea 13</margin>
<margin>Psalm 67</margin>
<margin>Psalm 138</margin>
<margin>18</margin>
And that passage in Hosea: "O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite" <note>Hosea 13:14; original: "Ero mors tua o mors, morsus tuus ero inferne"</note>. And in the Psalm: "Make a way for him who ascends over the sunset; the Lord is his name" <note>Psalm 68:4 in modern numbering; original: "Iter facite ei qui ascendit super occasum"</note>. Likewise: "I arose, and am still with you" <note>Psalm 139:18; original: "Exurrexi & adhuc sum tecum"</note>.
<margin><unclear>that [which] our people more [rightly?] call us with joy [?] sar</unclear></margin>
When Christ, by rising from the dead, fulfilled these and similar passages and made them intelligible, then (as has been said) the Lamb opened the third seal. Furthermore, the "third living creature"—or the third face of the one living creature—is the Resurrection itself. We hear its voice saying "Come and see" as often as the glory of that same Resurrection is preached to us through the mouth of the rejoicing Church.

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 4

<margin>
Death is here used to mean pestilence.
</margin>
...the name was changed, specifically to pestilence: for which specific name the general name, which is "death," was substituted. And rightly so, because clearly human fury will never reach the point of having power over pestilence—that is, the power to *create* a plague—as the Lord God does, in whose person the prophet says: 

<margin>
Isaiah 45 <note>Reference to Isaiah 45:7: "I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the Lord do all these things."</note>
</margin>
"I am the Lord making peace, and creating evil," meaning affliction: of which these four parts are those four worst judgments: the sword, famine, pestilence, and evil beasts. But [human fury] does not even have the power to create famine, except that by taking away bread it can kill someone through hunger. When it does this, it is nevertheless true what the scripture says: 

<margin>
Proverbs 10 <note>Reference to Proverbs 10:3: "The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish."</note>
</margin>
"The Lord will not kill the soul of the righteous with famine." For it is one thing when a persecutor, having imprisoned a righteous man, withdraws bread—which has often happened; it is another thing for a righteous man serving well (for example, preaching the gospel well) to lack bread, and for famine to kill him because God nowhere stretches out a hand to refresh him: something which no scripture records as ever having happened. Likewise, heretical fury cannot create evil beasts; it can only throw people to the beasts, and thus kill the body of a faithful soul. It can forge a material sword or whatever iron instrument of death, and kill with it: but it cannot create the matter itself. Of those four, pestilence alone is that which God alone can both create and kill by; and therefore rightly, instead of "pestilence," the general name—namely "death"—was placed here, containing or signifying many modes of death, whatever can be or be thought of, besides the deaths of the sword, of famine, and of evil beasts.

# Rupert’s Commentary, Book 4
### Page 184

<margin>Genesis 3: The robe is the worship or the word of God.</margin>
Robes were given to those who had been killed, or rather to the souls of the slain, because they were in need; for they had indeed been naked, suffering from that nakedness which our first parents <note>Adam and Eve</note> left to all their descendants. Concerning them it is written: *And when they knew they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.* <note>original: "Cumq; cognouissent se esse nudos, consuerunt folia ficus, & fecerunt sibi perizomata." quoting Genesis 3:7.</note> But was not the word of God and the testimony which they held—the very reason they were killed—already a robe or a covering for them? <margin>Exodus 32</margin> If the word, the name, or the worship of God were not a garment or a robe for the soul, the Scripture would by no means say: *When Moses saw the people, that they were naked (for Aaron had stripped them to their shame and set them naked among their enemies).* <note>Quoting Exodus 32:25. Rupert interprets "nakedness" here not as a lack of physical clothes, but as the loss of divine protection and worship.</note> Since, therefore, the worship of God and the word of God is the robe of the soul, and these souls had suffered for the word of God and for the testimony which they held, why is it said that "each was given a white robe," as if they were still naked? 

It should be noted, however, that it does not say merely "robes were given to them," but "**white** robes." For they did indeed have robes—that is, the righteousness of the word of God or the testimony for which they had been killed—but those robes were not yet white. Unless they were washed in the blood of Christ, they could not be bright. <note>Rupert is arguing that even the righteous martyrs of the Old Testament remained "stained" until purified by Christ's sacrifice.</note> One of them, Isaiah, bears witness to this; he undoubtedly held the word and testimony of God, for which he was also killed—for the Jews assert <margin>Isaiah 64</margin> that he was sawn in two by Manasseh. <note>A common medieval and ancient tradition that King Manasseh executed the prophet Isaiah by sawing him in half.</note> He says: *We have all become like something unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a menstrual rag.* <note>original: "pannus menstruatæ." A vivid biblical metaphor for ritual impurity and the inadequacy of human works.</note> And David says: <margin>Psalm 50</margin> *Sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.* <note>Psalm 51:7 in modern bibles.</note> And Zechariah: <margin>Zechariah 13</margin> *On that day there shall be a fountain open to the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the unclean woman.* Nothing is more "unclean" than such a woman, who makes whatever she touches unclean according to the Law. To this, all their own righteous acts were to be compared (as they themselves testify)—unless, of course, they were washed in the blood of Christ, in whom they believed and whom they awaited. Therefore, they already possessed "robes," but those robes were not yet white. Accordingly, regarding what was said: *and to each of them were given white robes,* thus in— <note>The text ends mid-sentence as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz's commentary on the Book of Revelation, specifically Chapter 6. Following the previous page's discussion on the white robes given to martyrs, Rupert now interprets the command for them to "rest for a little while" and expands on the theology of the "double robe"—the restoration of both soul and body.</meta>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 4
### Page 186

...into your sight the groaning of the prisoners: <note>original: "gemitus compeditorum," referencing Psalm 79:11.</note> as long as the earth—which is the Church—continues to cry out and say these or similar things, they will not rest in such a way that they cease their crying. Therefore, what was said to them—that they should rest for a little while longer—must be understood or implied as resting not from that cry demanding vengeance for their blood, but from their labors; just as we read in this same book:

<margin>
Below, chapter 14.
</margin>

"From now on," says the Spirit, "let them rest from their labors." <note>Quoting Revelation 14:13.</note> Since this is the case, why was it said that they should rest for a little while longer? Will their rest last only for a brief time?

<margin>
After the resurrection, the saints will have double robes.
</margin>

Certainly not; rather, it was said for this reason: because after a little while, when the number of their fellow servants and their brothers—who are to be killed just as they were—is complete, then something else great will happen, so that they may receive a bountiful increase of their rest. For they will rise again; and those to whom single white robes are given now, will then be given double robes, <note>The "double robe" (stola gemina) is a traditional medieval metaphor for the dual glorification of the soul upon death and the body at the final resurrection.</note> so that they may be blessed as much by the immortal happiness of the soul as by the blessed immortality of the body. For we know that when Adam sinned—in whom all have sinned—everyone was nonetheless stripped in him of the double robe: that is, of the happiness of both body and soul.

<margin>
Genesis 1.
</margin>

Concerning the first robe, which belongs to the soul, it is written: *And when they knew they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.* <note>original: "perizomata," the Latinized Greek term used in the Vulgate for the aprons/loincloths of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3:7.</note> Such a covering was surely the nakedness of the soul: because clearly the entire confusion of the flesh proceeded from within, from the place where beauty had perished.

<margin>
Garments of skin: a sign of misery.
</margin>

The other nakedness is the mortality of the body, concerning which God said: *Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return.* Also, as the Scripture says, the Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife. <note>Genesis 3:21.</note> For though thus clothed in garments, they were truly naked; they were stripped of the natural beauty of their bodies—which God had formed and which they were not ashamed of before they had any covering—and they bore in those very garments a sign of their nakedness and misery. This signified that their mortal bodies must grow old and fail in the same way that garments made of skin grow old. Therefore, in their first parent, they had lost the double robe—that is, the happiness of both soul and body; now, in the meantime...

<summary>Rupert explains that the martyrs' "rest" is a transition from earthly labor to a state of peace, which will culminate in the "double robe" of the resurrection. He contrasts this future glory with the loss of original dignity in the Fall of Adam, where humanity was stripped of its natural beauty and clothed in the "garments of skin" symbolizing mortality.</summary>

<header>On Revelation, Chapter 6</header>

<gloss><unclear>in the kingdom of heaven as the Seventy</unclear> <note>original: "Septuaginta"; referring to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note></gloss>

And I saw, when he had opened the sixth seal, and behold there was a great earthquake, and the sun became black like sackcloth of hair, and the whole moon became like blood, etc.

<margin>The sixth seal: the calling of the Gentiles.</margin>
<gloss><unclear>... concerning ...</unclear></gloss>
This earthquake, the blackness of the sun, the bloody redness of the moon, the falling of the stars, and the other portents of evils written here, most commentators refer to the final persecution and to the times of the Antichrist. We, however, are held by our set purpose; we strive to follow, as best we can, the path provided by the lamp of the scriptures and the clarity of the opened book. Let us therefore follow the order we have begun. When the Jews rejected the word of God and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, <margin>Acts 13</margin> the apostles turned toward the Gentiles. Subsequently, Jerusalem was surrounded by the Roman army, and the people fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive into all nations. Then, indeed, he opened the great sixth seal of the book: because clearly many things that had been written about this were then fulfilled. This is why the Lord himself says in the Gospel: "For these are the days of vengeance, so that all things which are written may be fulfilled." <margin>Luke 21</margin> 

For example: "Behold," says Isaiah, "look, all of us are your people: the city of your holy one has become a desert, Zion. Jerusalem has become a desert; the house of our sanctification and our glory where our fathers praised you has been consumed by fire: and all our precious things have turned into ruins. Will you restrain yourself over these things, Lord? Will you keep silent and afflict us vehemently?" <margin>Isaiah 65</margin> And the Lord answered: "They sought me who before did not ask; they found me who did not seek me. And I said: 'Behold, here I am,' to a nation that did not call upon your name." Explaining the reason why—namely because those same Jews had left their house a desert—he turns toward the Gentiles: "I have stretched out," he said, "my hands all day to an unbelieving people who walk..."

Now, let us traverse the spacious room of this same sixth seal, which has been unlocked. "When," it says, "he had opened the sixth seal, behold, there was a great earthquake." And the meaning is this: so that what was contained in the sacred scriptures concerning the dispersion of the Jews and the calling together of the nations might be fulfilled, the earth was moved—the Roman world was shaken—as Vespasian and Titus gathered their arms from every side and surrounded Jerusalem with their army. <note>Rupert interprets the "earthquake" of the Sixth Seal as the Jewish-Roman War (66–73 AD), which led to the destruction of the Second Temple.</note> Then "the sun," it says, "became black like sackcloth made of hair, and the entire moon became like blood, and the stars of heaven fell upon the earth, as a fig tree drops its unripe figs when it is shaken by a great wind."

<margin>Jerusalem</margin>
That earthly Jerusalem, in its own estimation, was like the sun and like the moon, especially since it had been the seat of David, in which that man had sat while reigning for a time. For they used to read what David himself sang in the Psalm, speaking in the person of God: "Once have I sworn by my holiness; I will not lie to David. His seed shall endure forever, and his throne as the sun in my sight: and as the moon, perfected forever: and a faithful witness in heaven." <note>Psalm 89:35-37. Rather, He spoke of holy men, who are truly the seat and city of Christ, who in the future will be like the sun in regard to their souls, and like the perfect moon in regard to their bodies—which certainly emits more light when it is perfect and full. Therefore, the scripture indeed said truly

<header>Commentary by Rupert, Book 4</header>

"...of heaven," he says, "fell upon the earth." <note>This refers to Revelation 6:13: "And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind."</note> In their own estimation, the Jewish people were also comparable to stars, especially since they would hear Moses saying:

<margin>Deuteronomy 1</margin>
"And I said to you at that time, I alone am not able to bear you, for the Lord our God has multiplied you; and today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the Lord God of your fathers add many thousands to this number." <note>Rupert quotes Deuteronomy 1:9-11, where Moses reminds the Israelites of God's promise to make them a great nation.</note>

<margin>Genesis 15</margin>
From this also, Moses spoke not out of human levity, but by divine authority; for he knew the Lord and had written that He said to Abraham: "Look up at the heaven and count the stars if you can." And again: "So," He said, "shall your seed be." <note>See Genesis 15:5.</note> And indeed, according to this authority, the seed of Abraham was comparable to the stars of heaven; however, not entirely or in every case, but on the part of the elect—that is, those who are children not only of the flesh, but of the promise.

<margin>Romans 9</margin>
For (as the Apostle says), "it is not those who are children of the flesh who are the children of God, but those who are children of the promise are counted as the seed." <note>original: "Etenim non qui filii carnis... hi filii dei..." from Romans 9:8. Rupert uses Paul’s theology to distinguish between physical descendants and spiritual heirs.</note> But were those [who fell] children of the promise, or only children of the flesh?

<margin>Isaiah 48</margin>
Even the prophetic truth reproached them for this, saying, "You who come forth from the waters of Judah." <note>original: "qui existis de aquis Iuda" from Isaiah 48:1, implying a physical origin that lacked spiritual depth.</note> Therefore, those who seemed to themselves to be the stars of heaven fell; they fell, I say—not the true stars of heaven, but like the <term>unripe figs</term> <note>original: "grossi." These are the early, unripened figs that are easily blown off the tree before they reach maturity.</note> of a fig tree shaken by a great wind—that is, greatly driven by a diabolical spirit. This is a truly fitting comparison, using the fig tree and its falling fruit, because clearly even those among the Jews who had believed in Christ at that time, and were like the first fruits of Christ's cross, fell away when the "great wind" moved—namely, the wind of envy. They hated the salvation of the Gentiles, and many of them zealously favored their own circumcision against the faith of the gospel, as the Acts of the Apostles testify.

<margin>Acts 15 & 21</margin>
And so, falling away of their own will from the grace of Christ, almost all the Jews rightly fell by the edge of the sword; and those who survived were led captive into all nations. They are comparable not to stars, as was already said, but to the dust which the wind blows from the face of the earth.

**And the heaven departed like a scroll rolled up.** <note>Quoting Revelation 6:14.</note>

The heaven in which they seemed to themselves to shine like stars was the knowledge of the law. In this law, they looked down upon all other nations as if they themselves were high and shining...

<summary>Rupert interprets the "falling stars" of Revelation as the Jewish people who, despite their prestigious lineage from Abraham, fell from grace due to envy of the Gentiles and rejection of the Gospel. He argues that their "heaven" was a prideful, legalistic understanding of the Law that collapsed during the Roman conquest.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s interpretation of the Sixth Seal in Revelation 6. Following the previous page’s discussion of the Roman siege of Jerusalem, Rupert now explores the symbolic meaning of the "mountains" and "islands," linking the biblical text to the historical downfall of the Jewish leadership and their failed reliance on their ancestral heritage.</meta>

<page-num>CXCV</page-num>
<header>On Chapter 6 of the Apocalypse</header>
<sig>R</sig>

...these [mountains are named] on account of pride: moreover, islands are rightly named on account of deep greed. It was not indeed in their own person that those men, Herod and Pontius Pilate, reached that evil of the siege <note>The Roman Siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD</note>, for each had previously received his own judgment <note>meaning they died before the city fell</note>. But truly, as many as were found at that time to be powerful men or princes, Pharisees and high priests, were moved from their places in the manner already described. Jesus cast them out altogether from his temple and from his place with the whip of his wrath <note>A reference to Jesus cleansing the Temple, here applied to the total destruction of the Jewish religious system</note>, as they fell by the edge of the sword, while that temple of theirs and the city collapsed equally before their eyes in the burning of fire; and those who remained were led away as captives into all nations. 

Meanwhile, they said in vain to the mountains and the rocks, "Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of the one sitting upon the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb." In vain, I say, were they hiding in the mountains and in the caverns of the rocks; nevertheless, in vain was hope held in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Also in Moses and the other fathers and prophets, who are indeed great mountains and living rocks. For those patriarchs did not protect them then; rather, they accused them. <margin>John 5</margin> For clearly the Lord says to them concerning Moses: "There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope." <note>original: "Est qui vos accuset Moses, in quo speratis."</note> 

And without doubt it is fitting to have said this to them: "Hide us from the face of the one sitting on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb." For they could not be ignorant in their fierce conscience that the Lamb whom they had killed lived again, and was powerfully angry with them. For, it says, "the great day of their wrath has come: and who will be able to stand?" The day of their wrath—that is, of the one sitting on the throne and of the Lamb, the Father and the Son, the Lord and his Christ, against whom these princes stood and gathered—has already come, and will yet come, because clearly all these things are the beginnings of sorrows. But the end of these same sorrows, an un-consumable end and an infinite completion, will be in <term>Gehenna|The valley of Hinnom, used as a name for the place of eternal punishment or hell</term>. 

<margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> For so God himself proclaims concerning these in the song of Deuteronomy: "A fire is kindled in my fury, and it shall burn even to the lowest depths of hell." <note>original: "Ignis succensus est in furore meo, & ardebit vsque ad inferni nouissima."</note> And who will be able to stand? Truly no one will be able to stand, no one will be able to resist. But it will be well for whoever, because he did not stand <note>meaning to stand in opposition</note> or resist Him, will then be able to flee the wrath.

<page-num>cc</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 4.</header>

...the soul of the human doing evil, the Jew first and then the Greek <note>original: *animam hoĩs operantis malū, Iudæi primum & Græci*. This is a direct reference to Romans 2:9, illustrating God’s impartial judgment.</note>. Rightly, therefore, are those numbered here in the first place who were sealed as Jews from every tribe of the children of Israel. And then it says: *After these things I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues* <note>Revelation 7:9</note>. The Apostle wishes all of these to be understood under the single name of "Greek" <note>In this context, "Greek" is used as a standard biblical shorthand for all non-Jewish peoples, or Gentiles.</note>.

<margin>The number 144,000 signifies a mystery. An arithmetic calculation based on 12 multiplied.</margin>
Furthermore, if you rightly examine the generation or composition of this number—one hundred and forty-four thousand—a beautiful and noble mystery shines forth from it. Let us say something that might perhaps be less clear or intelligible to the more simple-minded, but the present cause demands it; yet to "arithmeticians" <note>original: *arithmeticis*. In the Middle Ages, arithmetic was one of the seven liberal arts, often focused on the mystical properties of numbers.</note>, who best know the logic of the <term>abacus</term> <note>The medieval abacus was a counting board where columns represented different decimal places (units, tens, hundreds, etc.).</note>, it will immediately appear reasonable and pleasant.

The number twelve, which was the number of the first-born sons of Israel, is arranged so that a unit is placed in the tens column, while a two is placed in the units column <note>Rupert is describing the number 12 as 10 + 2.</note>. However, so that these twelve first-born may grow into the same number of thousands—that is, twelve thousand—that unit of ten passes through one and then another <term>limit</term> <note>original: *limitem*. In medieval mathematics, a "limit" refers to the vertical columns on a calculation board or the decimal places.</note> and settles in the third, becoming ten thousand. Likewise, the single two, which when joined to that unit of ten completed the twelve, passes through one and then another limit and settles in the third, becoming two thousand. These two thousand are then added to the ten thousand already mentioned (which were established in the second limit beyond them), and they become twelve thousand.

Thus, those who were only twelve sons of Israel, now multiplied into twelve thousand, are again multiplied twelve times and become one hundred and forty-four thousand. This number is arranged such that it is distinguished by three limits. For a unit is placed in the hundred-thousands place, a four in the ten-thousands place, and likewise a four in the thousands place <note>Rupert calculates 12,000 x 12 = 144,000, which he visualizes on the abacus as digits in three specific columns: 100,000 + 40,000 + 4,000.</note>. Note this diligently.

<margin>The mystery of the Trinity in this number.</margin>
The first twelve, or the "singles," ascend through three limits to become twelve thousand; and those same twelve thousand, led twelve times according to that same number of the sons of Israel, make one hundred and forty-four thousand—a number distributed, as has been said, into three limits. Why then do we think the holy grace of this revelation intends this, except to show that which all legal, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic truth teaches you...

<summary>Rupert explains the transition from the 144,000 sealed Jews to the "great multitude" of Gentiles and provides a complex medieval arithmetic breakdown of the number 144,000 to reveal a Trinitarian mystery.</summary>

<header>On Revelation, Chapter 7</header>

it is established that it is of no value for salvation that one is a son of Israel or Abraham according to the flesh, unless one is also a child of the same through faith <note>original: *per cā.*—likely a contraction for *conscientiam* (conscience) or a transcription error for *fidem* (faith), given the context of the following sentence.</note>. For is not faith perfected by the confession of three names? Indeed, the confession of faith in this time of revealed grace necessarily expresses the distinct persons of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Long ago, however, in that shadow of the Mosaic Law, this was signified by a hidden profession of just as many paternal names among that people of God, when everyone openly confessed and called upon the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.

<margin>Exodus 3</margin>
Now, indeed, the servants of God are signed on their foreheads with the seal of the cross and the blood of Christ, in the confession of the name of the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. But back then, they marked the doorposts of their houses under the aforementioned names of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, confessing one God, having been taught beforehand by the authority of that same God. For He had said to Moses: *Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.*

<margin>
The children of Israel
or Abraham
are so not by flesh,
but by faith.
Romans 9.
</margin>
*This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.* <note>Exodus 3:15</note> What then, I ask, do we understand by these numbers multiplied and arranged in such a way? It is as if the servants of our God were saying: these ones of ours who are sealed from among the Jews are those who are children of Israel or of the faithful father Abraham not only according to the flesh, but also according to faith. *For not all* (says the Apostle) *who are of Israel are Israelites; nor because they are the seed of Abraham are they all children; but "In Isaac shall your seed be called," that is, it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God, but the children of the promise who are counted as the seed.* <note>Romans 9:6-8</note> Therefore, by this finite number, an innumerable multitude of the entire Church is signified, which was brought forth from the patriarchs either by fleshly lineage or by the imitation of their faith.

<margin>
Here is another
order of tribes
than that found
in Moses.
</margin>
Furthermore, in this specific order of the names of the twelve sons of Israel, a <term>mystical reason</term> <note>Rupert refers to *ratio mystica*, the idea that the sequence of names holds hidden theological significance beyond literal history.</note> is not lacking. This is because they are found arranged here not according to the order of their generation—the order in which they were fathered or born according to the flesh. This certainly did not happen through ignorance, but for the sake of a specific mystery. Therefore, it should not be a burden to write down here the treatment of this subject in the same sense and the same words used by those who came before us.

<header>Rupert's Commentary, Book 4</header>

## Twelve thousand were sealed from the tribe of Judah, etc.

<margin>
Why the tribe of Dan is omitted here.
Genesis 49
</margin>
Appropriately, he begins with Judah, for it is from this tribe that our Lord arose. He omits the tribe of Dan, however, because it is said that the Antichrist will be born from it. As it is written: *Let Dan be a snake in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting the horse's heels so that his rider falls backward.* <note>original: "Fiat Dan coluber in via, cerastes in semita..." This prophecy from Genesis 49:17 was traditionally interpreted by medieval theologians like Rupert to mean the Antichrist would descend from Dan.</note> He chose to explain the virtues of the Church not according to the order of earthly generation <note>meaning their biological birth order</note>, but according to the interpretation of their names. The Church hastens from present confession and praise toward the "right hand" of eternal life. This is precisely what the names of Judah (who is placed first) and Benjamin (who is placed last) signify.

<margin>
Why the tribe of Judah is placed in the first spot.
</margin>
Judah is placed first, then, because his name is interpreted as *confession* or *praise*. <note>In Hebrew, *Yehudah* is related to the root for thanks or praise.</note> This is because no one can grasp the height of good works before the beginning of confession; unless we renounce our evil acts through confession, we cannot be shaped by righteous ones.

<margin>
Reuben
Psalm 127
</margin>
The second is Reuben, which is interpreted as *seeing the son*. The Psalmist <note>Rupert refers to the author of the Psalms, King David</note> testifies that "sons" designate "works" when he says, among other blessings for the blessed man: *Your children shall be like olive shoots.* And further on: *And may you see your children’s children.* <note>original: "Filij tui sicut nouellæ oliuarum." From Psalm 128:3 (127 in the Vulgate).</note> It is not that a man who fears the Lord cannot be blessed unless he has fathered sons and received grandsons—especially since a greater reward awaits faithful virgins—but rather, "sons" signify works, and "children's children" signify the fruit of those works, which is the eternal reward. Thus, Reuben follows Judah: after the beginning of divine confession and praise, the perfection of action follows.

<margin>
Gad.
Acts 13
</margin>
But because *it is through many tribulations that we must enter the kingdom of God*, <note>original: "per multas tribulationes..." Rupert cites Acts 14:22, though the margin notes Acts 13.</note> Gad follows Reuben. Gad is interpreted as *temptation* or *girded*. After the beginning of a good work, it is necessary for a person to be tested by greater temptations and to be girded for heavier wars, so that the strength of their faith may be proven, as Solomon says:

<margin>
Ecclesiasticus 2
</margin>
*Son, coming to the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.* <note>From the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 2:1. In the medieval period, this book was often grouped with the works of Solomon.</note>

<margin>
Psalm 17
</margin>
Likewise, the Psalmist says: *You have girded me with strength for the battle.* <note>Psalm 18:39 (17 in the Vulgate).</note>

<margin>
Asher
James 1
</margin>
And because *we call those blessed who have endured suffering*, Asher (which means *blessed*) is placed after Gad in a very fitting order. For *blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been proven, he shall receive the crown of life.* <note>James 1:12.</note>

<margin>
Naphtali
</margin>
Because truly hu— <note>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "hu," likely for "humilitas" (humility), which will continue on the next page.</note>

He notes the omission of Dan due to its traditional association with the Antichrist.</summary>

<page-num>cciiii</page-num>
<header>On Revelation, Chapter 6</header>

Secure in the faithful promise of right beatitude, they are not constrained; but rejoicing in hope and patient in tribulation, they sing along with the <term>Psalmist</term><note>The "Psalmographo" refers to King David, traditionally credited with writing the Psalms.</note>:
<margin>Psalm 4</margin>
"In tribulation, you have enlarged me." <note>original: "in tribulatione dilatasti me"</note> And likewise:
<margin>Psalm 119, 1 Samuel 2</margin>
"I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart," <note>original: "Viam mandatorum tuorum cucurri, cum dilatares cor meum"</note> and rejoicing with the mother of the blessed Samuel [Hannah], they say: "My mouth is enlarged over my enemies, because I have rejoiced in your salvation." <note>original: "dilatatum est os meum super inimicos meos, quia laetata sum in salutari tuo"</note> For this reason, **Naphtali** follows next, which means *breadth* or *latitude*.
<margin>Manasseh, Philippians 3</margin>
But **Manasseh** also follows him, whose name is interpreted as *forgotten* or *necessity*. By the mystery of this name, we are warned that, being taught by the pains of present temptations, we should "forget those things which are behind" and "stretch forward to those things which are ahead" according to the Apostle Paul, 
<margin>Romans 13</margin>
so that we care for the flesh not according to our desires, but by *necessity* alone, being bound by the human condition. 
<margin>Psalm 25</margin>
Concerning this, the Psalmist, sighing for better things, says in prayer: "Deliver me from my necessities." <note>original: "De necessitatibus meis eripe me"</note>
<margin>Simeon</margin>
After him is placed **Simeon**, which means *he heard sadness*, or the *name of a dwelling*. This is to indicate more clearly by the quality of this word what should be held onto here on earth and what may be healthfully expected in the future. For the joy of the heavenly dwelling will be given to those whose minds are saddened here by the waves of repentance. 
<margin>John 16, Levi, Proverbs 13</margin>
To them it is said: "Your sorrow shall be turned into joy." <note>original: "Tristitia vestra vertetur in gaudium"</note> Therefore **Levi** is joined next, which means *added*. By this we understand either those who "purchase" eternal things using temporal ones—as Solomon says: "The ransom of a man's soul are his own riches"—
<margin>Matthew 19</margin>
or those who, by following God's counsel, receive a hundredfold in this world along with tribulations, and in the world to come, eternal life. 
<margin>Ecclesiastes 1</margin>
To these people, what is written also fits: "He who adds knowledge, adds also labor." For the bitterness of tribulations was added to holy Job for this very reason: so that a greater reward of prizes might be returned to him once he was tested. 
<margin>Issachar, Romans 8</margin>
Whence, not without merit, **Issachar** rightly succeeds him in order, whose name is interpreted as *reward*. For as the Apostle teaches: "The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us." <note>original: "Non sunt condignae passiones huius temporis ad futuram gloriam..."</note> Indeed, the fight is fought more fruitfully when a certain reward is hoped for. This, however, God works and perfects in the "dwelling of strength," which is called 
<margin>Zebulun</margin>
**Zebulun**, when virtue is made perfect in weakness, and...

The author interprets their names as stages of spiritual growth, moving from enduring tribulation and forgetting earthly desires toward the final reward and strength found in God.</summary>

...wait a little time longer, until their fellow servants and brothers—who are to be killed just as they were—are fulfilled. <note>original: "rent tēpus adhuc modicum, donec impleantur cōserui & fratres eorū qui interficiendi sunt, sicut & illi." Afterward, however, one of the elders says: "These who are clothed in white robes, who are they and where did they come from?" <margin>Children of Abraham.</margin>

<margin>Romans 4.</margin>

"I saw," he says, "a great multitude, which no one could count." <note>Revelation 7:9.</note> The **number** of the saints in the scriptures is understood in two ways: sometimes indeed for their sheer quantity, but at other times for the manifold progress of their virtues. Regarding their quantity, it is used as in that place: "I will count them, and they shall be multiplied above the sand." 
<margin>Psalm 139.</margin>
<note>original: "Psal. cxxxviij." The Vulgate numbering is 138.</note> It is not that they are literally more numerous than the sand, but it is the same as if he were to say: "I will take up not a few, but many, and I will guard them in the manner of a thing carefully numbered and well-protected." 

Regarding the manifold increase of virtues or blessedness, it is used as in that place: "Lord, make me know my end: and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me." 
<margin>Psalm 39.</margin>
<note>original: "Psal. xxxviij." The Vulgate numbering is 38.</note> Not that there are many days there, but one alone more encompassing than all days together; there is an unending spaciousness, a number not passing away, but a state of permanent and eternal life. According to either sense, no one could count that multitude. For even in their plurality, those who already exist—together with those who, in the final persecution of the **Antichrist**, shall receive the robes and palms of victory as martyrs—are numbered or countable by God alone. And of how many "days" they are (of which it is said elsewhere for the consolation 
<margin>Psalm 91.</margin>
<note>original: "Psalm. xc." The Vulgate numbering is 90.</note> of the righteous: "With length of days I will satisfy him"), it cannot be estimated...

<summary>Rupert explains that the "great multitude" in Revelation consists of those who share the faith of Abraham, regardless of their ethnic origin. He also explores the symbolic meaning of "numbering" in Scripture, distinguishing between physical quantity and the spiritual "length" of eternal life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Book 4 of the Apocalypse. <page-num>ccvi</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 4</header>

...is possible, for indeed the number is infinite. "From all," he says, "nations, and tribes, and peoples, and languages." <note>A reference to Revelation 7:9.</note> 
<margin>Many tribes in one nation.</margin>
A nation and a tribe differ in this: that one nation contains many tribes. For a nation is a multitude arisen from a single origin, or distinguished from another nation according to its own specific grouping; just as from one Jacob—or Israel—came the one Israelite nation, which had twelve tribes. The Roman nation, moreover, was divided into thirty-five *curiae* <note>original: "curias." The *curia* was a traditional political and social division of the Roman people.</note>, by which name—though not strictly—they were called "tribes." Furthermore, "people" is accustomed to be used sometimes for a nation, and sometimes only for the inhabitants of a single city. Concerning "languages," this should be known: that although he listed nations, tribes, and peoples first, and then languages, languages did not give rise to nations, but rather nations arose from languages. In the beginning, there were as many languages as there were nations. <note>Rupert refers here to the biblical account of the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11, where the division of speech created the various nations.</note> Later, there were more nations than languages, because many nations arose from a single language.

<margin>The three sacred languages.</margin>
Let there be three sacred languages: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, which excel most in the whole world. For in these three languages, the cause of the Lord's death was written by Pilate above the cross. <note>Referring to the *Titulus Crucis*, the sign reading "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" (John 19:19-20).</note> Hence, and because of the obscurity of the Holy Scriptures, a knowledge of these three languages is necessary, so that one may turn to another if the speech of one language brings any doubt regarding a name or an interpretation. Therefore, it will no longer be permitted to boast in carnal Judaism or the circumcision of the flesh regarding what was originally written: "God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel," 
<margin>Psalm 75.</margin>
because behold, there are those from all nations, tribes, peoples, and languages in whom God is known, and in whom His name is great and victorious.

> Standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and with palms in their hands. <note>Quoting Revelation 7:9.</note>

<margin>Daniel 7.</margin>
Undoubtedly, this standing before the throne—or the throne itself—is that of which Daniel spoke after he had first said: "I watched until the thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat." Immediately after, he said: "His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels were a burning fire." Also: "Thousands of thousands served him, and ten thousand times a hun—" <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing as "a hundred thousand" (*centena milia*), quoting Daniel 7:9-10.</note>

<summary>Rupert of Deutz explains the differences between nations, tribes, and peoples, and emphasizes the importance of the three "sacred languages" (Hebrew, Greek, and Latin) for biblical interpretation. He argues that God is now known among all peoples, not just in Judea, as evidenced by the great multitude in Revelation.</summary>

...ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. <note>Rupert is completing a quotation from Daniel 7:10, describing the heavenly court.</note> For indeed, to those who are such people and who stand in such a way, that throne is not a flame of burning fire, but only a fire of illumination; but certainly for those who killed them, the flame will be a burning or melting fire, just as
<margin>Psalm 67</margin>

From Psalm 68:2 (67:3 in the Vulgate).</note> For what is it for these to stand before the throne, if not the same thing as it was for those earlier ones to cry out from beneath the altar of God? <note>A reference to the martyrs in Revelation 6:9-10.</note> Truly, both those standing and those crying out look forward to the same thing; they demand the same judgment and vengeance for their blood. <margin>Daniel 7</margin>
power, and honor, and a kingdom,* etc. <note>original: "Antiquus dierum" (Ancient of Days), a title for God the Father in Daniel's vision.</note> It is also fitting that those standing thus are clothed in white robes—it is understood they are washed white in the blood of the Lamb—so that they may be clearly similar to him before whom they stand. For his garment (as the same author says above) was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool.

->***And palms, he says, were in their hands.***<-

Because, without a doubt, they have conquered the four aforementioned angels—that is, the four principal kingdoms of the world—and although these kingdoms were willing to harm them, struggling and resisting with every effort, they were nonetheless sealed, and received the sign of the living God on their foreheads. Therefore, through the battle of the four winds after the passage of the four beasts (as the same author says above), the Ancient of Days came and gave judgment to the saints of the Most High, and the time arrived, and the saints obtained the kingdom. Thus, there are palms in their hands, and those same palms continue to bloom and grow in the meantime, until the fourth beast is utterly slain, and the power of the other beasts is also completely taken away, and at last the final judgment sits, and the kingdom, and the power, and the greatness of the kingdom, which is under all of heaven... <note>Rupert interprets the "palms" of victory as the result of the faithful surviving the persecutions of the worldly empires described in Daniel's prophecy.</note>

the kingdom is given to the people of the saints of the most high, with the individual robes <note>The "robes" or "stoles" (Latin: *stolis*) represent the glory of the saints. <margin>Death entered through one man. Romans 5</margin>
Destruction and death, which had entered into this world through one man, had passed into all men, because in him all had sinned. <note>Rupert is citing the traditional interpretation of Romans 5:12, where Adam’s "original sin" brings death to all humanity.</note> But just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death; so, says the apostle, through the one Christ, the condemnation and death of sin are overcome by the gift of eternal life. Just as the great multitude from all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues is a number comprehensible to no one, so also here (and above where the Lamb first took the book) the number of angels is not defined. It was already said of them there that, even if they were not redeemed through him (because they had not perished), they were nevertheless created through his divinity. And through his blood, as the Apostle also witnesses, they were reconciled to us, or made peaceful;

<margin>Colossians 1</margin>

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Chapter 7 of the Book of Revelation. On the previous page, Rupert discussed the saints’ confession of salvation through God and the Lamb. # On Apocalypse Chapter 7
### Page 209

<margin>
The number seven designates universality.
</margin>
There are seven words: blessing, wisdom, glory <note>original: "claritas," meaning brightness or divine splendor</note>, thanksgiving, honor, power, and strength. It is customary for the number seven to designate universality <note>The number seven was considered "perfect" in the Middle Ages, representing the sum of all things, such as the seven days of creation or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.</note>, both among secular philosophers and among church writers. Therefore, whatever praise, whatever glorification or jubilation the mind can conceive or the tongue can utter—whatever that language of angels might be—we do not doubt that it is proclaimed by those blessed spirits to our God on behalf of all the saints. For, as it is said of the lost son, they were dead and have come back to life; they were lost and have been found.
<margin>Luke 15</margin>

> And one of the elders answered and said to me: These who are clothed in white robes, who are they and from where did they come? And I said: My Lord, you know. And he said to me: These are they who came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; therefore, they are before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple.
<margin><insert>the way to paradise</insert></margin>

Since this manner of speaking—"Who are they, and from where did they come?"—is not a response but an interrogation or an inquiry, he is nevertheless rightly said to have "answered." This is because he intends to provide an answer: he asks the question so that, having made the listener attentive by the inquiry itself, he may then finally give the reply. "These," he says, "are they who came out of great tribulation." Truly, all the saints have come out of great tribulation, for the cause or the beginning of this tribulation was original sin.
<margin>2 Timothy 3</margin>
Indeed, all who have wished to live piously from that time onward have suffered tribulation or persecution. Nevertheless, in that tribulation, the martyrs shone more remarkably and brilliantly, like gold in a furnace of fire <note>A common biblical metaphor (from Wisdom 3:6) for how suffering purifies the soul of a believer.</note>. It is of these that he immediately adds, saying: "And they washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb." For even if the entire Church has been cleansed from every sin in the blood of Christ, these martyrs have been cleansed and made white much more so, for they shared in the blood of Christ to such an extent that they even shed their own blood for Christ. Therefore, they are before the throne of God precisely because they are clean, because they are white, and because they are remarkable in their white robes...

<summary>Rupert explains the significance of the "sevenfold" praise of the angels as representing total perfection. He then identifies the white-robed multitude as the saints and specifically the martyrs, who were purified through the "great tribulation" of original sin and their own sacrifice.</summary>

They walk gracefully; therefore they assist as familiars; thus they look joyfully upon the one who beholds them, and being full of sweetness and ineffably occupied with him whom they see, they cannot turn their mutual gaze away from his sight. He who sits upon the throne dwells both in them and over them; for they themselves are both his house and his throne. He dwells in them as their life; he dwells over them as their ornament and glory.

->### On Chapter 8 of the Apocalypse<-

# Page 211

...[sou]thern, this is what it says here: that the crowd which he saw was from all nations, tribes, and peoples, and tongues. Likewise in <margin>Luke 12.</margin> when the Lord had said, "Do not fear those who kill the body," <note>original: "Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt"</note> he immediately added: "And after this they have nothing more they can do." He magnificently amplifies this point here when he says: **They shall hunger no more, nor thirst anymore, nor shall the sun fall upon them, nor any heat.** For it was once in the power of those persecutors or murderers that the saints should hunger and thirst, that they should be afflicted by heat and cold, <margin>Hebrews 11.</margin> wandering about (as the Apostle says) "in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted, wandering in deserts, in mountains, and in caves and caverns of the earth." <note>A reference to the sufferings of the faithful in Hebrews 11:37–38.</note> But truly, it will no longer be in their power to do these things.

<margin>Those who hungered for righteousness are satisfied. Matthew 5.</margin>
But also regarding that praiseworthy hunger and good thirst which the saints held here—about which the Lord also said, "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness"—they shall hunger or thirst no more, for there they shall be satisfied and filled to overflowing. <note>original: "inebriabuntur," literally "inebriated," a common medieval metaphor for being overwhelmed by divine joy.</note> Finally, those fountains of water to which the Lamb who rules them leads them, those are the fountains—or rather that fountain and torrent—which the Psalmist foresaw when he said: <margin>Psalm 35 [36].</margin> "They shall be filled from the abundance of your house, and you will give them to drink from the torrent of your pleasure, for with you is the fountain of life." <note>original: "Inebriabūtur ab ubertate domus tuae... quoniam apud te est fons vitae."</note>

<margin>The ineffable joy of eternal life.</margin>
Who is sufficient to explain these things? Who will worthily treat or expound upon them? Indeed, who will perceive these things with the senses? How much or in what way does the scripture labor to intimate to us the feeling of divine clarity by saying: <margin>1 Corinthians 2.</margin> **And God shall wipe away every tear from their eyes?** We fail in this wonder, because eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him.

<insert><gloss><unclear>And besides / seven hours / until... </unclear> <note>These German glosses are difficult to read and appear to be a later reader's calculation or note regarding the timing of the "half hour" mentioned below.</note></gloss></insert>

<margin>Chapter 8.</margin>
**And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.**

<margin>The seventh seal, the day of judgment. Zephaniah 1.</margin>
When he who ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, comes to judge the living and the dead, then the seventh seal shall be loosened, because a no small or light momentum of the scriptures is being fulfilled. For example: concerning that day of judgment, the prophet Zephaniah says: "The day of the Lord is near..."

...[The day of the Lord is] great, it is near and very swift. The voice of the Lord’s day is bitter; there the strong man will be troubled. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and clanging over fortified cities and over the exalted angels. <note>original: "super angelos excelsos." While the biblical source (Zephaniah 1:16) usually refers to "high corners" or towers (angulos), this text reads "angels," perhaps interpreting the judgment as extending to spiritual powers.</note> And I will trouble men, and they shall walk as if blind, because they have sinned against the Lord. He says therefore: **There was silence in heaven for about half an hour.** <note>Revelation 8:1.</note> Silence in this place is rightly understood to signify that rest of which the Psalmist speaks:

<margin>Psalm 75.</margin>
**The earth trembled and was still, when God arose in judgment, to save all the meek of the earth.** <note>Psalm 76:8–9 in modern Bibles. Rupert interprets the "silence" as the peace that follows the storm of judgment.</note> For he had said just before: **From heaven you caused judgment to be heard,** using the past tense in the prophetic manner to refer to a future time.

<margin>Matthew 25.</margin>
And the meaning is this: When coming from heaven, you make judgment heard by saying to the righteous: **Come, you blessed of my Father,** and so on. Then the earth trembled and was still, that is, the wicked will fear and cease their evil-doing. But also the saints, who now cry out from under the altar of God (as written above) saying: **How long, Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood?** <note>Reference to Revelation 6:10, where the martyrs ask for justice.</note> then they shall rest, and put an end to their crying, because then it will be done, then it will be judged, their killers having been eliminated from every side, so that they can kill no more.

<margin>The silence of the saints.</margin>
This kind of silence or rest in heaven—that is, in the heavenly church—which will be without end, was signified by that "silence." Moreover, when he says, **for about half an hour**, this is sufficient both to signify the aforementioned peace and rest, and it serves to mark the separation between what has come before and what follows, because clearly the sequence of mysteries or revelation is now being summarized again from a new starting point. <note>Rupert refers to the "recapitulation" theory of the Apocalypse, where the narrative circles back to tell the same story of the Church from a different perspective.</note>

<summary>Rupert interprets the "silence in heaven" at the opening of the Seventh Seal as the eternal peace of the Church that follows the Day of Judgment. He explains that this silence marks the end of the martyrs' suffering and the beginning of a new section in the visionary narrative.</summary>

Just as Christ truly said that persecutors kill the body but cannot kill the soul, <note>Referencing Matthew 10:28.</note> so truly did Christ’s apostle say: **I labor even unto chains, but the word of God is not bound.** <note>Referencing 2 Timothy 2:9. His soul was expanded to such a great breadth that he could behold before him the mystical accounts of God's works, arranged through thousands of years and across almost many miles <note>The author uses "miles" (miliaria) metaphorically to describe the vast scope of the Holy Scriptures.</note> of all the scriptures. It leads and brings him back from the first ages to the very last, and from the last back to the earlier ones—namely, from the opening of the last seal (which is to be opened on the final day) back to the first trumpet. **Commentary of Rupert, Book 5**

<margin>Argument of the seven trumpets.</margin>
...that he will judge all on the last day. It is a laborious and yet very beautiful task to show from the Scriptures where, when, or how each of these angels sounded their trumpet; which "third part of the earth" was burned up by fiery hail; what "great mountain" was cast into the sea; which "third part of the sea" or its creatures died; which "third part of the rivers" was made bitter or turned into wormwood <note>original: <term>absynthium</term>; a bitter plant used here to symbolize divine punishment or suffering</note>; which—or of which sun or stars—a "third part" was struck and darkened; what "pit of the abyss" <note>Referring to the "bottomless pit" in Revelation 9</note> this is, and how a star falling from heaven opened it, from which smoke ascended and locusts emerged; who are the "four angels" bound at the great river Euphrates, but released at the voice of God’s command; what the "final woe" <note>original: <term>vae</term>; a cry of lament or judgment</note> is, and what are those voices of those saying: **The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.** <note>Revelation 11:15.</note> It is laborious, I say, to show all these things from certain places in the Scriptures, as they precede the last day of the Great Judgment with clear testimonies.

Furthermore, it should already be known here that when the aforementioned plagues began to occur—as a testament to or confirmation of the coming judgment of God—the preparation of mercy was not simultaneously lacking. This mercy is always ready for those fleeing that judgment and meets everyone. Therefore, it is beautifully said that after "I saw seven angels, and seven trumpets were given to them," but *before* any of them sounded their trumpet, "behold," it says, "another angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer," and so on. For this angel—or rather the action and character of this angel—designates the priesthood of Christ, our merciful and faithful High Priest <note>original: <term>pontificis</term>; literally 'bridge-builder,' a term for a high ranking priest or bishop</note>, which began to be prefigured there, where the angels' trumpets and the plagues began to occur, as the following parts of our discourse will declare as much as possible. Therefore, just as we recognize the Spirit of Understanding <note>Rupert is correlating the stages of the Apocalypse with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit found in Isaiah 11:2. The Seven Seals represented the Spirit of Understanding.</note> to have worked in the preceding seven seals of the book once they were opened, so in these seven trumpets of the angels, and in that other angel having the censer, we recognize that the Spirit of Counsel <note>original: <term>spiritum consilii</term></note> has worked or is working.

<margin>The Spirit of Counsel will open the mysteries of the seven trumpets.</margin>
Wherefore, after the trumpet-blast of the sixth angel, a mighty angel lifts his hand toward heaven, swearing by the one who lives forever and ever, that in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins...

<summary>Rupert explains that interpreting the seven trumpets is a difficult but beautiful task, detailing the various plagues they herald. He argues that the trumpets represent the "Spirit of Counsel" and emphasizes that Christ’s mercy, symbolized by the angel with the golden censer, is available even as the judgments of the last days begin.</summary>

### On Revelation Chapter 7.

<margin>The judgment by fire will not come suddenly.</margin>
...the trumpet sounds, the mystery of God shall be finished. For "mystery" <note>original: <term>mysterium</term></note> in this place is the same as a "secret counsel." And this was truly the great counsel of the great God: that he willed the final judgment by fire not to happen as suddenly or unexpectedly as that earlier judgment performed by water <note>A reference to the Great Flood in the time of Noah</note>. Instead, he sent many things ahead pertaining to that same judgment, through which it might not be doubted that it was coming—mercy being joined everywhere for those whom he foresaw were performing, or would perform, penance before the judgment itself. 

Therefore, since we have in this recapitulation <note>A method of biblical interpretation where the same events are described again from a different perspective to add depth</note> great matter regarding mercy and judgment—from which a grand discourse is rightly owed to us, except that we are weak in speaking—let us first speak of the instrument of mercy, according to the action or manner of this angel. The matter itself now seems to demand that we first inquire who this angel is estimated to be according to his person. Then we will say whose figure he bears or whom he signifies, according to the sense which the public use of the Holy Church has long since commended. 

<margin>The holy affection of the angels toward us. Luke 15; Luke 2.</margin>
Indeed, many testimonies of the Holy Scriptures commend that the devotion of all angels is holy and kind toward the human race, as for example that Gospel passage: **I tell you, there will be joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.** <note>Luke 15:10</note> They, rejoicing in our redemption, celebrated and exulted at the birth of the Lord in a great multitude, announcing as they sang, and singing as they announced: **Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will.** <note>Luke 2:14</note>

<margin>Matthew, last chapter; Acts 1.</margin>
These same ones, when the Lord rose and when he ascended into heaven, appearing in white robes, celebrated the festival of our salvation and hastened to make known that it should be celebrated by our faith. Nevertheless, above all others, Michael and Gabriel are before the Lord on our behalf; they busy themselves for us, and they come and go for our help, as both the Old and New Testaments testify. 

<margin>Daniel 8.</margin>
For in the Old Testament, let Daniel hear the voice of one saying to him: **Gabriel, make this man understand the vision.** <note>Daniel 8:16</note> This man who commanded Gabriel to speak, so that...

<margin>Gabriel, the overseer of battles.</margin>
...[The angel] makes Daniel understand the vision; though the Jews argue this was Michael. For it says: *A great battle took place in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon,* etc. Therefore, since (as has already been said) all the angels possess a pious zeal of goodwill toward us humans, we should feel this most strongly regarding these two, whom the famous proclamation of both the Old and New Testaments designates by name for such

# On Apocalypse, Chapter 8

<margin>The people of God, the sons of Abraham.</margin>
By the testimony of another, he is both said to be and is our prince—a prince in battle, a prince in the judgment of the world. Until the end of the age, this prince holds authority over the people of God, as witnessed by the same angel <note>The angel speaking to Daniel.</note> who said above when speaking to Daniel: *In that time shall Michael rise up, the great prince who stands for the children of your people, and there shall come a time such as never was from the time that nations began to be, until that same time.* <note>Daniel 12:1</note> When it is said to Daniel, "For the children of your people," we rightly understand this to mean ourselves. For truly, whoever of us is of the faith of Abraham is counted, along with Daniel and all the children not only of the flesh but of the faith of Abraham, as one people who are called and are so by the authority of the scriptures.

<margin>Romans 4 and 9.</margin>
With these testimonies supporting us, we truly recognize and say that this angel, who stood by the altar of the temple in such a form, is Michael the archangel, our prince. We do not doubt that through all the centuries of the past—before the Child was born to us from the Virgin, He who is called and is the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>A traditional title for Christ, often linked to Isaiah 9:6 in the Septuagint version.</note>—I say, since the nations began, since Abraham believed in God and it was credited to him as righteousness, Michael has stood for the children of that people and has been their helper.

<margin>The angel next to the altar of the temple is Michael.</margin>
<margin>Genesis 15.</margin>
From the time that Abraham believed God (as has already been said) and it was credited to him as righteousness, this angel stood beside the altar of the temple, having a golden censer in his hand. We have not yet touched upon the symbolic meaning of his "standing," about which we shall speak later, but we intend to commemorate the acts of his assistance by which he, as prince, personally helped the former people.

<margin>The altar of the temple is Christ; the temple is the Church.</margin>
Therefore, which altar of the temple, or by the altar of which temple, do we understand him to have stood? Doubtless, the holy temple of God is the holy universal Church, and the altar of this temple is Christ. Just as in a temple made by hands the visible altar stands out with every kind of religious dignity, so in His Church, Christ—as both God and man—prevails with both divine and royal majesty. In what way did this angel stand beside such an altar? He stood where that very altar was first founded in its temple: where Christ was placed through faith in the hearts of the patriarchs, who believed this word: *And in your seed shall all the nations be blessed,* <note>Genesis 22:18</note> which seed is certainly Christ.
<margin>Genesis 22.</margin>

<summary>Rupert identifies the angel with the golden censer in Revelation 8 as the Archangel Michael, arguing that Michael has served as the protector of God's people since the time of Abraham. He provides an allegorical interpretation where the Temple represents the Church and the Altar represents Christ.</summary>
