<page-num>218</page-num>
### Commentary of Rupert, Book V

From that time on, that angel <note>original: "angulus"; likely a transcription error or variant for "angelus" (angel), as the text refers to Michael the Archangel.</note> was made the prince of that nation, and for that reason he is rightly said to have stood beside the altar; for on account of faith of this kind, he was given to that people as a guardian and helper.

> He stood, therefore, it says, having a golden censer in his hand. <note>Revelation 8:3</note>

<margin>The golden censer is faith.</margin>
The golden censer was their holy faith—a pure faith, a golden faith—which was certainly proven through many tribulations of those same people wandering upon the earth, just as gold is tested in a furnace of fire. He held this faith of theirs in his hand like a censer; that is, he held it for them as a cause of righteousness, in order to obtain the benefits of God. Whence it also follows:

> And much incense was given to him, that he might offer the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne. <note>Revelation 8:3</note>

<margin>Incense represents the prayers of the saints.</margin>
He himself explained what he wished to be understood by the "incense" by saying: *That he might offer the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar.* Therefore, the incense given to him is the prayers of the saints. But what were those saints praying for, over whom this angel was prince in such a ministry, as the prophetic truth asserts? What were they praying for, or for what thing did they most especially offer prayers? Indeed, the divine pages are full of "cries" rather than the "prayers" of those who knew not how to call upon God except in times of necessity and for temporal safety.

<margin>Exodus 1.</margin>
<margin>Judges 3.</margin>
For example: *The king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel, groaning because of their labors, cried out to the Lord. And their cry rose up to the Lord because of their works, and He heard their groaning.* <note>Exodus 2:23-24; the margin incorrectly cites chapter 1.</note> Likewise: *The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and He delivered them into the hands of [their enemy], and they served him; and they cried out to the Lord, who raised up saviors for them and delivered them.* <note>Judges 3:8-9</note> The divine pages, I say, are full of such cries of theirs.

<margin>Which prayers may worthily be called incense.</margin>
But were these cries alone all those "prayers of the saints," and all the "incense" that was given to this angel? If they prayed for <note>original: "adorauerunt" (worshipped/prayed for)</note> nothing else, were their prayers then worthy to be called incense, and to be burned before the altar or before the throne in the sight of God?

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the "golden censer" in Revelation as the pure faith of God's people, which the Archangel Michael presents to God. He distinguishes between the desperate "cries" for physical relief found in the Old Testament and the spiritual "prayers" that truly constitute heavenly incense.</summary>

### On Revelation, Chapter VII <note>While the header says Chapter 7, Rupert is clearly commenting on the events of Revelation 8:3-4.</note>

<margin>Genesis 22. The prayers of David in the Psalms. Psalm 108, Psalm 140.</margin>
Therefore, the prayers of the holy fathers or patriarchs, which here deservedly earn the name of "incense," were those which they poured out for the sake of Christ. They prayed to obtain His arrival, which had been promised to the great father Abraham, so that through Him they might be blessed along with all the nations or families of the earth and be set free from that curse of the first transgression <note>A reference to "Original Sin" resulting from the fall of Adam and Eve.</note>. Saint David especially and clearly aims for this in the Psalms which he sings as prayers; indeed, because of the great importance of this goal, he judges those same prayers of his so highly that he utters many of the Psalms in the very person of the One whose arrival he sighs for. This is evident to anyone who pays close attention to their meaning.

For example: *O God, do not be silent regarding my praise* <note>original: "Deus laudem meam ne tacueris"; Psalm 109:1 (108 in the Vulgate).</note> etc. He says this instead of saying: "O God, do not be silent regarding the praise of Christ Your Son, for the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful man are opened against Him. They have spoken against Him with a deceitful tongue, and have surrounded Him with words of hatred, and have fought against Him without cause." Therefore, David was not ignorant that these and similar things were the true "incense." In a certain place, after he had said: *Lord, I have cried to You, hear me; listen to my voice when I cry to You,* he immediately added: *Let my prayer be directed like incense in Your sight* <note>original: "Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo"; Psalm 141:2 (140 in the Vulgate).</note>. The meaning is this: "Make it so that my prayer is directed, not in the sight of men—who think a prayer is 'directed' when they pray for bodily health, riches, and the like—but in Your sight, in Your good pleasure." It is the same as if he were saying: "Make me pray for that which ought to be prayed for." There follows, then:

->**And the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints ascended from the hand of the angel before God.**<-

<margin>The smoke of the incense is the affection. Galatians 5.</margin>
The "smoke of the incense" is the most sweet affection <note>In a medieval context, "affectio" refers to a deep, transformative emotional and spiritual state or devotion.</note> of holy prayers. It becomes sweet through faith working through love <note>A reference to Galatians 5:6.</note> and rises up before God just as when incense is melted by a burning fire, it creates a fragrant smoke, breathing a sense of its internal sweetness upward into open nostrils. In a beautiful progression, smoke of this kind ascends from the prayers of the saints to the hand of the angel, and from the hand of the angel...

<summary>Rupert interprets the incense of Revelation as the longing of Old Testament figures like Abraham and David for Christ’s coming. He explains that true prayer (the "smoke") is a sweet spiritual devotion that rises to God through faith and love.</summary>

# On Revelation Chapter 8

...and every surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and all the green things of the earth. Finally, under the names of the earth, the trees, and the grass, we are to understand men, as is well known by the authority of the Holy Scriptures. 
<margin>
Genesis 3.
Ecclesiastes 10.
Matthew 7.
Luke 6.
Isaiah 40.
</margin>
Take "earth," for example, when God says: *Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return* <note>original: "Quia puluis es, & in puluerem reuerteris"</note>, or: *You are earth, and to earth you shall go.* And elsewhere: *Why is earth and ashes proud?* Regarding "trees," the same Lord says: *A good tree does not produce bad fruit, nor does a bad tree produce good fruit.* Regarding "grass," the same Lord says through the prophet: *Cry out. All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the grass. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord remains forever.* Therefore, the "earth," the "trees," and the "green grass" were the men of Sodom, who were greedy, haughty, decadent, and indeed full of lust.

<margin>
Why the Sodomites are called a third part of the earth.
</margin>
But why were they called the "third part" of the earth or the trees—that is, of men? This was clearly for a twofold reason: because they were from the lineage of Ham, and because they were impenitent. Indeed, the lineage of Ham is rightly called and is a "third part" of men because, as is well known, there were three sons of Noah who came out of the ark: Shem, 
<margin>Genesis 10</margin>
Ham, and Japheth. Furthermore, Ham himself is the father of Canaan, from whose descendants the Sodomites were spread abroad, just as it is written: *By these the nations of the Canaanites were spread abroad; the borders of Canaan reached from Sidon as you come to Gerar even unto Gaza, until you enter Sodom and Gomorrah, and Admah and Zeboiim, even unto Lasha.* Therefore, by nature—that is, by race or nation—they were a "third part," because they were from the 
<margin>Genesis 9</margin>
lineage of the cursed Canaan, one of the descendants of Ham, whose father said: *Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.* This is the first reason why the Sodomites are rightly called a third part of the earth, or a third part of the trees.

<margin>
The impenitent are a third part of men.
Proverbs 2.
Isaiah 3.
</margin>
There is another reason, because as has already been said, they were impenitent, proclaiming their sin and not hiding it. For this reason, even to this day, a reason is given by God the Judge for why those who "rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the most wicked things" are condemned: *Because,* He says, *they have proclaimed their sin like Sodom, and they have not hidden it.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 3:9</note> For the impenitent are thus a third part of men

### On Revelation Chapter 8

...under the name of the **sea**, the nations are signified here, just as it says in the psalm: *And the mountains shall be moved into the heart of the sea.* <note>original: "Et transferentur montes in cor maris." Rupert cites Psalm 46:2 (Vulgate 45:3).</note> <margin>The sea signifies nations. Psalm 45. Job 9.</margin> For it is the same as if it were said: that the apostles shall pass from the Jews into the midst of the nations. Likewise, by the name of **ships**, the transitory life of men is designated, just as in the book of Job: *My days,* he says, *have passed away like ships carrying fruit.* <note>original: "Dies mei... sicut naues poma portantes." Rupert cites Job 9:26.</note> And so here, by the **third part of the sea** or of the ships (just as previously with the third part of the earth and the trees), the third part of mankind is rightly understood: namely, the descendants of **Ham** <note>Ham was one of the three sons of Noah. In medieval biblical interpretation, the world’s population was often divided into three parts based on Noah's sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.</note>. <margin>Egyptians from the lineage of Ham. Genesis 10.</margin> For the Egyptians arose from Mizraim, one of the descendants of Ham, for it is written: *The sons of Ham, however, were Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan,* and so on. But Mizraim fathered Ludim, and Ananim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim, and Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom the Philistines and Caphtorim came forth. The ancients record that the Egyptians also (as has been said) arose from this Mizraim. The Psalmist also asserts that his father Ham was the father of the Egyptians when he says: *And he struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstfruits of all their labor in the tabernacles of Ham,* <margin>Psalm 77 and 104. Impenitent Egyptians.</margin> that is, where the sons of Ham, sons of Noah, dwell. 

Nevertheless, there was another reason why the Egyptians constituted the **third part**: namely, because they were so **impenitent** <note>The "impenitent" are those who refuse to repent or change their ways despite divine warnings.</note> that even when signs and wonders were multiplied before them, they were hardened even further. For they hated the children of Israel and envied them; and therefore (as is typical of those who hate and envy), the more signs they saw performed for the Israelites—which were for their glory—the harder the Egyptians became, their hatred growing with every sign. Foreseeing this, the Lord himself said to Moses: *I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.* This is as if He were saying: I will indeed perform signs before him, but these will serve no purpose other than to make the envy of the hater grow and the hatred of the envious increase. They were therefore impenitent; and since (as stated above) there are three classes of men—some being **just**, others **penitent**, and others **impenitent**—these Egyptians belonged to the third part because they were among the impenitent.

->B<-

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the 'third part' of the sea in Revelation as the Egyptians and the descendants of Ham, categorizing them as the 'impenitent' portion of humanity who hardened their hearts against God's signs.</summary>

The burning star is the wrath of God.

**A great star burning like a torch.** This means a great wrath of God fell from heaven upon those nations. This wrath of God, I say, is a "star" to us, but a "torch" to them. To us, the wrath of God shines and provides knowledge of that same God; but to them, it is like a torch that consumed them, so that they burned in their own fury. First, the **just**, which were the children of Israel because of their worship of the one God. Second, the **penitent**, such as the house of Rahab the prostitute, who welcomed the messengers of the children of Israel. ...from there (it says) all the inhabitants of the land languished: but they were not, like her and her house, converted to repentance. <note>Rupert is contrasting the Canaanites who "languished" in fear with Rahab the harlot and her household, who were saved because they turned to God.</note>

<margin>The nature of wormwood</margin>
**And the name** (it says) **of the star is called Wormwood.** <note>original: "absynthium"</note> Wormwood is the Greek name for a herb that is very bitter in taste but sweet in scent, offering a healthy balance to the body; its crushed leaves, by their juice, induce vomiting, and it is proven most useful for removing pains or bruises from the body. To this herb, the wrath or judgment of God is rightly compared and called by its name—that judgment which came upon those nations so that it might remove them from the land. It was as if bad "humors" <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids; an excess of "bad humors" caused disease, which vomiting was thought to cure.</note> were cast out, so that the land's breast might be relieved and set free. For God Himself speaks of them in this way in <margin>Leviticus 18 and 20.</margin> the books of Leviticus: *The inhabitants of the land who were before you committed all these abominations and defiled it. Beware, therefore, lest it vomit you out also when you do the same, just as it vomited out the nation that was before you.* Rightly, therefore (as has been said), that falling star—that is, the judgment of God coming upon those nations—is called Wormwood, which produced such a necessary "vomiting" for that land.

**And a third of the waters became wormwood, and many people died because they were made bitter.**

<margin>The Canaanites became wormwood to the children of Israel. Exodus 23 and 33; Deuteronomy 7.</margin>
The "third part" became wormwood; that is, the cohabitation of those same nations was shown to be most bitter and exceedingly destructive to the children of Israel. Many of the Israelites died "of the waters"—that is, because of those nations—because they were made bitter. This is exactly what God Himself had foretold when warning Israel through Moses: *Beware that you never make alliances with the inhabitants of that land, who would be your ruin. Do not enter into a covenant with the people of those regions, lest when they have prostituted themselves to their gods and adored their idols, someone invites you to eat of what has been sacrificed,* and so on. For they did not listen to the Lord’s prohibition, but many "drank the bitter waters" and died; that is, they mingled among the nations and learned their works, and served their carvings <note>Rupert uses "sculptilibus" to refer to engraved or carved idols.</note>, and it became a stumbling block <term>scandalum|a trap or cause for spiritual falling</term> for them.

<summary>Rupert explains the "Wormwood" star as God's judgment purging the Canaanites from the Promised Land like a medicinal emetic, while warning that the remaining influence of these nations became a "bitter water" that led the Israelites into idolatry and death.</summary>

> **And the fourth angel sounded his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third part of them was darkened, and the day did not shine for a third part of it, and likewise for the night.**

<margin>The sons of Shem and Abraham are compared to the sun, moon, and stars.</margin>
The hand of the striker has been raised from the "third part" of the earth, sea, and rivers, toward the sun, moon, and stars. And so, a third part of them was struck. By this "third part," we mean—as has already been said many times—that the focus moves from the lineage of Ham <note>In medieval exegesis, the descendants of Noah's son Ham were often associated with earthly, sinful, or pagan nations.</note> (that is, the third part of men or nations who love the earth, make themselves bitter, and always flow into vices and sins) to the lineage of Shem itself: to the very seed of Abraham and the stock of Jacob. For just as those who do not seek God and do not look up to heaven are, for this very reason, called "earth," "sea," and "rivers," so conversely the seed or sons of Abraham are the "sun," the "moon," and the "stars." They are the "sun" because of Christ, the true sun, the singular "seed" promised to Abraham. They are the "moon" because they constitute the Church. They are the "stars" because of the diverse grace of heavenly light which each individual possesses. Moses, looking forward to this, said: *And you are today as numerous as the stars of heaven.*

<margin>Deut. 1</margin>
For he knew, and had written, that God said to Abraham: *Look up at the heavens and count the stars if you can*; and he immediately added: *So shall your seed be.*

<margin>Gen. 15</margin>
Furthermore, to prove that under the names of the sun, moon, and stars, that nation—or rather the fathers, mothers, and individual children of that nation—should rightly be understood, this testimony alone is sufficient:

<margin>Gen. 37</margin>
*I saw,* said Joseph, *as it were the sun and the moon and eleven stars bowing down to me.* When he had related this to his father, Jacob replied: *What does this dream that you saw mean? Shall I and your mother and your brothers actually come to bow down to the ground before you?*

<margin>The fourth trumpet sounds against the murmuring children of Israel in the desert.</margin>
Therefore, **the fourth angel sounded his trumpet**; that is, the "murmuring" <note>original: "murmuratio." This refers to the frequent episodes in the Book of Exodus and Numbers where the Israelites complained against God and Moses.</note> of the children of Israel in the desert, in the presence of the angel who went before them in a pillar of cloud, became so stirred up that it reached the ears of the Lord. Wherefore Moses said: *Come before the Lord, for I have heard your murmuring.* For a long time, that trumpet...

He links this "darkening" to the Israelites' sinful murmuring against God during the Exodus.</summary>

### On Apocalypse Chapter 8

<margin>
For the murmurers, neither the true sun nor the night shone.
</margin>
...that is, of the holy people: but in truth, the third part, that is, those pertaining to the third part of men or of nations—the portion of Ham and the portion of Canaan. <note>Rupert is using a medieval geographic and genealogical framework where the world is divided among the three sons of Noah: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. He associates the rebellious Israelites with the cursed line of Ham/Canaan.</note> Thus it happened that for the day, this third part did not shine, and likewise for the night. That seed of Abraham, or the Israelite nation—in which respect they were like the sun and moon—was at the same time a bright day and a luminous night. A **bright day**, specifically for the Christ, related to them by blood and promised to the fathers as the eternal sun. A **luminous night**, for the favorable outcome of temporal matters, the promised possession of the land of Canaan, and the earthly kingdom illustrated by many of God’s miraculous signs. But those faithless murmurers, whoever in their pride disparaged God, were called by the mouth of God "the worst multitude." For example, when He said: *How long does this worst multitude murmur against me?* <note>original: "Vsquequo multitudo hæc pessima murmurat contra me?" — referencing Numbers 14:27.</note> They deserved to see neither Christ the sun in the life to come, nor the temporal inheritance of the fathers in the present life. Therefore, that part of the day and night alike, which was thought to belong to the day and the luminous night, when instead it pertained (as was said) to that third part in which Canaan was counted, did not shine and was not made bright, but left a dark memory behind it.

> And I saw, and I heard the voice of a single eagle flying through the midst of heaven, saying with a great voice: "Woe, woe, woe to the inhabitants of the earth, because of the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound the trumpet." <note>This is Revelation 8:13. While many modern translations say "angel," the Latin Vulgate used by Rupert reads "aquila" (eagle).</note>

<margin>
The flying eagle is Holy Scripture.
</margin>
This eagle, flying and announcing, is **Holy Scripture**. It should be noted that no eagle announced the preceding four strikes <note>Rupert refers to the judgments of the first four trumpets just described.</note>, because, clearly, for the Sodomites who were to be destroyed by heavenly fire or sulfurous rain, for Pharaoh and the Egyptians who were to perish in the Red Sea, and for the Amorites who were to be punished once their iniquities were complete and were to be "vomited out" from their land, no scripture and no written law threatened or foretold it. They were judged and condemned only by the **natural law** <note>The "natural law" refers to the moral code believed to be inherent in all humans by nature, even without written revelation like the Ten Commandments.</note>. 

<margin>
The vengeance against the murmurers was not foretold in the scriptures.
</margin>
Similarly, the murmuring children of Israel, whose bodies were laid low in the desert—they had not heard the penalty for their murmuring and rebellion that they were about to suffer through a foretelling scripture or by the indication of scripture; indeed, they began to murmur even before...

...before the scripture was established or the law was written—at least before the first tablets of the ten commandments were written by the finger of God, which were themselves made before the written law—woe hung over that people. <margin>Exodus 32</margin> For example: when the Lord spoke regarding the guilt of the calf which Aaron made: *I see that this people is stiff-necked; let me alone, that my fury may burn against them and I may destroy them.* <note>original: "Cerno quod populus iste duræ ceruicis sit..." Rupert refers to the Golden Calf incident where Moses intercedes for Israel.</note> And when He was not "let alone," because Moses stood in the breach—that is, in great humility of mind in His sight—He said at last: *But in the day of vengeance I will visit even this sin of theirs.* <margin>In the same place</margin> The law, I say, had not yet been written or certainly not yet recited, and for that reason the "flying eagle" is not described here as having foretold that specific woe. The three woes that <margin>The three final woes are foretold in the scriptures. Psalm 105</margin> remain were foretold by Holy Scripture. The **first**, namely, is that which the children of Israel suffered when, because of their sins, they were handed over by the Lord into the hands of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them, and their enemies troubled them, and they were humbled under their hands. The **second** is what they endured when they were led into captivity and miserably sustained the overbearing strength of the **four kingdoms**—namely the Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman—on account of their sins. <margin>Daniel 7</margin> Of these, the fourth—namely the Roman Empire—was a *terrible and wonderful beast, exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth,* which devoured them and broke them in pieces, and stamped the rest with its feet. <note>Rupert is quoting Daniel 7:7, a passage traditionally interpreted by medieval scholars as a prophecy of the four great world empires leading up to the end of the world.</note> The **third** will be the woe of the final judgment, when those to whom the law was written, and all the nations, will receive what they deserve; <margin>Romans 2</margin> because, clearly, *whoever has sinned without the law will perish without the law, and whoever has sinned under the law will be judged by the law.* <note>original: "quicunque sine lege peccauerunt, sine lege peribunt..." — quoting Romans 2:12.</note> These three things, I say, God willed to announce through His scripture before they happened, and therefore the "woe" is rightly proclaimed three times by the eagle here, concerning the remaining voices of the three angels who were about to sound their trumpets. And for whom or what kind of people is the woe? "For those dwelling on the earth," he says—that is, for those whom the earth drags down and earthly affection holds back so that they do not look upward at all. And Holy Scripture is rightly compared to a flying eagle—to an eagle, I say, flying through the midst of heaven—because...

<margin>Chapter IX.</margin>
*And the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, and I saw a star had fallen from heaven to earth, and the key to the shaft of the abyss was given to him, and he opened the shaft of the abyss,* etc. up until *one woe <margin>Afflictions of the children of Israel in the time of the Judges. Judges 3 & 4.</margin> has passed.* This first woe—great and long-lasting—repeats many great things briefly and marvelously: the mocking evils of the various enslavements of Abraham’s children. Specifically, that after the death of Joshua they sinned against the Lord, serving Baalim and Ashtaroth <note>These were local Canaanite deities; their worship represented a betrayal of the covenant with God.</note>, and because of this He handed them over into the hands of Chusan-Rishathaim <note>original: "Chusanrataim."</note>, king of Mesopotamia. # On Revelation Chapter 9 [page] 244

...the locusts grew to the size of horses, or what is more marvelous, these men were so diminished that, in comparison to them, the locusts seemed to have the size of horses. Undoubtedly, this latter explanation is what occurred by the judgment of God—not by a physical shrinking or lessening of their bodies, 

<margin>
The children of Israel became like locusts before their enemies.
</margin>

but by a failure of their souls. For those who, because of a contemptible life, were as locusts in the eyes of the Lord, remained as locusts—namely, the wanton peoples of the Canaanites. However, those who ought to have been men were deservedly diminished, and in a certain sense were made "locusts of locusts," <note>original: "locustæ locustarum" — a Hebrew-style superlative suggesting they were even smaller or weaker than the insects themselves.</note> fearing those who should have been in fear of them. For the Just Judge was paying them back in kind, 

<margin>
Numbers 13 and 14
</margin>

because they were the children of fathers who were detractors and murmurers. They followed the sins of those who had spoken ill of that same land, saying: "The people we looked upon are of tall stature. There we saw certain monsters of the sons of Anak <note>Anak was a forefather of a race of giants mentioned in the Old Testament; the scouts sent by Moses claimed they felt like grasshoppers next to them.</note> from the race of giants, compared to whom we seemed like locusts." Therefore, as if in pursuit of them, God said at that time: "As you have spoken in my hearing, so I will do to you: your carcasses shall lie in this wilderness." <note>A paraphrase of Numbers 14:28-29.</note> In a similar way, this flying eagle, pronouncing "Woe," <note>The eagle from Revelation 8:13 who announces the three final woes.</note> speaks to their descendants and says: "As you have spoken, so shall it be done to you. Those locusts, in comparison to you, shall be like horses; you, compared to them, shall seem like locusts." Likewise: "As you have spoken—'Would that we were dead, would that we might perish'—so shall it be done to you. You shall seek death, and it shall not come; you shall desire to die, and death shall flee from you." Nor is it without significance that when he had said "like horses," he added, **prepared for battle**. This expresses the great confidence of those locusts and the great force of their hostile spirits, so that they come forward to battle and seek with arms those whom they previously fled from. Histories plainly report that this came to pass.

**And upon their heads as it were crowns like gold.**
The kings or princes of those nations, who are rightly understood to be the "heads," were like crowned victors—yet not truly crowned. This is because they did not conquer by their own virtue, but rather these men [the Israelites] were conquered on account of their own sins. They themselves...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 5

<margin>
Crowns not truly of gold, but like gold.
Judges 3
</margin>

The crowns are called not truly golden, but "like gold," <note>original: "similes auro"</note> because surely whatever they boasted regarding victory—as if they were wise and strong—was false. For the "gold" of their prevailing was not from their own virtue, but from the examination of divine providence, by which Israel was tested for their own self-knowledge. For Scripture also shows this: *These are the nations which the Lord left, that he might instruct Israel by them, and all those who had not known the wars of the Canaanites, and afterwards their children might learn to fight with enemies and have the practice of warring.* <note>Quoting Judges 3:1–2. Rupert argues that the "golden" success of Israel's enemies was a tool used by God to train the Israelites.</note>

## And their faces were like the faces of men. And they had hair like the hair of women, and their teeth were like the teeth of lions, and they had breastplates like iron breastplates.

<margin>
What the hair of women, the teeth of lions, and the breastplates signify.
</margin>

All these things can be understood as the diminishing of the children of Israel, by exalting the supposed greatness of those "locusts," so that (as has already been said) the Israelites themselves, compared to them, seemed like locusts. Specifically, however, in the human face we see the simulation of reason; in the hair of women, loose and effeminate morals; in the teeth of lions—which are accustomed both to tear apart and to carry a natural stench—we see a ferocity of mind. In the iron breastplates, all military armor is correctly understood, which was so great among them that they even abounded in scythed chariots. <note>original: "falcatis curribus" — ancient war chariots equipped with curved blades on the wheels to mow down infantry.</note>

<margin>
Judges 4
</margin>

For this is also written of the king of Canaan: that he had nine hundred scythed chariots, and for twenty years he vehemently oppressed them. <note>Refers to King Jabin and his general Sisera, described in Judges 4:3.</note>

## And the sound of their wings was like the sound of many horses rushing into battle.

<margin>
The sound of wings: the exaltation of pride.
1 Kings 4
</margin>

The "sound of the wings" represents the exaltation of the pride of such locusts, a sound we have indeed heard. For example: in the first book of Kings <note>original: "primo libro Regum" — In the Vulgate, this refers to what is now called 1 Samuel.</note> when the enemies said to themselves: *Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you serve the Hebrews, as they have served you: take courage and fight.* <note>Quoting 1 Samuel 4:9.</note> Truly, to say this—"Take courage and fight"—was a sound like that of many horses rushing into battle.

## And they had tails like scorpions, and stings...

Now for the third time those locusts—namely, the enemies of Israel—are shown to be like **scorpions**: that is, appearing harmless in their faces, but preserving poisons in their hind parts. First, where it is written (which we mentioned above) that the children of Moab called them to their sacrifices. While this sounds like modern pest control, in a medieval context it means "The Destroyer" or one who drives others beyond the boundaries.</note>. This angel of the abyss is clearly the opposite of the "Angel of Great Counsel" <note>A traditional title for Christ derived from the Greek version of Isaiah 9:6.</note>; a king contrary to a king, the king of the children of pride against or opposite the king of the children of wisdom. For both the writing of this name and the writing of that other name—recorded in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—proclaims that one as evil and this one as good, to be recognized by all nations.

<margin>
John 19
</margin>
For we know it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: "Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews." That name is "Jesus" in Hebrew, "Soter" <note>original: "σωτηρ"</note> in Greek, and "Savior" <note>original: "Saluator"</note> in Latin. This one, I think—as we now have it before us—is "Abaddon" in Hebrew, "Apollyon" <note>original: "απολλυων"</note> in Greek, and "Exterminator" in Latin. I say this "exterminator" had to be recognized by those by whom that Savior was recognized: so that while it is known how novel this destroyer is, it may be better known how truly and rightly He who saves us from him is called the Savior.

<margin>
This Exterminator was prefigured in the smiter of Egypt, Exodus 12.
</margin>
Furthermore, divine authority previously explored the name of the "exterminator" in the Old Scripture when it says: "For the Lord will pass through striking the Egyptians." And when He sees the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, He will pass over the door, and will not allow the smiter <note>original: "percussorem."</note> to enter your houses and harm you. One and the same is the angel king of the abyss, the exterminator or smiter; and just as there he was not permitted to harm anyone except in the houses that did not have the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, so here he has a command with his locusts to torment only those men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads.

The first woe has passed, and behold, two more woes are coming. ...to the angel who had the trumpet: "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates."

<margin>
Isaiah 45.
The golden altar is Christ.
</margin>
This voice which he heard, commanding the four angels to be released, was a permission and a judgment of "evil"—that is, the act of a just Creator bringing affliction upon men because of their sins, exactly as it says in Isaiah: *I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil.* <note>original: "Ego dñs faciẽs pacẽ & creans malum." In this context, "evil" refers to calamity or disaster sent as punishment, rather than moral wickedness.</note> Furthermore, this golden altar is the very one we encountered above, where it was written that an angel came and stood before the altar, having a golden censer in his hand, and so on. We have already stated previously that this altar represents the faith of Christ, founded in the hearts of the holy fathers 

<margin>
Genesis 22.
The horns of the altar are the patriarchs and prophets, etc.
Psalm 117.
</margin>
from the moment God first spoke to Abraham, saying: *In your seed all nations shall be blessed.* What, therefore, are the "horns of the altar," if not the patriarchs, prophets, kings, and leaders or judges of that people? They were the princes of that same faith, which they both sang of in their writings and prefigured through their mystical deeds. Indeed, there is one "greatest horn" of this altar, of which the Psalm says: *Appoint a solemn day in thick crowds, even to the horn of the altar.* <note>original: "Cõstituite... diẽ solennẽ in cõdensis usque ad cornu altaris." Nevertheless, there are as many horns of the altar

<margin>
Psalm 47.
The four angels are the four principal kingdoms.
</margin>
as there are participants in that same Christ, of whom the Psalm says elsewhere: *God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.* Why was a voice heard from such horns of the altar saying, "release the four angels"? It was spoken in a prophetic manner, by way of concession. For those who possessed foresight predicted it, and those consenting to divine justice permitted it: namely, that the four kingdoms <note>Rupert refers here to the traditional interpretation of the four world empires—Babylonian, Persian, Greek, and Roman—which appear in the visions of the prophet Daniel.</note> which were to rise up should be "released" from the earth. That is, they were no longer to be restrained by any obstacles from the holy angels—and especially not by Michael the prince <note>A reference to Daniel 10:21 and 12:1, where Michael is described as the angelic protector of the Jewish people.</note>—from taking the Jewish people (of whom he was the prince) into captivity, killing them, reducing them to slavery, and dispersing them among all nations. For example: Jeremiah, considering within himself the sins of the people who persecuted the prophets and killed many of 

<margin>

</margin>
them, and who were even destined to kill Christ himself, said: *And you, O Lord of hosts, prover of the just, who sees their reins and hearts...* <note>original: "renes eorũ," literally "their kidneys." But after a long time, the prophet himself, as a type <term>typus: a person or event in the Old Testament that foreshadows a future spiritual reality</term> of God, frees the people from captivity. Nevertheless, even after their return, they did not follow God's commands, but followed foreign gods, and in the end even laid hands upon the Son of God. Thus they wasted away in eternal perdition, just as that loincloth rotted and was fit for no use. These things from the prophet Jeremiah are brought up in this place so that it might not be doubtful or unknown how, or in what way, those angels were bound at the great river Euphrates. Namely, as long as that loincloth clung to God’s loins, those angels were held bound by that same loincloth or belt. But when, at the Lord's command, Jeremiah hid it in the Euphrates, they were released. This is to say: as long as the people of Israel or Judah kept the law of their God, those pagan kingdoms did not tear them apart, nor did the Assyrians or Chaldeans take them captive. <margin>The mystery of numbers.</margin>
One may understand something entirely different by the fact that he said it thus: "twenty times a thousand, ten thousand times," than if he had said, "ten thousand times twenty thousand." So that what we now wish to say may become clearer and more intelligible, let us first say a few things about the nature of multiplied numbers.
<margin>Abacists, calculators of numbers on the abacus.</margin>
Unity—that is, the character <term>character<gloss>The symbol or digit used in calculation.</gloss></term> which (as the <term>Abacists<gloss>Medieval mathematicians who performed complex calculations using an abacus or counting board.</gloss></term> know best) in the first "limit" <note>Rupert is describing the columns or "limits" on a medieval abacus. The first limit represents ones, the second tens, and so on.</note>, which is called the singular, signifies "one," but when moved across to the fifth limit, it designates "ten thousand." Likewise, the <term>binary<gloss>The character or digit for the number 2.</gloss></term>—that is, the character which in the aforementioned singular limit signifies "two"—when moved to the same fifth limit, which is called the <term>milenus nuleuus<gloss>Rupert's terminology for the position of the ten-thousands on the abacus board.</gloss></term>, designates "twenty thousand." There are, therefore, in one and the same tenth limit both the unity to be multiplied and the binary as the multiplier; namely, the unity as ten thousand, and the binary likewise...

# On Chapter 9 of the Apocalypse
**page 255**

<margin>The mystery of why the number two multiplies the power here</margin>
...twenty thousand times ten thousand. <note>This completes the phrase from the previous page, translating the Latin *vicies millenus dena milia*.</note> We believe there is a significant mystery hidden in this: that in this specific quantity of the cavalry army, unity and the binary <term>binary; the number two, which Rupert often associates with division or impurity</term> lie within one and the same boundary. It is not that unity multiplies the binary in such a way that it would be said, "ten thousand times twenty thousand have I heard the number of them," but on the contrary, the binary multiplies unity, saying: *and twice ten thousand times ten thousand I heard the number of them.*

<margin>Genesis 7. Unity designates the Hebrews, the Binary designates the Gentiles.</margin>
For what does the "unity of ten thousand" signify, if not the Hebrew nation, the worshipper of the one God? Furthermore, what does the "binary of ten thousand" signify? In Holy Scripture, this number is sometimes associated with ill repute, as in that passage regarding the Great Flood: *of the unclean animals, indeed, they shall enter the ark two by two.* <note>original: "de immundis vero bina & bina ingredientur in arcam." From Genesis 7:2.</note>

Therefore, unity lies in the same boundary as the binary because, evidently, the Israelite nation—which ought to have been the people of the one God—was placed in the land of the unclean Gentiles and those who commit abominations. In that place, the Israelite nation surely did not convert the unclean and idolatrous nations to a clean life and the worship of the one God; but on the contrary, the unclean and idolatrous nations perverted that nation toward uncleanness and abominations.

<margin>1 Ezra 9</margin>

From Ezra 9:6, 13-14.</note>

<margin>The Jews as idolaters under the Greeks.</margin>
Furthermore, when they were under the kingdom of the Greeks, they did not convert the Greeks to the worship of the true and one God; on the contrary, the Greeks perverted them into laws opposed to the true God.

<margin>1 Maccabees 2</margin>
For this is what Mattathias, along with his sons, lamented with torn clothes in the book of Maccabees, saying: *Woe to me! Why was I born to see the destruction of my people, and the destruction of the holy city, and to sit there while it is given into the hands of enemies?* <note>original: "Væ mihi, vt quid natus sum videre contritionem populi mei..." From 1 Maccabees 2:7. Mattathias was the priest who sparked the Maccabean Revolt against Greek-Syrian oppression.</note>

### On Revelation, Chapter 8
**page 257**

...says, **breastplates of fire, and of hyacinth, and of sulfur**. For the malignant spirits, who preside over the hearts of these horsemen, are most closely clothed in their own punishments; and just as they transform those whom they possess, so they appear in this present vision. For what kind of people do they make them, if not **greedy, proud, and lustful**? 

Indeed, what is meant by **fire** but **greed**? <note>original: "cupiditas"</note> What is meant by **hyacinth**—which is a color said to imitate the appearance of the sky—but **pride**? <note>In medieval thought, the blue of the hyacinth stone represented the heavens; here, it symbolizes the "heavenly" ambitions of the proud who seek to exalt themselves.</note> What do we understand by **stinking sulfur** but **lust**, <note>original: "libidinem"</note> and especially that which is against nature? Such, indeed, were the nations of those kingdoms: burning with greed, swelling with pride, and stinking with lust. 

<margin>What fire, smoke, and sulfur signify.</margin> 
Rightly, therefore, after he spoke of the riders, he added almost the same things regarding the horses: **and from their mouths**, he says, **shall come fire, and smoke, and sulfur**. <margin>Psalm 36</margin>

For such men are like the malignant spirits that sit upon and inhabit them, though demons have less in this regard—that is, they are lustful only in will and not in act, since they are without flesh. And who could be ignorant that those enemies of the Lord were greedy, proud, and lustful?

Furthermore, regarding their **smoking pride**, it is sufficient proof that their kings, though mortal men, wished to be held as gods.

# On Chapter 9 of the Apocalypse

...men, by the fire, and the smoke, and the sulfur, which proceeded from their mouths.

<margin>The Three Plagues: Psalm 101; Genesis 3.</margin>
“By these three plagues,” that is, on account of these three plagues—just as it says in the Psalm: *By the voice of my groaning, my bone has cleaved to my flesh.* <note>original: "A voce gemitus mei adhæfit os meum carni meæ" — Psalm 102:5 (Psalm 101 in the Vulgate).</note> This is understood as being on account of the voice of the devil saying, *Eat, and you shall be as gods,* <note>original: "Comedite & eritis ficut dij" — Genesis 3:5.</note> which was the source and beginning of my groaning; I wasted away and was made mortal. And on account of that voice being believed, just as in a wasting body the bone cleaves to the flesh, so in me <term>rationality</term> <note>the higher, reasoning part of the soul</note> consents to <term>sensuality</term> <note>the lower, physical desires</note>. Likewise: *Because I ate ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping, before the face of your wrath and indignation,* <note>Psalm 102:9-10</note> that is, on account of the face or the presence of your wrathful indignation. And so, “by these three plagues,” that is, on account of these three plagues, a third part of men was killed by the fire, smoke, and sulfur. This means that on account of this fire, smoke, and sulfur—which we have already said were the sins of those nations or kingdoms—namely, **concupiscence** <note>intense worldly desire or greed</note>, **pride**, and **Sodomitic lust**.

<margin>The Jews did the same things as the Gentiles.</margin>
For they themselves did the same things, and those who were handed over to punishment were their equals in guilt. It is more than enough for us to prove this with the testimonies of the Scriptures, just as the Apostle did when, after recounting the crimes of the Gentiles, he turned to the Jew who was blaming and judging those from among the Gentiles who had believed. He says to him: <margin>Romans 2.</margin> *Wherefore you are inexcusable, O man, whoever you are who judges. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself; for you do the same things that you judge.* <note>Romans 2:1</note> Therefore, this part of men—specifically the Hebrew nation—was justly killed, because it had been wounded before God by these three plagues of sin. For this reason, it is called a “third part of men,” as it is reckoned in the portion of **Ham** <note>original: "Cham"</note>, who was one of the three sons of Noah; he was a sinner and deserved to be cursed. These plagues are said to “proceed from the mouth of the horses” because it was obviously through the conversation and fellowship with the Gentiles that the Jews contracted the influence to do such things.

<margin>2 Maccabees 4: The crimes of Jason the Jew.</margin>
For example: **Jason**, the brother of **Onias** (as we read in the Book of Maccabees), by favoring the wicked commands of **Antiochus**, overthrew the legal...

Psalm 23. <note>In the medieval Latin Bible (the Vulgate), this is Psalm 23; in modern English Bibles, it is Psalm 24:8: "Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty."</note>

...other angel, <note>The text begins mid-word with "lus," completing "angelus" (angel) from the previous page.</note> who could this be but the "Angel of Great Counsel," <note>original: "angelus magni consilii" — a title for the Messiah from the Septuagint version of Isaiah 9:6.</note> the angel of God’s covenant, of whom much has been and will be said? Is he not truly "another," and far different from all other angels? The author calls this angel "mighty," for he is truly strong; indeed, he is the Prince of Strength. And he who was God was made man; and he who was the Word in the beginning was made flesh, not by the divinity being changed into flesh, but by the flesh being assumed into God.

<margin>
Clothed in a cloud.
</margin>
This is what he means by **clothed in a cloud**. For both here and in many mystical passages of the Scriptures, the "cloud" signifies his human flesh. This is a beautiful and fitting comparison: for just as the sun is covered and hidden by a cloud, and yet is known to be present even when its full circle is not visible, while it still brings daylight to the entire world; so too in that flesh, God lay hidden and yet could be recognized as present. He contained his divinity (as it always was) in an invisible state, and yet he illuminated the whole world through his visible works.

A rainbow on his head.
Genesis 9.
</margin>
*And a rainbow*, he says, *was on his head.* The rainbow—the celestial arc—designates the mercy of this same Mighty One. It is the sign, or given as the sign, of propitiation <note><term>propitiation</term>: an act that makes God favorable or merciful toward people; an atonement for sin.</note>, as the Lord said to Noah: *Never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood*, and further: *This is the sign of the covenant between me and you. I will set my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign between me and the earth.* Therefore, the rainbow is on his head, meaning that mercy is the highest and primary intention of his coming. For this reason, he came thus "clothed in the cloud of flesh," so that he might prepare us and make us the kind of people who can stand on that Day of Judgment when the final trumpet sounds. This preparation consists of the remission of sins...

**And his feet, he says, were as a pillar of fire.**

### On Chapter 10 of Revelation

Their voices were certainly like thunders before, because just as thunder sounds both terribly and yet gives no articulate or intelligible sound, so the voices of the Law and the Prophets sounded both terribly and yet what was signified by those same voices, the common people...

### On Chapter 10 of the Apocalypse

<margin>The mysteries of the Scriptures were not unknown to the apostles.</margin>
<margin>Luke, final chapter.</margin>
<margin>John 16.</margin>
<margin>Why the apostles did not explain the scriptures.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 5.</margin>
"I," he said, "was about to write." <note>original: "Ego, inquit scripturus eram." This refers to Revelation 10:4, where John is told by a voice from heaven to "Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not."</note> What does it mean to "write those things which the seven thunders spoke," if not to explain all the mysteries of the Scriptures through the use of pen and ink? This he did not do, nor did the other apostles. Why? Was it because they did not know or understand them? Far from it. On the contrary, they were the very "friends" from whom nothing ought to be hidden, just as the Lord himself said: *I no longer call you servants, but my friends, because everything I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.* <note>John 15:15</note> He said "I have made known to you" as a way of saying "I will make known," because clearly, when he was saying this, what he was soon to do was as certain as if he had already done it. For soon, by rising again, he was to open their senses so that they might understand the Scriptures, giving them the **Spirit of Truth**, who would teach them all truth—even though they had been, until that point, unlettered and common men <term>idiotæ</term>. <note>The word "idiotæ" here follows the Latin Vulgate's description of the apostles in Acts 4:13, meaning "ordinary" or "untrained" rather than the modern derogatory sense.</note>

Why then did they not write? Was it because they did not want to, or did they shrink away because they lacked the patience for the labor? Certainly not. For John says, "I was about to write," which means "I wanted to write." What, then, stood in the way, if not the command or the rule of holy discretion? For all things could not be fulfilled at once or at the same time because of the slowness of men, who were then still unrefined and too weak to hear wisdom of that kind. 

This is why the apostle Paul, after saying: *And being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him, called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek,* <note>Hebrews 5:9-10</note> immediately added: *Of whom we have much to say, and hard to be explained in speaking, because you have become weak to hear.* <note>Hebrews 5:11</note> *For whereas for the time you ought to be teachers, you have need to be taught again what are the basic elements of the words of God; and you have become such as have need of milk, and not of solid food,* etc. <note>Hebrews 5:12</note> Therefore, the reason that John and the other apostles did not write the things spoken by those "thunders" was not a lack of ability or will, but rather the weakness of the understanding of those who would then be hearing or reading. Otherwise, the timing would have been inappropriate for such a purpose—just as the same apostle [Paul] occasionally provided a small taste of a subject according to the time and the matter. # Commentary of Rupert, Book VI

...in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the mystery of God will be finished, just as he announced <note>original: "euangelizauit"; literally "evangelized" or brought the good news</note> through his servants the prophets. You have put all things under his feet.* <note>Psalm 8:5-6</note> Truly, this very lifting of the hand—that is, the magnificence or omnipotence of so great an angel—began from that exaltation

# On Chapter 11 of the Apocalypse, page 281

...like a rod. "Therefore, it is necessary for you," he says, "to prophesy again," as if he were saying: "I have known for a long time that you wish to be released from the body, desiring with your whole heart to see my face; my scent has stirred the desires of eternity within you, and because of this, you have asked me many times that you might come to me. I told you as often as you asked, and now I say to you: wait, so that you may free the people who will believe in me. For this reason, it is necessary for you to wait; it is necessary for you to prophesy again to the peoples, and nations, and tongues, and many kings." This means that the peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings should read and hear your words with the highest reverence. 

For behold, while you are in exile, in the meantime Cerinthus <note>Cerinthus (c. 100 AD) was an early Gnostic teacher who was a contemporary of John the Apostle; tradition says John fled a bathhouse because Cerinthus was inside.</note> is acting with insanity, Marcion <note>Marcion of Sinope (c. 85–160 AD) was a famous heretic who rejected the Old Testament and the God of the Jews, believing the God of Jesus was a different, superior deity.</note> rages, Ebion <note>Ebion represents the Ebionites, a group of Jewish Christians who believed Jesus was the natural son of Mary and Joseph and not the pre-existent Son of God.</note> begins his blasphemy, and other "antichrists" <note>original: *antichristi*</note> rave against the word of faith—against the majesty and ancient divinity of the Son of God. They say that he did not exist before Mary, and that he is such a "recent god" that he only began to exist from her. 

Furthermore, it is destined to happen that Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) was a priest in Alexandria whose teachings led to the Council of Nicaea. He taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> will come, a stubborn henchman of the devil, who will speak to and persuade the peoples, nations, and many kings that this same Son of God is a creature, that he began to exist in time, and that "there was a time when the Son was not." <note>original: *fuerit tempus quando idem filius non fuerit*. This is the famous slogan of the Arian heresy.</note> Because of these men, it is necessary for you to prophesy again and to provide for the peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings, so that you may free the Christian people—those who will believe in me—from these plagues. How should he prophesy? He says:

<margin>Chapter 11</margin>
> AND there was given to me a reed like unto a rod,
> saying: Rise and measure the temple of God and the
> altar, and those who worship in it. But the court, which
> is outside the temple, cast it out, and do not measure it,
> because it has been given to the nations.

<margin>A reed like a rod.</margin>
A reed like a rod signifies the power of writing <note>original: *facultatem scribendi*</note> joined with the authority of a teacher. For the reed <note>original: *calamus*—a writing tool made from a hollow stalk</note> belongs to writers, but the rod <note>original: *virga*—a staff used for discipline or as a scepter of office</note> belongs to masters. There are, or have been, some to whom a reed was given, but not one "like a rod"—meaning they had the ability to write, but not with that authoritative dignity of a master, such that no member of the Church would be permitted to doubt their opinion or their phrasing. For this...

To first taste that which may more quickly open the door of understanding: among even numbers, some are <term>superfluous</term> <note>Also known as "abundant numbers" in mathematics, where the sum of the factors is greater than the number itself.</note>, others are <term>diminished</term> <note>Also known as "deficient numbers," where the sum of the factors is less than the number itself.</note>, and others are <term>perfect</term>. If these are reduced into one sum, the whole body of the number is found through its own parts—that is, an entire six is restored from them.

A number is called **diminished**, however, when its parts, composed in the same way, are fewer, and they are surpassed by the magnitude of the number to which they belonged. As an example: the **number eight**. For eight has a half part, which is four; it has a fourth part, which is two; and it has an eighth part, which is one. All of these, when reduced into one, total seven, resulting in a sum smaller than the eight was.

Furthermore, they name those **superfluous** whose parts extend themselves beyond what is sufficient. As an example: the **number twelve**. For the parts of this number total a greater sum than twelve itself was. For the half of twelve is six; the third part is four; the fourth part is three; the sixth part is two; and the twelfth part is one. This entire heap overflows into sixteen, a sum certainly greater than twelve.

Now, there is (as both secular and church philosophers say) a great similarity in these to **virtue and vice**. For the **perfect** number bears the likeness of the virtues, while the **diminished** and **superfluous** bear the likeness of the vices. <note>In medieval thought, virtue was seen as a "mean" or balance, while vice was an error of either excess (superfluous) or deficiency (diminished).</note> Undoubtedly, it is from the superfluous ones that these numbers come which this Scripture has presented to us—namely, **forty-two** and

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 6

<page-num>286</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 6</header>

<margin>Even numbers are of three kinds.</margin>
Let us first taste that which may more quickly open the door to understanding. Among even numbers, some are **superfluous** <term>abundant numbers</term>, some are **diminished** <term>deficient numbers</term>, and others are **perfect**. Those are called **perfect** which are equal to their own parts <note>Rupert is referring to "proper divisors"—numbers that divide into a sum without a remainder, excluding the number itself.</note>; they are neither swollen with abundance nor do they suffer from poverty. For example, consider the number **six** <note>original: "senarius"</note>. For six has a half part, which is three; a third part, which is two; and a sixth part, which is one. If these are reduced into a single sum, the number is found to be equal to its parts throughout its whole body; that is, the complete six is restored from them <note>3 + 2 + 1 = 6</note>. Truly, that number is called **diminished** whose parts, when composed in the same way, are fewer, and are surpassed in multitude by the very number of which they were parts; for example, the number **eight** <note>original: "octonarius"</note>. For eight has a half part, which is four; it also has a fourth, which is two; and an eighth, which is one. When all these are reduced into one, they collect to seven, concluding in a smaller sum than the eight was. Furthermore, they name those **superfluous** whose parts extend themselves beyond what is sufficient; for example, the number **twelve** <note>original: "duodenarius"</note>. For the parts of this number collect into a greater sum than the twelve itself was. For the half of twelve is six, the third part is four, the fourth part is three, the sixth part is two, and the twelfth part is one. All this heap overflows into sixteen, which is certainly a greater sum than twelve was <note>6 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 16</note>. Moreover, there is (say the philosophers, both secular and ecclesiastical) a great similarity in these to **virtue and vice**. For the perfect number has a likeness to virtue, while the diminished and the superfluous have a likeness to vices.

<margin>The parts of the number 42.</margin>
Undoubtedly, those numbers which this Scripture has offered to us here—namely **forty-two** and **one thousand two hundred and sixty**—are of the superfluous kind. For this number, forty-two, has a half part, which is twenty-one; a third, which is fourteen; a sixth, which is seven; a seventh, which is six; a fourteenth, which is three; a twenty-first, which is two; and a forty-second, which is one. Indeed, these parts, when reduced into one, collect together a greater sum than the forty-two was. For they make **fifty-four**. Thus, this number...

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 6

<page-num>cclxxxviii</page-num>

<margin>The abundance of iniquity is signified.</margin>
it is the case that the opinion of all philosophers, both secular and ecclesiastical, is the same: that the likeness found in numbers of this kind, which are or are called "superfluous" <term>abundant numbers; numbers whose proper divisors sum to more than the number itself</term>, represents vice rather than virtue. What do we think the author of this Scripture intends when he prefers to say "forty-two months" and "one thousand two hundred sixty days," rather than "a time, times, and half a time" <note>original: "tempus & tempora, & dimidium temporis"; a phrase from Daniel and Revelation often interpreted as three and a half years.</note> or "a year, two years, and half a year"? What, I say, does he intend except to signify—through these "superfluous" numbers—that **abundance of iniquity** which the Lord predicted would come to pass at that time? For He Himself said: *And because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold.* <note>Matthew 24:12</note>

<margin>Matthew 24. Psalm 40.</margin>
But it is also written elsewhere: *I have announced and spoken; they are multiplied beyond number.* <note>Psalm 40:5 (Psalm 39 in the Vulgate). Rupert interprets "beyond number" as referring to those who are technically "extra" or not part of the "elect."</note> The truthful Scripture conveys both: first, that as Christ the Lord announced, those who would be called believers or Christians would be multiplied "beyond number"—with many taking up the empty profession of this name who do not belong to the number of the elect—and second, that in the time of persecution, as iniquity abounds, the charity of many would grow cold. Therefore, both the number of forty-two months (which is quite "superfluous") and the number of one thousand two hundred sixty days (which is "superfluous" to the greatest degree) are presented here to readers. This is so that both the multiplicity of those professing faith—of whom it was said, *I announced and spoke, they are multiplied beyond number*—and the abundance of iniquity—of which it is written, *And because iniquity has abounded, the charity of many will grow cold*—might be signified through a beautiful and venerable symbolism to those who deserve to know the mystery of the kingdom of God. Furthermore, who are these two witnesses, or what do they mean, concerning whom he says:
->**And I will give power to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy.**<- <note>Revelation 11:3</note>

<margin>Who those two witnesses are, who shall prophesy.</margin>
Has this Lord and author of the prophets had, or will He have, no more than two men as witnesses to prophesy? Are not all His witnesses—to say nothing for now of the other confessors—apostles and martyrs? Truly, this utterance in the mouth of the Mighty One is great, very grave, and of immense weight; for though He has so many [witnesses]...

# On Revelation Chapter 11.

...to overwhelm the rule of truth with the storms of heretical wickedness, the judgment of damnation shall come out of their mouth, so that they may anathematize <note>To "anathematize" is to formally excommunicate or pronounce a curse against a person or doctrine, cutting them off from the community of believers.</note> them and deliver them to the eternal destruction of Satan. Why did he prefer to understand it this way: "And if anyone wants to harm them, fire shall come out of their mouth and devour their enemies"? 

<margin>2 Kings 1</margin>
Why, I ask, except because a mystical example of this power preceded in that often-mentioned Elijah? For it is written: "And he"—namely Ahaziah <note>Ahaziah was the King of Israel who turned to the false god Baal-zebub; Rupert uses him here as a precursor to the Antichrist.</note>—"sent to him a captain of fifty and the fifty who were under him." He went up to him while he was sitting on the top of the mountain and said: "Man of God, the king commands that you come down." And Elijah, answering, said to the captain of fifty: "If I am a man of God, let fire descend from heaven and devour you and your fifty." And fire descended from heaven and devoured him and the fifty who were with him. 

<margin>Fire came out of Elijah’s mouth</margin>
He sent another captain of fifty and fifty with him, and likewise fire came out of his mouth—that is, it descended at the command of his mouth—and devoured them. From this it is clear that they spoke with the intention of doing harm when they said: "Man of God, the king commands that you come down." "Man of God, thus says the king: Hurry, come down." Therefore, he said: "Let fire descend from heaven and devour you," and the result followed the word. Surely, just as visible fire then came out of his mouth and devoured his enemies who brought royal commands with pride, so invisible fire shall come out of the mouths of these witnesses—that is, the judgment of damnation—and it will devour those who, flattering impious kings and the head of impious kings, the Antichrist, wish to harm or hurt them. 

Likewise, although he could have said: "These have the power of binding in heaven and on earth," so that no favor or remission of sins comes upon their enemies all the days of their ministry or office (that is, until the end of the age or forever), why did he prefer to say: "These have the power to shut the sky, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy"? Why, I ask, except because the mystery of such rain, and of the power to withhold such rain, shone forth in that same Elijah? 

<margin>The power of Elijah</margin>
For he "prayed with prayer" <note>This phrasing reflects the Hebrew idiom for "praying earnestly," as cited in James 5:17.</note> that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain...

<summary>Rupert explains that the "fire" from the mouths of the Two Witnesses is a spiritual judgment of damnation, paralleling the literal fire Elijah called down upon King Ahaziah's soldiers. He argues that their power to "shut the heavens" also mirrors Elijah's historical drought, representing the withholding of God's grace from the wicked.</summary>

# On Revelation Chapter 11

...they crushed <note>original: "contriuerunt"</note> them, until the Egyptians, struck by the final plague, were rolled with their king into the depths of the sea. There follows:

**And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that ascends from the abyss will make war against them, and will overcome them, and kill them. And their bodies will lie in the streets of the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified.**

"When," he says, "they have finished their testimony." Truly, for each of the faithful witnesses, a pre-defined time and a specific number has been set—namely, how long they are to perform the duty of testifying, or to what measure the heap of their merits must be completed. Those who are still living in the body, journeying as pilgrims away from the Lord, are ignorant of this; 

<margin>2 Corinthians 5</margin>

sometimes in their haste they desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ. In the rush of their desire, panting upward toward God, they do not pay attention to whether they have finished their testimony or not. He, however, knowing and foreseeing what or how much still remains for their progress, delays the fulfillment of their desire. We read of this in the deeds of this very John <note>Rupert refers here to St. John the Apostle, the traditional author of Revelation.</note>: when he asked many times to be allowed to depart from here and come to Christ, he reports that the answer given to him was: "Wait, so that you may deliver the people who will believe in me." Likewise, the impious persecutors, hating the progress of the Word of God and the glory of its testimony, hurry to remove the holy witnesses from the earth. 

<margin>Persecutors are not permitted to kill the witnesses unless their testimony is already finished. Luke 13.</margin>

God, however, preserves them, and He anticipates and frustrates the efforts of those lying in wait—until they finish their testimony. Thus Herod also hurried to kill the "Faithful Witness" <note>A title for Christ from Revelation 1:5.</note> himself, and the Prince of faithful witnesses, Christ, but he was not permitted to do so until Christ finished His testimony. Luke records it this way: Some of the Pharisees approached Him, saying: "Go out, and depart from here, because Herod wants to kill you." And He said to them: "Go and tell that fox: Behold, I cast out demons and I perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am finished." <note>original: "consumor" — meaning to be perfected, completed, or to reach the end of one's course.</note> Nevertheless, it is necessary for me...

<summary>Rupert explains that the martyrdom of the Two Witnesses can only occur once their divinely allotted time of testimony is complete, drawing parallels to the lives of St. John and Jesus.</summary>

What kind of war? Truly, the kind that usually exists between truth and falsehood. For these witnesses against whom he makes, or will make, war, are accustomed to fighting not with a material sword, but only with the word of truth. He will therefore make war against them, meaning he will attack the truth with a forcefully established lie.

### And he will overcome them.

<margin>Luke 5, Matthew 24.</margin>
That is, he will weigh them down almost to the point of victory: just as it is said elsewhere: *And they filled both little boats, so that they were sinking* <note>Rupert draws a parallel to the miraculous catch of fish in Luke 5:7, where the "sinking" represents being overwhelmed by pressure rather than total defeat</note>; it must be understood that they were pressed toward the point of submersion. At that time, therefore, the pious martyr will not perform signs amidst his torments, but that beast will perform lying signs through his prophets, and in this, he will seem superior. What then?

### And he will kill them.

<margin>2 Thessalonians 2.</margin>
He says. Who will kill, if not he who is accustomed to killing? For he has not yet come in his own person—he who is properly called the **Antichrist**, and it is certain that he is to come—but in his spirit, **Nero** <note>The Roman Emperor Nero was often viewed by early and medieval Christians as a precursor or "type" of the Antichrist due to his brutal persecution of the Church.</note> has already come, and others after him, in whom that "son of perdition" (who is to be revealed in his own time) has already worked the ministry of iniquity for a long time and in many ways.

### And their bodies, he says, will lie in the street of the great city,

<margin>The Beast ascending from the abyss. Luke 12.</margin>
The **beast** which ascends from the abyss—that is, from the secret and unknown depth of malice and darkness where the devil, the adversary of God, now resides—before he enters that lost man and is properly called the Antichrist; once he has killed the body, after this he will have no more... <note>Rupert is alluding to Luke 12:4: "Be not afraid of them that kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do."</note>

# On Chapter 11 of the Apocalypse
## Commentary of Rupert, Book VI

<page-num>301</page-num>

<margin>The mockery of the Jews toward Christ hanging on the cross.</margin>
...[as those slayers of] the martyrs, when the legions of martyrs were struck down, they rejoiced and were glad; indeed, even reclining in the midst of the corpses, they feasted with lavish banquets, as if they had achieved great triumphs over their greatest enemies. But one example regarding their Lord, who was crucified, is sufficient. For when they had crucified Him, they rejoiced and were so glad that, shaking their heads, they said: "Aha! You who would destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days." <note>A reference to the mockery of Christ in Matthew 27:39–40.</note> Furthermore, they sent Him to one another like a gift, leading Him first to **Annas**, then to **Caiaphas**, then to **Pilate**, then to **Herod**, and then back to **Pilate**. Thus they sent Him to one another as if He were a gift for a spectacle, and for this gift of theirs, they felt an impious gratitude. Finally, Annas considered it an honor to himself that Jesus was led to him first, because he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas.

<margin>Luke 23</margin>
Moreover, **Pilate** and **Herod** became friends on that very day; for previously they had been enemies to one another. <note>Rupert cites Luke 23:12 to show how the shared act of persecuting the righteous creates a false peace among the wicked.</note> They rejoiced and were glad to such an extent, as if they had been liberated from an immense torment. This was because, clearly, just as it has now been said that these **two prophets** tormented those who dwell upon the earth, so also the Lord of the prophets Himself had tormented them much more vehemently—so much so that He was a burden to them even to look upon. This was because they themselves were "dwellers on the earth"—meaning they clung to the earth and to earthly desires no less in heart than in body—while He spoke of heavenly things and reproved their earthly greed. Nevertheless, regarding what is said of these two witnesses—*and they shall not allow their bodies to be placed in tombs*—they were not permitted to do this to their Lord, who was crucified. For the Holy Spirit had provided for Him through a precept of the sacred and mystical Law of this kind:

<margin>Deuteronomy 21. The law concerning one hanging on a tree.</margin>
**"When a man has committed a sin punishable by death, and being condemned to death, he is hung on a gallows, his corpse shall not remain on the tree, but shall be buried on the same day, because he who hangs on a tree is cursed."** <note>Rupert is quoting Deuteronomy 21:22–23. This law explains why the body of Jesus had to be taken down and buried quickly.</note> In this sentence, it should be noted that it is not the punishment that makes one cursed, but the guilt; for the text prefaces and diligently determines it thus: "When a man has committed a sin that is pun[ished by death...]" <note>The Latin text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

<summary>Rupert compares the rejoicing of the wicked over the fallen "two prophets" in Revelation to the way the Jewish and Roman authorities rejoiced and "exchanged gifts" during the trial and crucifixion of Christ. He also explains that while the prophets' bodies were left unburied, God’s Law in Deuteronomy ensured that Christ was buried the same day.</summary>
