The burial of Christ.
</margin>
...is to be considered, and finally he adds: "and having been sentenced to death, he was hung on a gallows" <note>Rupert refers to the legal custom mentioned in Deuteronomy 21:22–23 regarding those executed and hung on a tree.</note>. But those men, in their own judgment, wished him who had no fault to be considered "accursed" because of the nature of his punishment. Nevertheless, as has already been said, with the authority of the Law supporting it, they were not allowed to prevent his burial. Thus, even in this, they unknowingly served our salvation: so that while his soul descended to the underworld <note>original: "ad inferos" — a reference to the 'Harrowing of Hell,' the theological belief that Christ descended to the realm of the dead to liberate the souls of the righteous.</note> to free all the souls of the chosen through the power of his indwelling divinity, his body—its burial not being forbidden—was placed in the earth. This was to grant the bodies of the dead the power to spring forth from their tombs in the future resurrection. It should be noted, however, that he circumscribes the time periods such that he says: "for three and a half days they shall see their bodies," and again:

**"And after three and a half days, the spirit of life from God entered into them, and they stood upon their feet."**

For as much time as he had indicated above by saying: **"And they shall trample the holy city for forty-two months,"** and likewise: **"And they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days,"** he signifies just as much now by saying: "for three and a half days," and likewise: "and after three and a half days."

<margin>
Why a day is used here instead of a year.
</margin>
<margin>
John 21
</margin>
Therefore, "a time, and times, and half a time"—that is, three and a half years—he here calls "three and a half days." Why is this? Why is it that while these witnesses were prophesying, the time of their prophecy was predefined as one thousand two hundred and sixty days (which is three and a half years), but after they have finished prophesying, after the beast has killed their bodies—having nothing more it can do—it pleased the author to say or write "three and a half days" instead of "three and a half years"? Surely it is because to the holy witnesses of God, struggling for the truth in a very painful contest, the time of anguish seems long to the senses of their most fragile flesh while it presses upon them, while it is present, and while **"they are led where they do not wish to go."** <note>original: "quo nolunt ducuntur" — Rupert quotes John 21:18, where Jesus tells Peter that in his old age he will be led where he does not wish to go, signifying his martyrdom.</note> But once that time has passed—so that there is no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away—then at last, placed in blessed eternity, as they look back...

<summary>Rupert explains that Christ's burial was allowed by Law to ensure his physical resurrection and his soul's descent to liberate the dead. He further argues that the "three and a half days" mentioned in Revelation represent years, but are described as days because, from the perspective of eternity, the suffering of martyrs is brief.</summary>

# On Chapter 11 of the Apocalypse

[...trou]bles behind them, it will seem that what they endured was brief. Then they will truly understand how rightly the Apostle spoke when he said that the <margin>Romans 8</margin> sufferings of this time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us <note>original: "non sunt condignae passiones huius temporis ad futuram gloriam quae revelabitur in nobis" — This is a quote from Romans 8:18, a common source of comfort for those facing persecution.</note>. He says, therefore: *And after three days and a half, the spirit of life from God entered into them*, which is to say, after a short time—though it may seem like much—it shall come to pass that the spirits, returning by the command of the Almighty, shall return to their own limbs. Then, those who had lain dead in their graves, or were even cast out unburied, shall rise again. The tenses of the verbs have changed here; whereas until now the declaration was made in the future tense—"they will trample the holy city," "I will give to my two witnesses," "they will prophesy," "their bodies will lie in the streets," and "those from the peoples will see and rejoice"— <margin>Why he speaks here first in the future, then later in the past.</margin> now it is spoken in the past tense: *the spirit of life from God entered into them and they stood*. Surely this change indicates a shift in the persona speaking. This is because from the point where it was said above: "But the court which is outside the temple, cast it out, and do not measure it, for it is given to the Gentiles and they will trample the holy city," these and the rest of the words up to this point were the words of that persona who gave the reed <note>The "persona" here refers to the angel or the divine voice instructing John in Revelation 11:1–2.</note>. But here, the persona of John begins to speak again, using the same tense—namely the past—in which he was speaking earlier. It is well known that this is not unusual in prophetic discourse. For quite often, while they are foretelling future events, they use verbs in the past tense <note>This is a linguistic feature often called the "prophetic perfect," where a future event is described in the past tense to emphasize the certainty of its fulfillment.</note>.

**And they stood, he says, upon their feet.**

<margin>Wisdom 5</margin> 
It is understood: "in great steadfastness." For this is what is implied by the addition of the phrase "upon their feet." For then, as Wisdom says: *The just shall stand in great steadfastness against those who have troubled them, and who have taken away their labors* <note>original: "Stabunt iusti in magna constantia..." — This quotes the Book of Wisdom 5:1 from the Deuterocanonical/Apocryphal books.</note>. Those seeing this shall be troubled with horrible fear. Regarding this fear of the wicked, and simultaneously the status of the saints, it is immediately added here:

**And great fear fell upon those who saw them. And they heard a great voice from heaven saying to them: "Come up here." And they ascended into**

<summary>Rupert explains the resurrection of the two witnesses, interpreting the "three and a half days" as a brief period of suffering followed by eternal glory. He also provides a grammatical analysis of why the biblical text shifts from future to past tense, attributing it to a change in the speaker's persona.</summary>

## And seven thousand names of men were killed in the earthquake.

<margin>Seven thousand men: that is, all the wicked. Psalm 49, Isaiah 5, Matthew 25.</margin>
For "seven thousand men" is the same as if he were to say: the entire assembly of wicked men. However, he preferred to say the **names of men** rather than simply "men," by which we understand those who were famous and renowned in this world. These are the kind of people of whom it is written in the Psalm: *Their dwellings are from generation to generation; they have called their names upon their lands.* <note>original: "vocauerunt nomina sua in terris suis" — From Psalm 49:11 (Vulgate 48). Rupert suggests these "names" represent the worldly fame and pride of the wicked.</note> And in Isaiah: *Therefore hell has enlarged its soul, and opened its mouth without any limit, and its strong ones shall descend, and its people, and its high and glorious ones into it.* <note>original: "Propter hoc dilatauit infernus animam suam..." — From Isaiah 5:14, describing the consumption of the proud by the underworld.</note> How has that tenth part of the city fallen (or how is it about to fall), and how are the names of men to be killed in the hour of such a great earthquake? Surely by the command of the same Lord who says to his witnesses, "Ascend here"—that is, "Come, you blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom." By that same Lord, I say, saying: "Fall there"—that is, "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire." They shall fall and go into eternal punishment. <note>Rupert contrasts the "ascent" of the faithful with the "fall" of the wicked, seeing the "earthquake" as a metaphor for the final separation of the Last Judgment.</note>

## And the rest were struck with fear, and gave glory to the God of heaven.

<margin>The righteous also will fear then; so great will be the upheaval. Job 41.</margin>
Who are, or will be, "the rest," if not all the elect who will stand on the right hand? But will these people fear, or be struck with fear, when the devil is cast down in the sight of everyone? They will certainly fear, because we have heard or read the Lord speaking thus to blessed Job: *When he is raised up, the angels will fear, and being terrified they shall be purified.* <note>original: "Cum sublatus fuerit, timebunt angeli..." — From Job 41:25 (Vulgate). Rupert interprets "angels" here not as celestial beings, but as the "holy preachers" or the elect on earth.</note> Indeed, the fortitude of even the holy preachers—whom scripture is accustomed to call **angels**—will be disturbed by such a great weight of terror. But there will be in them, in some way, a "joyful trembling" and a "secure fear": because they will be certain of being rewarded with the heavenly kingdom, yet the flesh will tremble due to its weakness through the dread of such a great whirlwind.

Namely, marvelling at the power of the Most Strong, who will so strongly cast down one who was so strong and so proud. In such a manner regarding...

### The second woe has passed; behold, the third woe comes quickly.

Rather, they pertain to the praise of Christ and the magnificence of His glory and mercy. Just as the Psalmist, speaking in the person of [Christ] himself against them, testifies: "My enemies have spoken evil against me: When will he die and his name perish?" <note>original: "Inimici mei dixerunt mala mihi. Quando morietur & peribit nomen eius?" This is Psalm 41:5 in modern Bibles (40:6 in the Vulgate).</note> For having first said, "Because you have taken your power and have reigned"—that is, being incarnated from your Holy Spirit and having cast out the prince of the world—they immediately add:

### **And the nations were angry.**

<margin>
The nations and the Jews were angry against Christ. Matthew 20, Luke 18.
</margin>
For why were the nations angry, or what did the nations wish to achieve by their anger, except this: that he should not exist? Clearly, the Jews are not excluded here from the name "nations" <note>original: *gentium*. While "Gentes" usually means Gentiles/non-Jews, Rupert argues here that the Jewish authorities are included in this group because of their shared opposition to Christ.</note>, because they were the first to be angry and were most envious, handing him over to the nations to be mocked, scourged, and crucified, saying (as we have already recalled), "When will he die and his name perish?" Wherefore also in the Psalm, the Holy Spirit, vehemently insulting them, reproaches them: "Why have the nations raged, and the people meditated on vain things?" Truly they have meditated on vain things, because you, O Lord, were God even before you became man; and now, after the nations were angry and 

<margin>Psalm 138</margin>
raged by killing you, you have risen and you *are*. Hence it is that you say to the Father, likewise in the words of David: "I have risen, and I am still with you." <note>original: "Exurrexi & adhuc sum" from Psalm 139:18 (Vulgate 138:18). Rupert interprets "still being" as the proof of Christ's eternal nature despite the crucifixion.</note>

Following the previous page’s discussion on Christ’s eternal existence ("who is and who was") and the elders' thanksgiving, Rupert now interprets the "anger of the nations" as a catalyst for God's righteous judgment.</meta>

<page-num>311</page-num>
<header>On Apocalypse Chapter 11</header>

with you. Therefore, "the nations were angry," that is, they killed you, and (as has already been said): in killing you they roared. But what follows?

**And your wrath came, they say,**

<margin>After the wrath of the sinner comes the wrath of God.</margin>
Rightly and in an ordered fashion, because the nations were angry first, and afterwards "your wrath came." This is the legitimate order of justice: that God is angry with no one except the person who was angry first—by swelling with pride, by resisting, and by defending their own guilt in imitation of the transgression of Adam <note>original: "preuaricationis Adæ." Rupert refers to the "original sin" of Adam as the archetype for all human resistance to God.</note>. Where someone is angry and resists, there at last God is angry and resists; and against the "strong" man he uses his own power, which cannot be endured. <margin>Psalm 75</margin> Hence the Psalmist, when he had said: "You are terrible, and who resists you?" immediately added: "From then on, your wrath" <note>original: "Extunc ira tua." This refers to Psalm 76:7 in modern Bibles (75:8 in the Vulgate).</note>. It is as if he says: Your wrath does not start from the moment a person first sins, but from the moment they multiply their sin by defending it and resisting your justice. Then comes your wrath, which no one is able to <margin>Job 9</margin> resist, just as it is written elsewhere: "God, whose wrath no one can resist" <note>original: "Deus cuius iræ nemo resistere potest." See Job 9:13.</note>. This order of judgment is preserved both specifically in individual people and universally in the whole human race. Therefore they say: "and the nations were angry, and your wrath came." It is as if they say: Because the nations were unwilling to accept the repentance you preached, but on the contrary were more angry and roared, and "imagined vain things," and "the kings of the earth stood up, and the princes gathered together as one, against the Lord and against his Christ" <note>Rupert is quoting Psalm 2:1-2, which was traditionally interpreted as a prophecy of the Passion of Christ.</note>, justly now at last your wrath has come, just as was written about you in that same place: "Then he will speak to them in his wrath, and in his fury he will trouble them." For, explaining what they meant by "and your wrath came," they follow up and say:

**And the time to judge the dead, and to give reward to your servants, and the prophets, and the saints, and those who fear your name, the small and the great, and of destroying those who corrupted the earth.**

The effect of his wrath which has arrived is to destroy those who corrupted the earth. For to give reward to the saints...

<summary>Rupert explains that God’s wrath is a just response to human pride and the "anger" of the nations who rejected and killed Christ. He argues that divine judgment follows a specific order, targeting those who stubbornly defend their sins rather than repenting.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Book 6 of the Apocalypse, focusing on the final judgment sequence in Revelation 11:18. Rupert emphasizes that God’s mercy toward the faithful precedes his punishment of the wicked. He then transitions into Book 7 of his commentary.</meta>

<page-num>312</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 6</header>

<margin>Reward is given first to the good, then the wicked are destroyed.</margin>
it is not wrath, but "grace for grace" <note>original: "gratia pro gratia." This is a famous theological phrase from John 1:16. Rupert interprets it here as the gift of eternal life being given in exchange for the gift of faith.</note>—the grace of blessedness in exchange for the grace of one’s calling, or the blessedness of faith that earns its reward. And the discourse is rightly woven or ordered in this way: it was said first that he would "give reward to his servants," and then: "And to destroy those who corrupted the earth." For according to the true order—or the "ordered truth" of the Gospel—reward is given first to the servants at God's right hand, and then those on the left are destroyed. For that King will first say to those on his right: "Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom," and only then to those on his left: "Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire" <note>Rupert is referencing the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats from Matthew 25:34-41 to explain the sequence of events in Revelation.</note>. For in such a manner will the reward be given to the servants of God, and the corruptors of the earth will be destroyed. But who are these "corruptors of the earth," if not those who corrupt both bodies and souls by serving their every desire? For in the judgment of God, no cause of corruption is prosecuted except that by which the rational creature is corrupted. That creature, which ought to be the "earth of God" and bring forth the fruit of faith, holiness, and peace or love, has instead become so corrupted within itself that it produces the bitter thorns of unbelief and every lust, and is therefore destined for a curse.

<margin>There will be no more time—namely, for repentance.</margin>
Thus, in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when the trumpet begins to sound, the mystery of God will be completed. And just as that strong angel swore—he who stood upon the sea and upon the land and lifted his hand to heaven—"time will be no more" <note>original: "tempus amplius non erit." See Revelation 10:6. Rupert interprets "time" here specifically as the "time available for repentance."</note>. The time for repentance will no longer be granted to sinners, who were sufficiently forewarned by the many terrifying sounds of the preceding hosts which we have already enumerated. Not partially, as happened during the other trumpet blasts, but all the corruptors of the earth will perish together and be destroyed at the command of the reigning Lord, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, so that they may never again cause any offense to the kingdom of God.

<margin>The Spirit of Fortitude is proclaimed here.</margin>
...before the throne. Thus, with the seven angels to whom trumpets were given arranged on one side, and on the other the angel who had the golden censer, it was first set out what was done through each blast of the trumpets, and the seven punishments for sins were recorded. And now, having returned to the beginning, it is written what was done through the office of the angel holding the golden censer, and the great war and lengthy struggle of the angel—who is here called Michael—is narrated. He battles with the great red dragon of seven heads, and the distinguished victories of the martyrs are proclaimed, who finally, after the labors of their battles, sing as it were a new song. Here, the works of the **Spirit of Fortitude** <note>original: "spiritus fortitudinis." This refers to one of the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit. Rupert associates this gift with the strength required for martyrdom.</note> are manifest and proclaimed; this Spirit is found fourth in the order of the seven spirits, joined to the **Spirit of Counsel** <note>original: "spiritui consilij." The gift of right judgment.</note>, whose providence we mentioned above regarding the seven sounding trumpets. Therefore, he says:

**And the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven.**
<margin>When the temple of the Lord was opened: Daniel 10.</margin>
By this conjunction where he says, "And [it] was opened," he leads us back to the earlier things, where he had said: *And another angel came and stood before the altar,* etc. For it happened at the same time that the temple of the Lord was opened and the angel stood near the altar. For then the temple of the Lord was opened when holy men received the faith of the Lord and the promises of Christ in their hearts; and then the angel stood near the altar when, on account of that same faith, Michael was appointed as the prince for the race of the righteous, just as we have shown more fully in its proper place with the authority of the Scriptures. Therefore, the temple of the Lord was opened in heaven—that is, they believed—and by believing in the Christ who was to come, the holy fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, became the temple of the Lord.

**And the ark of his testament was seen in his temple,**
<margin>The ark of the testament is the incarnation of Christ.</margin>
That is, the **Incarnation of Christ** <note>Rupert follows a common medieval allegory where the Ark of the Covenant, which held the Law, represents the body of Christ, who contains the fullness of God.</note>, the Son of God, was foreseen and hailed from afar. This is now seen in his temple—that is, in his Church—shining with the purest gold, which represents the great brightness of his divinity. <meta>Continuity from page 315: Rupert has finished discussing the signs accompanying the opening of the temple (lightnings and voices) as symbols of the Law and the Spirit. He now moves to the next major vision in Revelation 12: the Woman Clothed with the Sun.</meta>

<page-num>316</page-num>
<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book 7</header>

<margin>The woman is called the Church.</margin>
Truly, this sign was great and of a great matter. For that woman signified the **Holy Church**, whom we find called a "woman" in many places of the prophetic scriptures, joined and beloved by her husband—that is, God—and indeed sometimes rebuked as an adulteress when part of her people turned to the vices and sins of serving idolatry. This woman is then rightly said to be **clothed with the sun**, from the moment she received Christ, the true "Sun of Justice," <note>original: "solem iusticiæ"; a reference to Malachi 4:2, frequently used by medieval theologians to identify Christ as the source of spiritual light.</note> in the promise. The **moon under her feet** signifies the brightness of temporal goods under her management. For the moon, because of its changeability, rightly signifies the shifting goods of this world, which the fool serves, but the wise man commands. 

Therefore, it is to the praise of the holy fathers <note>The Patriarchs of the Old Testament.</note> that they were indeed wealthy, as the sacred histories record, but they did not allow those riches to rule their hearts; rather, they themselves ruled over the riches, dispensing them as private or public need required. Thus, such wealthy men are laudably excused, because the sin is not in the wealth itself, but in the attachment to it. On the contrary, whoever believes in Christ but clings to and serves the profit of temporal things in his heart is a slave and not their master; it cannot rightly be said of his soul that it is a "woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet." Instead, he perversely strives to be clothed by the moon <note>clothed in worldly, changing status</note> and seeks to keep the sun under his feet. It follows:

-> **And on her head a crown of twelve stars.** <-

On the head of this woman, a crown of twelve stars is seen, because in the beginning of the nascent <note>The early or "born" church.</note> church twelve patriarchs are numbered, and likewise at the beginning of its rebirth <note>The New Testament era.</note>, twelve most well-known and splendid apostles are counted.
<margin>Twelve stars, twelve tribes of Israel. Genesis 37.</margin>
Now, following the order of these heavenly wonders, we understand the crown of twelve stars to represent the number of the twelve sons or tribes of Israel. For as Joseph said when telling his dream: *I saw,* he said, *the sun and the moon and eleven stars worshipping me.* <note>Genesis 37:9. Joseph’s dream is treated here as a "type" or foreshadowing of the Church.</note> For the father himself, on account of the Christ whom he held in the promise, was like the sun; the mother, however—whichever of them was the most excellent (since his natural mother had died)—was the moon, shining with the faith of that same Christ. But the eleven...

<summary>Rupert interprets the "Woman Clothed with the Sun" from Revelation 12 as the Church, explaining that she is "clothed" in Christ and tramples upon the changeable "moon" of worldly wealth. He connects the twelve stars on her head to both the twelve Patriarchs of Israel and the twelve Apostles.</summary>

<page-num>317</page-num>

<header>On Chapter 7 of the Apocalypse, 317</header>

the brothers to whom he was telling [his dream], there were to be eleven stars, and Joseph himself was the twelfth star. Therefore, on the head of the woman was a crown of twelve stars, and in the beginning of the church, there was a chorus of twelve sons, or the twelve tribes of Israel.

->**And being with child, she cried out in labor, and was in pain to be delivered.**<-

<margin>Genesis 22; Galatians 3</margin>
What did it mean to "have in the womb," if not to preserve the faith of the promise in the secret of the heart? For when God first spoke to Abraham, saying: *And in your seed shall all the nations be blessed* <note>original: "Et in semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes"; from Genesis 22:18.</note> (which "seed" is certainly Christ <note>A reference to Paul’s argument in Galatians 3:16 that the "seed" promised to Abraham is a singular person, Jesus.</note>), Abraham believed the one making the promise. Because his descendants hoped in that same faith from then on, the woman <note>The Church in her Old Testament form.</note> began to have a child in her womb. Moreover, it was God who had promised who was the husband of this same woman, as well as the father and author of that conception—that is, the faith through which Christ, who was yet to come, already inhabited the hearts of the believing fathers. As the multitude of believers increased through the ages, Moses and the prophets followed; they signaled the faith they had received by both speaking and writing, and they did so with a great intensity of longing. It follows, therefore:

->**And she cried out in labor, and was in pain to be delivered**<-

When he said, *And she cried out in labor*, he repeated the idea—or rather, he completed it—by adding, *and was in pain to be delivered*. Indeed, it would have been too little to say only "she cried out in labor." It might have seemed as though he wanted nothing more to be understood than if he had said: "When she gave birth, she began to cry out." But she, before she gave birth, before she brought forth her offspring, was in labor and cried out. For "to be in labor" <note>original: "parturire"</note> means to be in pain *before* the birth, because "to be in labor" is a word describing a state of reflection or preparation, whereas "to give birth" <note>original: "parere"</note> is a word of completion. 

Therefore, just as a woman who is physically pregnant, when the hour of birth is pressing in, is entirely focused on the thought of her delivery and is occupied by expectation, enduring pain until she gives birth—so too is that woman who is spiritually pregnant. *She cried out*, he says, *in labor, and was in pain to be delivered*. We could bring forward many of her cries, but for the sake of an example, this one passage from the prophet Isaiah is enough.

<summary>Rupert explains that the Woman’s pregnancy represents the Old Testament Church’s long-held faith in the promised Messiah, interpreting her labor pains as the intense longing and suffering of the patriarchs and prophets before Christ's birth.</summary>

Almost all ecclesiastical writers have handed down the tradition that at the end of the world, when the Roman kingdom is to be destroyed, ten kings will arise who shall divide the Roman world among themselves. Then, an eleventh "little king" will rise, who is to overcome three of those ten kings—specifically the king of the Egyptians, the king of Africa, and the king of Ethiopia. <margin>A little horn in the midst.</margin>

which clearly signifies that this horn will be the Antichrist. However, in this present text—where we see not just the "fourth beast" (which in Daniel signifies only the Roman kingdom) but the dragon himself (that is, the devil), and where his seven heads are described without any mention of three horns being plucked out—it is permitted to offer another interpretation that may be joined to our established theme by the authority of the Scriptures. There are indeed only seven heads of the dragon, yet ten horns are seen. This is because one of the aforementioned kingdoms, the Macedonian kingdom, was divided into four kings. 

<margin>The Macedonian Kingdom after the death of Alexander.</margin>

<margin>Daniel 8</margin>

Finally, although other parts of the divided kingdom sometimes ravaged Judea, it remains a certain fact that the king of the one part who held Syria (and with it Judea) acted as the dragon’s agent against the Woman and carried out the devil's intent against the law of God.

# On Revelation Chapter 12

...might devour her son. <margin>Matthew 2; Micah 5</margin> That bloody head <note>The "bloody head" refers to Herod the Great, whom Rupert sees as one of the heads of the dragon, manifesting the dragon's murderous intent.</note> raged most especially in Herod, when he was moved by that prophetic oracle he had heard: *And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means the least among the princes of Judah, for from you shall come a leader who will rule my people Israel.* He sought the boy to destroy him, and sent [his men] to Bethlehem and killed all the boys who were in it and in all its borders, as if it were impossible for that child not to be killed along with them. 

But how did that foolish dragon, who was raging within Herod, think he could void the counsel or purpose of God? For that Child was destined to rule the nations with an <term>iron rod<note>original: "virga ferrea"; a symbol of unyielding power and absolute authority, frequently applied to Christ's reign in medieval exegesis.</note></term>, and this had been preordained in the scriptures of truth. <margin>Psalm 2</margin> For example, He Himself says in the Psalmist: *The Lord said to me, "You are my son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall rule them with an iron rod."* How then did the malicious foolishness of the dragon hope to devour Him so quickly, when it had been written of Him that He would rule the nations with an iron rod? Truly "with an iron rod" means with inflexible justice. 

<margin>Isaiah 9</margin> Likewise, when he mentions a **male son**, it is the same as if he said "a most strong son." For a "male"—that is, a strong son—was then born to us, just as the prophet had foretold: *And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God.* <margin>Psalm 40 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 41.</note></margin> Yet that dragon did as much as he could, not ceasing to pursue that son in order to devour Him—that is, to erase His memory—saying that which we hear in the Psalm: *When will he die, and his name perish?* By saying these things, he impatiently brought it about that He was crucified; and by doing this, he thought He was "devoured" and that His name had perished. 

But see what follows.

<margin>Matthew 27</margin> **And her son was caught up to God and to his throne.**

Who does not know how truly this was done? Who has not heard? For when He was thought to have been devoured—inasmuch as He was buried in the earth and shut in the ground with a sealed stone—then, the "pains of hell being loosed" <note>A reference to Acts 2:24, explaining that death could not hold Christ.</note> because it was impossible for Him to be held by it, He rose again and ascended into heaven. Now He sits at the right hand of God, while the truth of Scripture triumphs, which says in David: *The Lord said...*

The dragon and his messengers also fought with material weapons, as has already been said. Every time it shook itself for battle, it rained blood upon the whole world.

# On Revelation Chapter 12
### 344

...idols having been destroyed, it lost its usurped glory of what seemed like divine worship. Now, with the Roman Empire at its peak adoring the son of this woman—who was snatched up to God and to his throne <note>A reference to Revelation 12:5, interpreted here as Christ's ascension and his subsequent worship by the Empire.</note>—and with the Christian emperor **Constantine** carrying the sign of the cross of **CHRIST** upon his forehead, **Arius** <note>Arius (c. 256–336) was a priest in Alexandria whose teachings led to the Arian controversy, which debated the nature of Christ's divinity.</note>, that great priest and <term>heresiarch</term> <note>A leader or founder of a heretical movement.</note>, broke out too insolently into blasphemy against Christ, the Son of God, under the "Christian" name and with intolerable talkativeness. We shall recognize how truly and how appropriately, according to the nature of the events, this was demonstrated in the vision and thus spoken or written. For what is truer than what it now says: that after the dragon saw he was cast down to the earth, he persecuted the woman, sending forth water like a river from his mouth after her? <note>Revelation 12:13-15</note> For the devil saw that his old idolatry could no longer stand, once the highest princes had inclined toward accepting the profession of the Christian name; therefore, he turned the whole abundance of his malice toward corrupting the truth of the Scriptures, and in this way began to persecute the woman who gave birth to the male child. See what the text says: for it does not say, "he persecuted the male son," but he persecuted, it says, "the woman who gave birth to the male child."

<margin>
Arius led the faithful away from the Church into the synagogue.
</margin>

For the dragon, pouring out impious doctrine through the mouth of **Arius** and other heretics of that sort, did not openly demand of anyone that they deny Christ or the Christian name; but rather that anyone confessing Christ should receive a rule of confession or faith other than what the apostolic truth had handed down. Intending this—or rather, contending for it—he persecuted that woman so that **Satan** might make the Church of Christ into his own <term>synagogue</term> <note>The author uses "synagogue" here in a pejorative, symbolic sense common in medieval polemics to mean a gathering of unbelievers or heretics, referencing the "synagogue of Satan" from Revelation 2:9.</note>. Doing this with excessive talkativeness and noisy contention, that serpent sent forth "water like a river" from his mouth. Note that he did not say, "he sent a river from his mouth," but "he sent water *like* a river." Finally, the water which that serpent sends from his mouth can have the appearance of a river, but it cannot truly be a river. For the true river—the river of living water in Holy Scripture—is the true and <term>Catholic</term> <note>original: "catholica." In this 12th-century context, it refers to the "universal" or "orthodox" faith of the Church as opposed to heretical sects.</note> doctrine, which the Church (who is this woman) is accustomed to send forth from the fountain...

<summary>Rupert interprets the dragon's pursuit of the Woman as the rise of the Arian heresy following the conversion of Emperor Constantine. He argues that the devil, unable to use pagan idolatry anymore, used Arius's "talkative" false doctrines (the "water like a river") to try and corrupt the Church from within.</summary>

...of truth, which having within itself, she is the garden of the Lord, as is said in the Song of Songs:

For in such a way, and into such diverse indeed contrary states, are all those dragged away who follow the flowing talkativeness of blaspheming heretics with wondering ears.

### And the earth helped the woman, and the earth opened its mouth, and swallowed up the river which the dragon cast out of his mouth.

<margin>The Council of Nicaea</margin>

For from almost the entire earth, from the whole circle of the lands, illustrious men gathered: religious men from all nations, famous men, skilled in debate, and practiced in every art of eloquence, who sat together to defend the church of Catholic truth.

One of these was **Paphnutius** of Egypt. There, indeed, was seen a people of athletes...

...of the saints and martyrs of CHRIST gathered in one place. That is, it annihilated and condemned the sect of wicked doctrine which had been uttered by the diabolical spirit. 

For there the dogma of **Arius** <note>Arius taught that Jesus was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father; his views were condemned at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD.</note> was destroyed. Likewise also later, when the **Council of Constantinople** <note>Held in 381 AD; it expanded the Nicene Creed and addressed heresies regarding the Holy Spirit.</note> was celebrated, the error of **Eunomius and Macedonius** was proven wrong. And when the **Council of Ephesus** <note>Held in 431 AD; it addressed the teachings of Nestorius regarding the nature of Christ and the Virgin Mary.</note> was held, in which the impiety of **Nestorius** was judged. And then when the **Council of Chalcedon** <note>Held in 451 AD; it defined the "two natures" of Christ (divine and human) against the teachings of Eutyches.</note> was celebrated, in which the depravity of **Eutyches and Dioscorus** was rejected, the earth opened its mouth and absorbed a river of this kind, while the woman escaped, flying with two wings, just as was predicted here:

> Because there were given to the woman two wings of a great eagle, so that she might fly into the desert into her place, where she is nourished for a time, and times, and half a time, from the face of the serpent.

<margin>That eagle is Sacred Scripture.</margin>
For the **great eagle** (as we have already said in another place above) is **Holy Scripture**, and its **two wings** are the **two Testaments** <note>The Old and New Testaments.</note>, which were given to this woman—that is, they were made understandable to her—so that she might have the means to lift her heart toward heaven, and not fall into the river that flows through the earth: the diabolical river, the snare-ridden river of heretical talkativeness, full of deceptive nets. Having wings of this kind, she flies into the desert, into her place; that is, she pursues **holy leisure** <term>otium</term> <note>Rupert uses "otium" not as "laziness," but as the "holy leisure" of monastic life—freedom from worldly business to focus on God.</note>.

<margin>Wisdom in leisure and solitude.</margin>
She does this so that she may be free to serve the meditation of the scriptures, according to that saying of the Wise Man: *“The wisdom of a scribe comes in a time of leisure, and he who is lessened in activity shall gain wisdom.”* <note>original: "Sapientiam scribae in tempore ocii, & qui minoratur actu [sapientiam percipiet]." From Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:24.</note>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 7
### 346

<margin>
Ecclesiasticus 38.
Genesis 25.
</margin>
...will receive her. **He who is lessened in action** <note>original: *minoratur actu*; Rupert is quoting the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:25, suggesting that one who has fewer worldly distractions can better attain wisdom.</note>, that is, who is less occupied by physical labor—just like **Jacob**, who lived simply at home, not doing as much as **Esau**, who was physically strained as a hunter. For this reason, Jacob received wisdom, while for the other, the physical exercise in which he was engaged profited him but little. Accordingly, the **Apostle** <note>The "Apostle" always refers to St. Paul.</note>, instructing his vigorous disciple, says:
<margin>1 Timothy 4.</margin>
**Train yourself for godliness. For bodily exercise is of little profit, but godliness is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come.** Therefore, this Woman, flying away into that desert—into such a place of her own, a "holy leisure" for the exercise of godliness—is understood, in another sense, to be occupied by the contemplation of truth and sacred readings. Moreover, she is sustained even in her physical needs (as has been said elsewhere) by the generosity of the support provided by her children. In this way, I say, she is removed **from the face of the serpent**, meaning she does not fear the serpent.

<margin>
The times of the Church's persecution.
</margin>
That is, for three years and a half—the length of time the **Antichrist** will vex the world with his persecution. Therefore, this specific timeframe is rightly understood to represent the entire duration in which the Church suffers persecution because she lives godly in Christ. Thus, the "river" (or the phantom river of serpents) was "swallowed up" when that holy assembly, the **Council of Nicaea**, condemned the wicked dogma of **Arius** <note>Arius (d. 336 AD) was a priest whose teachings denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>. The dragon’s anger against the woman through the Emperor Constantius.

What does he imply by this, if not the difficulty of that time and the excess of tribulation? Into the portion of Seleucus (as we already said in that place where we treated the dragon, its heads, and its horns) Syria fell along with the Jews, and only his descendants—of whom that most wicked Antiochus Epiphanes <note>A Hellenistic king of the Seleucid Empire who famously persecuted the Jews, leading to the Maccabean Revolt.</note> stood forth—attacked the name of the Lord, as we have from the recorded deeds of the Maccabees. It is right, therefore, that there are as many diadems as there are horns, because everywhere there are kings, there will be as many ministers of this impiety.

Regarding the kingdom of Israel <note>Rupert refers here to the Northern Kingdom of Israel, which broke away from Judah and often fell into idolatry.</note>, it is certain that Jezebel committed blasphemy, not only by forcing Baal to be worshipped as god, but also by perverting the oath of the name of the Lord commonly used at that time. <margin>Nebuchadnezzar. Daniel 3. Judith 3.</margin>

<margin>Haman. Esther 3 and 13.</margin>

When he says this, he expresses clearly enough that the arrogant man <note>Haman.</note> was demanding for himself not just any kind of respect, but that worship which is owed to God alone. ...of the Macedonians. For it is a very swift beast, which is carried headlong toward blood and rushes into death with a leap. Therefore, the kingdom of the Macedonians—the kingdom of Alexander—is compared to it, for nothing was swifter than his victories. Indeed, he traversed the land from the Illyrian and Adriatic Sea all the way to the Indian Ocean and the Ganges River, not so much by battles as by victories, and in six years he subjugated a part of Europe and all of Asia to himself. The beast I saw, he says, was like that leopard-like kingdom, namely according to the wickedness of the aforementioned Antiochus <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Hellenistic king who persecuted the Jews and is often seen as a "type" or precursor to the Antichrist.</note>, who (as the same Daniel foretold) was magnified even to the strength of heaven, or to the prince of strength, and took away from him the continual sacrifice <note>original: "iuge sacrificium"</note>. Therefore, it was like a leopard; that is, the Antichrist will fulfill that which was prefigured about him through Antiochus.

### And its feet, he said, were like those of a bear.

<margin>Daniel 7.</margin>
<margin>The feet of the beast are his wickedest legates <note>A "legate" is an official messenger or representative.</note>.</margin>
<margin>Esther 3.</margin>
In that same vision of Daniel, the bear signifies the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, clearly because of the harshness and ferocity of that same kingdom. The feet of this beast are compared to the feet of that bear. Who, then, will be his feet, if not the satellites <note>henchmen or followers</note> of his wickedness, the carriers of the most evil embassies throughout the whole world to shed blood? And who were the feet of that bear—that is, of that kingdom of the Persians and Medes—if not the accomplices of Haman <note>original: "Aman"</note> the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews? These were the men who hastened to carry the cruel letters received, or rather demanded, from the king concerning the killing of the Jews, which contained savage commands. Therefore, when he says, *and its feet were like a bear's*, it is the same as if he were to say: "and his ministers, like Haman, will be swift to shed blood."

### And its mouth was like the mouth of a lion.

In that same vision of Daniel, it is not a lion, but what is even fiercer, a lioness <note>original: "leena"</note>, that signifies the Babylonian kingdom, clearly on account of its savagery and cruelty, or on account of its luxury and a life serving lust. Therefore, *its mouth was like the mouth of a lion*, namely when it speaks proud and cruel things, just as that king of Ba— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, referring to the King of Babylon.</note>

The Antichrist is one and the same as the "man of sin" <note>A title from 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note>; he was called the "beast of seven heads" a little earlier, and here he is called "one of the heads" of the beast. For the beast has so many heads to represent its body, which is the generation of the wicked; however, he is called one head to represent his own person, because of his lordship during that time when he is to be revealed over all the **sons of pride** <note>original: "filiorum superbiæ." A reference to Job 41:34, often interpreted as the followers of the Devil.</note>. Truly, what is said here—that this head of the beast was as if killed unto death, and the wound of death was healed—he repeats this same thing a bit later, calling it the head of the beast itself, when he says: *That they should make an image of the beast which has the wound of the sword, and lived.* 

Where, I ask, was this head struck down? Where did it receive the wound of the sword? How was it healed after death? How did it live? Indeed, how does this relate to the name of the Antichrist, that is, the one "contrary to Christ"? 

It does so, truly, in a wonderful way, yet also in an execrable way. The true Christ received the wounds of the nails and the wound of the spear, and he **died unto sin** <note>Rupert alludes to Romans 6:10, meaning Christ died to destroy sin.</note>; but now his death is healed, and he himself lives unto God. But this one—O, what a wonder—having been subjected to judgment in heaven before the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and before the whole court of heaven and the holy senate of blessed angels, received a capital sentence for the crime of pride. He was struck by the sword of eternal damnation, and so, having died to God, he lives for sin, and lives even now. 

<margin>The Devil, dead to God, lives for sin.</margin>

He lives, certainly he lives, because he defends himself with extreme stubbornness; nor does he wish to be considered dead, but wants to be held as a god. Indeed, **he exalts himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped** <note>A direct quote from 2 Thessalonians 2:4.</note>. Was the wound of his death truly healed then? It was not healed, but he, a rebel against the sword and a rebel against the sentence of God, contends that the wound has not harmed him at all. 

For what of it? Even before the Devil enters into him—that <term>vessel</term> <note>Rupert uses "vas" (vessel) to describe the Antichrist as a container for the Devil's influence.</note> of his own, the <term>son of perdition</term>—and although he was struck in heaven, he sought out for himself temples and altars and priests and sacrifices as if he were a living god. And after he has entered into that man, he will obtain the kingdoms of the world and will sit in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God. How will such a one concede—or even be in agreement with his own conscience—that he was ever killed, or ever wounded, or that he ever *ought* to have been wounded or killed?

<summary>Rupert explains that the Antichrist's "healed wound" is a parody of Christ’s Resurrection; while Christ died to sin and lives for God, the Antichrist (and the Devil within him) is "dead to God" but continues to live in stubborn rebellion and pride.</summary>

# On Revelation Chapter 12 <note>Though the header says Chapter 12, the text continues the commentary on the Beast from Chapter 13.</note>

<margin>Powerful people who despise excommunication act like the devil, because they live despite being struck unto death.</margin>
O tyrant, tyrant! We wonder from where such foolish hardness, such hard foolishness, comes to you, or how it arises? And yet, we read of many among our own kind who are like you and taught by you; we see them follow your example, becoming hardened and foolish. For whoever is convicted of a crime and assigned to judgment yet acts against their own conscience, and—conscious of their guilt—defends themselves, they strike back against the sentence. For example: suppose a powerful person is guilty of adultery or murder and is rebellious. While he, through his own power, resists the **sword of anathema** <note>original: "gladiū anathematis." Anathema refers to a formal curse or excommunication by the church, often described as a "spiritual sword."</note> by which he is justly struck, we judge that person correctly and truly: he has the "wound of the sword" and yet he lives. This means that in his conscience he is condemned by his own judgment, and yet through stubbornness, he defends himself as if he were righteous. It follows:

<margin>
A reproof of the worldly, because they receive the Antichrist.
</margin>
**And the whole earth marveled after the beast, and they worshiped the dragon who gave power to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight with it?"**
Here, that generation is especially blamed which is destined to receive that man <note>The Antichrist.</note>, according to the heavy and truthful complaint of that Man who comes blessed in the name of the Lord, saying: *I have come in my Father’s name, and they did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him they will receive.* <note>Rupert is quoting John 5:43.</note> For those people are "earth" and savor earthly things; and this "reception" by which they will receive him is the very "marveling" of which it is now said: *And the whole earth marveled after the beast.* In this, therefore, they are blamed, and in this they are reproached: for unless they were merely "earth," if they savored anything of the things that are above, they would not marvel at him. They would not highly prize his earthly height, his earthly power, or his earthly glory, which the true Christ valued so little that at the time when he was first 
<margin>Matthew 21</margin>
greeted by the crowds of Israel saying, "Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord," he chose to sit upon a **donkey** <note>original: "asello." Referring to Christ's humble entrance into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday.</note> out of contempt for all earthly high-status. Furthermore, he strikes them with what he subjoins:

**And they worshiped the dragon who gave power...**

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 8

One and the same is the **man of sin**, the **Antichrist**. Just a moment ago he was called the **Beast of seven heads**, and here he is called one of the heads of the Beast. Specifically, the "Beast" refers to the many heads of his "body," which is the entire generation of the wicked; however, he is called "one head" in reference to his own person and to the period of his reign when he is to be revealed as the king over all the "children of pride" <note>A reference to Job 41:34, often associated by medieval commentators with the Devil and the Antichrist.</note>.

Certainly, what is said here—that this head of the Beast was "as if slain unto death" and "the wound of his death was healed"—is the same thing repeated a little later when the head itself is called the "Beast," saying: *That they should make an image to the beast which has the wound of the sword and yet lived.* <note>original: "Vt faciant imaginem bestię quę habet plagam gladiij, & vixit." See Revelation 13:14.</note>

Where, I ask, was this head slain? Where did it receive the wound of the sword? How was the wound of its death healed? How did it live? Moreover, how does this relate to the name of the **Antichrist**—that is, the one "contrary to Christ"? 

In truth, it is in a way both marvelous and execrable. The **True Christ** received the wounds of the nails and the wound of the spear; He died to sin, but now "His death is healed" and He lives for God. But this one <note>The Antichrist/the Devil</note>—O, what a strange thing—was subjected to judgment in heaven before the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, in the presence of the entire court of heaven and the holy senate of blessed angels. For the **crime of pride**, he received a **capital sentence** <term>capital sentence<note>In this context, a "death sentence" that is spiritual rather than physical—the "death" of eternal separation from God.</note></term> and was struck by the sword of eternal damnation. Thus, while he became dead to God, 

<margin>The Devil, though dead to God, lives in sin.</margin>
he "lived" in sin, and lives in it still. He lives, certainly he lives, because he defends himself with such stubborn persistence; he does not wish to be regarded as dead, but as God. Indeed, he exalts himself above everything that is called God or that is worshiped. 

Has the wound of his death truly been healed, then? It has not been healed, but he, being a rebel against the sword and the sentence of God, contends that the wound has done him no harm. For what then? Even before the Devil enters into that "son of perdition" <note>The human figure of the Antichrist.</note> as his own vessel, and despite having been "struck" in heaven, he has already sought out temples, altars, priests, and sacrifices for himself as if he were a living god. After he has entered that man, he will seize the kingdoms of the world and sit in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God. How could such a one ever concede—or even admit to his own conscience—that he was slain or wounded, or that he ever deserved to be wounded or slain?

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the "mortal wound" of the Beast not as a physical injury, but as the divine judgment of damnation cast upon the Devil for his pride. He contrasts Christ’s redemptive wounds with the Antichrist’s stubborn refusal to acknowledge his spiritual death and his subsequent claim to divinity.</summary>

### On Chapter 12 of the Apocalypse <note>Though the header says Chapter 12, the text comments on Revelation 13:3–4. In medieval manuscripts, chapter numbering often differed from modern Bibles.</note>

O tyrant, tyrant! We wonder from where such foolish hardness, such hard foolishness, comes to you, or how? And yet, we read of many in our own human race who are conformed to you and pre-taught by you; we see them, following your example, becoming hardened and made foolish. For whoever is convicted of a crime and sentenced by judgment, yet acts against their own conscience and, being conscious of their crime, defends themselves, they reject the sentence. For example: some powerful person, guilty of adultery or homicide and rebellious, while they reject the sword of **anathema** <note>original: "gladiū anathematis"</note> by which they are justly struck, we judge rightly and truly of them: that they have the wound of the sword and yet live. This means that in their conscience, by their own judgment, they are condemned, yet through defiance, they defend themselves as if they were righteous. It follows:

-> *And the whole earth wondered after the beast, and they worshiped the dragon who gave power to the beast, and they worshiped the beast, saying, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight with it?"* <-

<margin>A rebuke of earthly people because they receive the **Antichrist**.</margin>
Here, that generation is most blamed which is destined to receive that man <note>The Antichrist</note>, according to the heavy and true-speaking complaint of that Man who comes "blessed in the name of the Lord," who says: *I have come in the name of my Father, and they have not received me; another will come in his own name, and him they will receive.* <note>Quoting John 5:43.</note> For they are "earth" and they savor earthly things, and that "receiving" by which they will receive him is this "wondering" of which it is now said: *And the whole earth wondered after the beast.* In this, therefore, they are blamed; in this they are reproached: because unless they were "earth"—if they savored anything of the things that are above—they would not wonder at, nor would they highly value, his earthly height, his earthly power, or his earthly glory. 

The true **Christ** valued such things so little that at the time when he was first greeted by the crowds of Israel saying, "Blessed is
<margin>Matthew 21</margin>
he who comes in the name of the Lord," he chose to sit upon a donkey, in contempt of all earthly loftiness. Furthermore, the text strikes them even more in what it adds next:

*And they worshiped the dragon who gave power...*

There, when the silver garment caught the first rays of the sun, it shed a reflected splendor that cast a shimmering metallic glow—a double light—upon the onlookers, so that a terror of the sight struck the eyes of those watching. Because of this, his calculated arrogance <note>original: *artifex arrogantia*</note> feigned something more of him than belongs to human nature. Immediately, the voices of the flattering crowd rang out, sounding with honor but bringing destruction; from here and there, he was called 'god' by those shouting, and he was humbly entreated to be favorable, the people saying that..."

Rupert is finishing a thought on the chain of salvation for the elect.</note> Furthermore, as for the book of evil—the book of death—in which are written all those, and only those, who do not belong to that purpose of God, the cause was sin. This began when sin first entered into this world through the envy of the devil, as Scripture bears witness. For it was not before, but after the act of that same sin that God said to the woman: *I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions.* <note>Genesis 3:16. Rupert interprets the "multiplicity of conceptions" as the origin of the vast number of the reprobate.</note> This multiplicity, or rather "superfluity" of conceptions, has from the very beginning always violently oppressed the children of blessing—who are born more slowly and sparingly—by its sheer numerical force. <margin>Genesis 4.</margin> This began with Eve’s firstborn, Cain, who killed his righteous brother Abel; and in those last days (which are the subject of our current discussion), the one who worships and says, "Who is like the beast, and who can fight against it?" will persecute and kill the remnants of the children of that same blessing. <margin>

Matthew 26.

<margin>Exodus 21.</margin>
The author wished to rouse us vehemently and make us attentive to hearing by first stating: *If anyone has an ear, let him hear.* But who would hesitate at such a voice? Who would not immediately grant that the proposition he states is true: *He who leads into captivity shall go into captivity; and he who kills with the sword must likewise be killed*? For this is the same thing that was said to Peter: *Put your sword back into its place,* to which was immediately added: *For all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword.* <note>Matthew 26:52</note> In this, it must be understood—unless they have performed penance—just as in the Law, where it is said of one who has done this or that. For example: *He who strikes a man, intending to kill him, let him die the death* <note>Exodus 21:12</note>; here, too, it must be understood: *unless he has performed penance.* Otherwise, the rule of sound doctrine will not stand. Therefore, once this true proposition has been heard or accepted, look and consider that this beast—this "man of sin" <note>A common title for the Antichrist, derived from 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note> who claims to be Christ, but is in fact a beast—has taken up the sword, led others into captivity, and killed with the sword by making war with the saints, just as this Scripture says later on.

<summary>Rupert explains that the "book of death" originated with the first sin in Eden, contrasting the overwhelming number of the wicked with the "few" children of blessing. He then interprets the warning about the sword as a universal law of justice that applies to the Beast (the Antichrist), though he notes that for humans, divine judgment always allows for the possibility of penance.</summary>

A question concerning the other beast.

We have already stated that the beast with seven heads represents the entire <term>generation of the wicked</term> <note>Rupert uses "generation" to mean the lineage or collective group of people throughout history who oppose God.</note>, and those seven heads were or are the seven kingdoms of the world whose power at various times crushed the saints of the Most High—the seventh head of which will be the Antichrist. What then is this other beast which he saw rising out of the earth? Or how can there be two beasts, since there is only one "body" for the wicked and perverse generation, just as, conversely, there is only one "body" for the one holy and elect generation?

<margin>
The answer is the magical art.
</margin>
To this it must be known: although the wicked generation is one, it is nevertheless called "this beast" and "another beast" because of its double power—namely, its **warlike or royal power**, and its **magical power**. Regarding this magical power, the scripture begins this narrative of the divine vision when it says: **"And I saw another beast rising up out of the earth."** When do you think this other beast rose up, which he saw rising? Surely at one and the same time when that first beast rose up, having seven heads, the seventh head of which will be the kingdom of the Antichrist. For as soon as the generation of the impious subjected the generation of the saints to servitude, and afflicted them, and brought them to bitterness through hard labor...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book V

->[Page] 374<-

...and to take up his loftiness, by which he is exalted above everything that is called God or that is worshipped. <note>Rupert is quoting 2 Thessalonians 2:4, referring to the pride of the Antichrist.</note> How did he do this? He says:

> **And he performed great signs, even making fire come down from heaven to earth in the sight of men.**

Great is the power, great and wonderful the effectiveness, of the spirit of deception. But to whom will this seem great? Surely to those who are perishing (as the Apostle <note>The "Apostle" refers to St. Paul.</note> says) because they did not receive the clarity of the truth so that they might be saved. <margin>2 Thessalonians 2</margin> This must be carefully observed. This is a key concept for Rupert: inner spiritual health protects against outer deception.</note> He clearly asserts that unless they had already perished inwardly, they would not be led astray; unless they had first abandoned the love of the truth within themselves, they would by no means yield to lying wonders on the outside. Is this not the customary and ancient order of perishing? Finally, we almost all know the same regarding the first human beings: 

<margin>Those tempted would not have yielded so quickly unless they had first perished within.</margin>

that unless they had first perished within through pride, and unless they had abandoned the love of the truth, they would not have yielded so easily when tempted from without; they would not have bowed so quickly to the miraculous speech of the serpent—a brute animal—nor believed its promises. Therefore, regarding that which the Apostle now says universally—that they did not receive the love of truth so that they might be saved—God will for this reason send them a **working of error** <note>original: "operationem erroris." Often translated in Bibles as "strong delusion."</note> so that they might believe a lie, and so that all who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity might be judged. By an example most lamentable and harmful to us, it is a constant and indubitable truth that it happened this way to our first parents. Because they did not receive the love of truth, God sent them a "working of error" in that serpent. Therefore, let us not marvel as if what will happen to them is something new—that such a beast should perform great signs in their sight and deceive them, just as the Scripture says in the following words:

> **And he deceives those who dwell on the earth because of the signs...**

...which were granted to him to perform in the sight of the beast, telling those who dwell on the earth to make an **image of the beast** that had the wound of the sword and yet lived. And it was granted to him to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might speak.

Indeed, he will lead no one astray except those who have already perished, those who have abandoned the love of the truth. <note>original: "charitatem veritatis." Rupert maintains that inner spiritual corruption must precede outer deception by the Antichrist.</note> But what truly great or unheard-of magnitude do these "greatest signs" actually possess—those which he is able to perform, and which Scripture has highlighted here for their excellence? For one is found in what it says: **that he would even make fire come down from heaven in the sight of men.** Another miracle is in what it says: **And it was granted to him to give breath to the image of the beast, so that the image of the beast might speak.**

Are these things of such a kind or so great that the devil has never done them before? Did he not also make fire descend from heaven in the sight of men, when power was given to him to tempt Job? "The fire of God" (said that messenger, who did not know what was really happening or what Satan was plotting), "the fire of God fell from heaven and, striking them, consumed the sheep and the servants, and I alone have escaped to tell you." <margin>Genesis 3</margin> <note>Though the text here quotes Job 1:16, the margin points to Genesis 3, likely to link the Devil's actions in Job to his first appearance as the deceiver.</note> Likewise, did not that same devil give breath to his "image" and cause his "image" to speak, when the serpent spoke those wicked, death-bearing words? For through whatever image of his the devil intended to speak at that time, it is certain that the serpent who deceived the first man was his image—especially since that reptile has, from that moment on, hated the human race almost naturally.

<margin>Those who believe in the Antichrist on account of signs are without excuse.</margin>

How then will they be excusable, those who, seduced by signs of this kind, worship that beast? Can they be excused on the grounds of ignorance? Surely, if they are ignorant—if they have not read that such an "image of the beast" (namely the serpent) spoke to the first humans, and that he made fire descend from heaven upon the sheep of the blessed Job—then they are lacking in sense. But if they do know, if they have read these things, and yet do not guard themselves, they are foolish. <margin>Psalm 43</margin> <note>Rupert cites the Psalms to warn the "foolish" (insipiens) and "stupid" (stultus). In the Vulgate numbering used here, this refers to the warnings of the destruction of the ungodly.</note> As the Psalmist says, the senseless and the foolish shall perish together.

<summary>Rupert argues that the Antichrist's miracles—bringing down fire and making statues speak—are merely repetitions of the Devil's ancient tactics seen in the Book of Job and the Garden of Eden. He concludes that those who fall for these tricks are without excuse, as the warnings are clearly laid out in Scripture.</summary>

This is that perverse change: This <note>The Antichrist or the Second Beast.</note> is the one who is far dissimilar, yet seeks to be "like the Most High." <note>A reference to Isaiah 14:14, traditionally associated with the fall of Lucifer and his prideful desire to equal God.</note> For the Most High will make all—small and great, rich and poor, free and slave—without distinction of persons or origins, whether Jews or Greeks; all, I say, He will make to have His own character <note>original: "characterē"; here referring to the spiritual "mark" or "seal" impressed upon the soul.</note> equally on their foreheads and on their hands, by legal as well as Gospel authority.

<margin>Deuteronomy 6.</margin>
For in the Law it says: *The words which I command you, you shall meditate upon while sitting in your house, and walking on the journey, while sleeping or rising, and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand...* <note>original: "verba quę ego pręcipio tibi meditaberis sedēs in domo tua... & ligabis ea quafi fignum in manu tua." See Matthew 28:19.</note> For when all are baptized, whether small or great, they receive on their foreheads the character of the name of Christ, and the seal of the cross.

<margin>The number of the name of the Lord.</margin>
And they receive the number of the name of the Lord—that is, the number of the three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, they receive this number so that they may profess it of the one Christ; for Christ is not only man or only God, but is both God and man, consisting of a rational soul and human flesh, with the divinity of the Word in one person. The false prophets <note>Rupert identifies the "Second Beast" of Revelation as the collective body of false teachers or a specific "pseudo-prophet."</note> will attempt to take away this number from the foreheads, hearts, and mouths of all, so that, on the contrary, the character of the name of the beast and the number of his name may be inscribed.

<margin>The number of the beast.</margin>
He <note>John the Evangelist, author of Revelation.</note> wants the listener to be vigilant, as if pointing out the place with a finger and looking around. *Here*, he says, *is wisdom.* And immediately: *If anyone has wisdom, let him calculate the number of the beast.* What kind of number, or why should he calculate the number of the beast? *For it is*, he says, *the number of a man, and his number is six hundred sixty-six.* What is this, that he himself writes out the number, and yet says: "He who has wisdom, let him calculate the number of the beast"? Does he intend this: that by calculating wisely, you should search through this whole matter to see how many <term>monads</term> <note>From the Greek 'monas'; refers to individual units or the number one.</note> or certainly <term>decades</term> <note>From the Greek 'dekas'; refers to groups of ten.</note> are in that number? ### On Apocalypse Chapter 13

...in such a great writing, would one search or propose that it be searched? Therefore, since no one is summoned here to calculate except he who has wisdom, perhaps the problem lies in the number. 

<margin>Ancient consideration of the fathers.</margin>
And indeed, illustrious men, commentators on this scripture before us, vigorously handling this number, noticed certain names—three Greek and one Gothic: **A N T E M O S**, **A R N O Y M E**, **T E I T A N**, **G E N S E R I C O S**. <note>original: "A N T E M O S  A R N O Y M E  T E I T A N  G E N S E R I C O S"</note> Of these, the first is interpreted as "contrary to honor"; the second as "I deny"; the third as "the sun"; and the fourth as "seducer of nations." <note>These interpretations rely on Greek gematria, where letters double as numbers.</note>

<margin>The number 666 in each of these four names.</margin>
The letters of each of these names contain within themselves the number six hundred sixty-six. For the first letter of this name, which is **A N T E M O S**, the letter *a* signifies one, *n* fifty, *t* three hundred, short *e* five, *m* forty, short *o* seventy, and *s* two hundred. Similarly with the other name, **A R N O Y M E**. For *a* shows one, *r* one hundred, *n* fifty, short *o* seventy, *u* four hundred, *m* forty, and short *e* five; which, when drawn together, make six hundred sixty-six. Furthermore, in the name which is **T E I T A N**, the letter *t* expresses three hundred, short *e* five, *i* ten, likewise *t* three hundred, *a* one, and *n* fifty; which, joined together, make six hundred sixty-six. Moreover, the Gothic name written in Greek letters in this way, **G E N S E R I C U S** <note>original: "GENSERICUS"; likely referring to the Vandal King Genseric, an Arian persecutor of the Church.</note>, shows *g* as three, *e* five, *n* fifty, *s* two hundred, *e* eight, *r* one hundred, *i* ten, *c* <note>The Greek kappa.</note> twenty, *o* seventy, and *s* two hundred.

This investigation of the fathers is to be praised; nevertheless, there is still that which might be inquired of not without purpose. Would that beast wish to be called by such names, or to be saluted by such titles? 

<margin>Insufficient consideration of the fathers.</margin>
Would he reward with his peace those by whom he is called "contrary to honor" or "seducer of nations," so that they might be able to sell or buy? For you have it here, that no one can buy or sell unless they have the mark or the name of the beast, or the number of his name. Would he decree this: that "contrary"—which is Satan—or **A N T E M O S**, or "denier," or "seducer of nations" be proclaimed, and that whoever has proclaimed this shall be free, and able to sell or buy? Or would he be content with the giant-like name that is **T E I T A N**, since he exalts... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the critique of why these traditional names might not fully satisfy the prophecy's requirements.</note>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129) was a Benedictine theologian. This work is his "Commentary on the Apocalypse."</note>

...above all that is called God or that is worshipped, showing himself as if he were God? <note>A reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:4, describing the Antichrist.</note> Among us Latins, the letters with which **D I C L V X** <note>original: "D I C L V X"</note> is written contain the same number. For **D** signifies five hundred, **I** one, **C** one hundred, **L** fifty, **V** five, and **X** ten: which, collected into one, similarly make six hundred sixty-six. But even if the Scripture in this place openly ascribed that name to him and said the number of this name was six hundred sixty-six, would there not then also remain the task of seeking how this number pertained to that man?

<margin>This number is to be sought in the scriptures.</margin>

Therefore, since this number is placed here, and yet wisdom is required for its calculation by saying: *If anyone has understanding, let him calculate the number of the beast*: let us seek wisdom, let us consult the Holy Scripture, without which we can find or say nothing constant or certain, whether about the number of God or about the number of the beast that exalts itself against God.

<margin>Judges 14</margin>

For just as that Samson was able to say truly: *If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle* <note>original: "Si non arassetis in vitula mea, non inuenissetis propositionem meā" — Judges 14:18.</note>: so our Lord Jesus Christ—whose riddles or problems are surely all the profound mysteries contained in this book—might truly say to us: "If you had not plowed in other scriptures, you would not find the solution to this number, which the present scripture has marked."

First, it must be carefully noticed that earlier, when it was said that no one might buy or sell except those who have the mark or the name of the beast, or the number, the text pointedly added: *of his name*. But later, when it says: *If anyone has wisdom, let him calculate the number*, it made no mention of the name, but only said, *let him calculate the number of the beast*, and then, *and his number is*—without any mention of the name—*six hundred sixty-six*.

<margin>The beast signifies one thing, his name another.</margin>

Why is this, unless because the name of the beast signifies one thing, and the beast itself is another? For the beast itself is a man, and the devil dwells within him; however, the name which he usurps for himself—which if one does not confess, they will not be able to buy or sell—is **God**. For he opposes and exalts himself, as has been said many times now, above all that is...

<margin>2 Thessalonians 2</margin>
