# On Revelation Chapter 13

<margin>Two numbers are to be considered here.</margin>
...as God, or as that which is worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as if he were God. <note>Continuing the reference to 2 Thessalonians 2:4 regarding the Antichrist.</note> Therefore, it is necessary to understand two numbers here: one of the name that the beast usurps for himself—namely, the name of God—and the other of the beast himself, which is the number of the man he shall be. For the number of God is one thing, and the number of man—indeed, of every rational creature that does not attain the grace of the Creator, whether man or angel—is another. Indeed, the number of the Creator and the creature should have been one; but the creature chose another number for itself by disagreeing with the Creator.

<margin>The number of the Creator is the septenary <note>The "septenary" refers to the number seven.</note></margin>
What is that number of the Creator? The septenary number, as the Scripture says: 
> And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had carried out. And he blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it he had ceased from all his work that God created so that he might act. <note>Genesis 2:2–3.</note>

<margin>Genesis 2. The number of the creature is the senary <note>The "senary" refers to the number six.</note></margin>
But what is the number of the creature? The senary number: because, clearly, Scripture encompasses the entire creation within the six-day number, and on the sixth day—indeed, the sixth day itself—is the creation of man. And man was indeed created for this purpose: that after the work of obedience was completed, he might keep the Sabbath <note>original: "sabbatizaret" — to observe a period of rest.</note> with God on the seventh day, that is, to find rest, and thereby be filled with the good signified by the saying: *And God completed his work on the seventh day which he had made.* 

<margin>Hebrews 4, Psalm 95 <note>The original margin cites Psalm 93, but the text quotes Psalm 95, which corresponds to the Vulgate's Psalm 94.</note></margin>
For the seventh day signifies the reward for good work, as the Apostle <note>Rupert refers to Saint Paul, the traditional author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.</note> also testifies when he says: 
> For we who have believed enter into rest, just as he said: *As I swore in my wrath, they shall not enter into my rest.* And indeed, although the works were finished from the foundation of the world, he spoke in a certain place concerning the seventh day thus: *And God rested on the seventh day from all his works,* and in this place again: *if they shall enter into my rest.* Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again defines a certain day, "Today," saying through David after so long a time, as was said above: *Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts,* etc. <note>Hebrews 4:3–7.</note>

<margin>Psalm 95</margin>
So that, I say, he might enter into that rest of the day, so that in the sabbath-rest <note>original: "sabbatismo" — a technical term for the eternal rest of the saints.</note> of that septenary number with God...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz contrasts the "Number of God" (seven, representing rest and completion) with the "Number of the Creature" (six, representing the work of creation and man's incomplete state). He argues that the Antichrist's number (666) stems from the creature's failure to transition from the labor of the sixth day into the divine rest of the seventh.</summary>

# Commentary of Rupert, Book 8

...that man might keep the Sabbath; for that very reason he was created. But neither did man enter [into that rest] then, nor will the devil, who deceived him, ever enter. For both, without God—indeed, against God—wished to glory in the created world and in themselves. Therefore, he says:

**For it is the number of a man.**

<margin>The number of man, not of God, is in the Antichrist.</margin>
He had previously stated: "If anyone has wisdom, let him calculate the number of the beast." <note>Revelation 13:18.</note> It is as if he were to say: "If anyone has wisdom, when they see that man of sin, the son of perdition <note>A title for the Antichrist from 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note>, powerful and wealthy, extolling himself and resisting, killing, and glorifying himself magnificently in all things, let him reconsider and weigh carefully that whatever he speaks and whatever he does does not belong to that rest [of the Sabbath]. It is not of that seventh day of the Creator, nor of the Word of God, nor of the kingdom of charity. Instead, all of it belongs only to the created world, to the lust of the eyes, and to the pride of life." <note>A reference to 1 John 2:16, describing worldly temptations.</note> And so, as if confirmed by a certain argument, let the wise man know and say that this man is not who he claims to be; he is not God, but deceitfully displays himself as if he were God. When, therefore, he said, "for it is the number of a man," a simple or singular six could be understood, if indeed that man were only a man and not also the devil. But in truth, that man is indeed a man by nature, but the devil will be entirely within him with all his power and all his fullness; and the coming of that same man, as the Apostle says, will be according to the operation of Satan. Therefore, there follows:

**And his number is six hundred and sixty-six.**

<margin>1 John 2.</margin>
<margin>His number is 666.</margin>
Behold, the number six is repeated three times—indeed, it is multiplied tenfold, and then hundredfold. What we now say is very well known to arithmeticians or those who use the abacus. <note>Rupert refers to "abacists," scholars who used the abacus for calculations, which was the standard method for mathematics in the Middle Ages.</note> The character for six, passing from the first (that is, the singular) limit into the second (that is, the tenth) limit, makes sixty; and likewise, being carried over into the third (that is, the hundredth) limit, it makes six hundred. When, therefore, he says, "and his number is six hundred and sixty-six," the number six—which was the number of man, as has already been said—does not reach the seventh day, the Sabbath (which is the rest of God), because of his transgression. The transgression of the second and third limits...

He uses medieval arithmetic to show how the "number of man" is amplified through the ones, tens, and hundreds places to represent the fullness of evil.</summary>

# On Chapter 13 of the Apocalypse

<margin>The number 666 signified the three-fold transgression of the devil. **I**</margin>
...it has been multiplied. What is this, (dearest reader), except that the devil Satan—by whose operation that man [the Antichrist] will come and who will dwell entirely within him—multiplied his labor a second and third time after he once shook himself loose from the rest of God, from the heavenly Sabbath? Let us note and trace back where, when, and how that ancient transgressor—that industrious multiplier—multiplied his number in this way.

**I.** First, when heaven and earth and all their adornment were perfected, on the seventh day God completed the work which He had done, and rested from all the work He had performed. He [the devil], however, did not rest with the resting Creator on His seventh day; indeed, long ago, because of the restlessness of his pride, he had been cast down from heaven into this dark air. 

<margin>Psalm 11</margin>
"The wicked walk in a circle" <note>original: *in circuitu ambulat impius*; Rupert quotes Psalm 12:8 (Psalm 11 in the Vulgate) to suggest the devil is trapped in the repetitive cycle of the "six days" of creation, unable to reach the "seventh day" of eternal rest.</note> and he was laboring. Therefore, he was in the number six <note>original: *senario*; the number associated with the six days of creation and manual work.</note>, within this six-day creation.

<margin>Psalm 38 **II**</margin>
In this number six, the penitent man, grieving that he is held back and sighing for the seventh day, says in the Psalm: "Lord, make me know my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me." <note>Psalm 39:4 (Vulgate 38:5). Rupert interprets "what is lacking" as the seventh day of rest which follows the "number of days" (the six days of life).</note> 

**II.** But that wicked and transgressing angel did not do so; rather, since he was outside of rest or the seventh day, and while his "six" was still simple or singular [6], he was not content with his own labor. Instead, through envy, he added to it so that he might drag the human race into the same labor with him by deceiving the <term>protoplast</term> <note>From the Greek *protoplastos*, meaning "first-formed," referring to Adam.</note>. By doing this, he certainly increased his transgression; and rightly, just as his own labor is imputed to him, so too is the labor of man. 

**III.** Therefore, his first "six" was multiplied, and his number has now become sixty-six [66]. But not even content with this, he will add yet more so that he may entirely enter that "man of sin, the son of perdition" <note>2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note>. Through him, he will do that which we now marvel at regarding the malignant beast in this present passage. There, undoubtedly, by a third transgression, his "six" will be multiplied. This occurs when he—who first deceived the first man by guile without force—will now use both guile in lying wonders and force (the sword) as the manifest enemy of God and men. This he does with persisting envy, through which he brought death into the world, and with a pride that persists and indeed increases for the worse, through which he exalted himself in heaven against God. Therefore, when the Apostle had well said, "For it is the number of a man," he added:

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the number 666 as a three-stage progression of evil: the devil's initial fall (6), his deception of Adam (60), and his final possession of the Antichrist (600).</summary>

# On the Apocalypse of John the Apostle, Book IX of the Commentaries

<margin>Concerning the spirit of knowledge.</margin>
Where we go now, and where we direct the course of our discourse, is shown to us by the radiant order of the seven spirits of the Lord <note>The "seven spirits" refer to the gifts of the Holy Spirit listed in Isaiah 11:2-3: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord.</note>, whom we have proposed to follow closely. For it was not in vain that this John, at the beginning of this volume, wrote of grace and peace from the seven spirits who are in the presence of the throne of God to the seven churches.

<margin>Isaiah 11.</margin>
Moreover, in the order of those same spirits, according to the prophetic proclamation of Isaiah, the fifth is the **spirit of knowledge**. This follows the one whose great works we beheld in the preceding vision during the battles of the martyrs—namely, the **spirit of fortitude** <note>original: *fortitudinis spiritum*; Rupert is mapping the structure of his commentary to the traditional sequence of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He identifies the previous section on the martyrs' struggle with "Fortitude" and this new section with "Knowledge."</note>. The supreme or final contest of those battles will be the one which the first beast shall carry out by itself—the beast whose number we calculated just a little while ago. This beast, of course, will be the Antichrist, who must be shut out in his own time. Therefore, where we go now we know not, but

<meta>This page continues Rupert’s transition into Book IX of his commentary. Following the discussion of the "spirit of fortitude" (associated with the martyrs' resistance to the Beast), he now moves to the "spirit of knowledge," linking the vision of the 144,000 on Mount Sion to the historical revelation of God's Law through Moses and the Evangelists.</meta>

<margin>Exodus 12.</margin>
This radiant order of spirits (as has already been said) leads us to consider that a recapitulation <note>original: *capitulationem*; a theological term for when a narrative "circles back" to retell history from a different perspective.</note> is occurring here. We are filled from this place with those things which the holy spirit of knowledge performed in the world, where the Lamb is seen standing upon Mount Sion. For where the knowledge of God first began to be given or written, there Christ, the Lamb of God, began to be prefigured. Indeed, where Moses—that writer through the knowledge of God—wrote the Law, there the lamb began to be sacrificed as a type <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of Christ.</note> of Christ, and the doorposts of the sons of Israel were anointed with its blood. Furthermore, in these one hundred and forty-four thousand singing a kind of new song before the throne, and before the four living creatures and the elders, and in the four angels flying through the midst of heaven, having the eternal gospel—the fourth of whom is John himself, who says: *And I heard a voice from heaven saying: Write, blessed are the dead who die in the Lord*—and in the seven wings of the seven angels; in these, I say, we understand all the builders or arrangers of heavenly knowledge (that is, of Holy Scripture). According to these men, or according to these studies, the wondrous holy spirit of knowledge enters to preach.

->**And I saw (he says) and behold, a lamb stood upon Mount Sion.**<-

<margin>The true Lamb prefigured in the Law.</margin>
This vision suddenly brings John’s eye back from the end of the ages—where a moment ago he had seen the Beast (that is, the wicked head of the beast and the Antichrist) struck by the sword of eternal damnation—to the beginnings of the ages, namely to the times of the promise or the faith of the patriarchs. It is from there that all these recapitulated things run and return again. Truly, this Lamb is Christ, who now indeed stands in his own person upon Mount Sion, above all the dignity of the Church, above all sovereignty, and all the powers of the heavens. 
<margin>Exodus 12.</margin>
But back then, when the promise was being made or had recently been fulfilled, he stood in figure (as has already been said), when from that time the lamb was sacrificed in the houses of the children of Israel. By its blood the doorposts were marked while the flesh was eaten, and the firstborn of the Egyptians died, and the children of Israel...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 9 <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129) was a Benedictine abbot and influential theologian whose works often focused on the symbolic meaning of Scripture.</note>

<margin>Exodus 3.</margin>...[the God of] Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. But because faith alone without works is not enough for perfection or for life, twelve thousand are again multiplied by twelve <note>The number twelve represents the "duodenary" or the foundation of the people of God (the twelve tribes and the twelve apostles).</note>, and they become one hundred and forty-four thousand. By this number, both the confession of faith and the abundance of good works are signified. Therefore, so many saints standing with the Lamb, having the name of that same Lamb and the name of his Father written on their foreheads, are all the perfect children of Abraham from that time—the time, namely, when Christ (who was to suffer for the whole world) was prefigured every year through the sacrifice of the Passover lamb. The present text immediately commends their perfection in a magnificent and wonderful way. For it follows:

> And I heard a voice from heaven, like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of great thunder, and the voice I heard was like that of harpers playing on their harps. And they sang as if it were a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders, and no one could learn <note>original: *dicere*, literally "to say" or "to speak," but used here in the sense of reciting or mastering the song.</note> the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand who were redeemed from the earth. These were redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and the Lamb, and in their mouth no lie was found. They are without blemish before the throne of God.

First, regarding this chapter, the argument requires me to address the fact that when he had said, *And no one could learn the song except those one hundred and forty-four thousand who were redeemed from the earth*, he immediately—as if he had been asked by what merit they alone could sing such a song—adds: *These are those who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins.*

# On Apocalypse Chapter 14
B iij

<margin>Bodily virginity has a great privilege. 1 Corinthians 7.</margin>
Regarding the virginity of the flesh <note>The author is distinguishing between physical celibacy (virginity of the flesh) and spiritual purity or faithfulness to God (virginity of the mind).</note>, this praise can indeed be taken quite usefully. It is very effective for encouraging, comforting, and strengthening that sweet vow of virginal beauty, in which one is permitted to "think on the things of the Lord" <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 7:34, where Paul discusses the advantages of the unmarried state for devotion to God.</note>. For truly, devoted virginity of the body, when joined with virginity of the mind, possesses a great privilege. Nevertheless, so that we may maintain the planned order of our discussion, something else must be said—something against which no authority from the Scriptures or reason can be proven to conflict. For no one would lightly dare to attribute so much to bodily virginity as to judge that a certain song to be sung by the holy virgins would be "unsingable" for all others, no matter how great some of those others might be. For example: take the apostle Peter from the New Testament, and Moses from the Old Testament. Concerning them, it is well known that, according to the flesh, they were not of a virginal state <note>original: *virginalis propositi*, referring to the fact that both Peter and Moses were married men.</note>. Therefore, having briefly set these matters aside, let us now follow the order of the text.

### "And I heard," he said, "a voice from heaven like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of great thunder."

<margin>The voice from heaven is Holy Scripture.</margin>
With the Lamb standing upon Mount Zion with his marked ones, a voice from heaven began to be heard like the voice of many waters, and like the voice of great thunder. This is because, clearly, when the passion of Christ, the Son of God, began to be prefigured through the symbolic sacrifice of the Passover lamb in Egypt, then also the voice of God began to be heard through Scripture. For it was then that Moses wrote the Law, which he certainly received not from the earth, but from heaven—not from man, but from God. After this, the other just men and prophets wrote down the knowledge of God, and they too spoke not from the earth, but from heaven. Whence comes that saying: "For Holy Scripture was never brought by human will, but holy men of God spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Spirit." <note>original: *ii. Pe. i.* (2 Peter 1:21). The author is arguing that the Bible itself is the "voice from heaven."</note> "I heard, therefore," he said, "a voice from heaven." Furthermore, Holy Scriptures are sometimes signified by the name of "waters," as in that passage: "All you who thirst, come to the waters" <note>Isaiah 55:1.</note>. It is also usually compared to "thunder," clearly because of the terrifying threat of the future judgment, according to that: "And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High [gave his voice]" <note>Psalm 18:13.</note>.
<margin>2 Peter 1.</margin>

...He gave His voice. Indeed, the first judgment has already been carried out through water <note>A reference to the Great Flood in the time of Noah, described in Genesis 7.</note>, but these same Scriptures testify, as if thundering at some future time, that the second judgment shall be through fire. Therefore, it rightly describes that voice—the voice of the heavenly Scriptures—as the "voice of many waters" and as the "voice of great thunder." <margin>
The holy prophets and apostles are like strings on harps, stretched out through afflictions.

*And the voice which I heard was like harpists playing on their harps.*

Finally, just as there is the harshness of terror in thunder, but the sweetness of delight in sounding harps, so in the Holy Scriptures the threat of judgment terrifies and healthfully disturbs sinners, while the promise of rewards soothes and gladdens those who perform good works. And it should be noted that the sounding strings in harps delight those who listen, but the strings themselves "labor" in their own stretching. 

<margin>Numbers 11.</margin>
In this way, those through whom the Holy Scripture was established delighted good listeners by promising good things in their own time; yet they themselves labored within themselves and were frequently worn out. Hence the first of them, Moses, said to the Lord: *Why have you afflicted your servant? Why do I find no grace before you? Why have you laid the weight of all this people upon me?* <note>original: "Cur afflixisti seruum tuum?..." from Numbers 11:11. Moses is expressing the heavy burden of leadership and prophecy.</note> And further: *If it seems otherwise to you, I beseech you to kill me, that I may find grace in your eyes, lest I be afflicted with such great evils.* 

<margin>Hebrews 11.</margin>
But those saints were also worn out in various other ways, just as the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul, traditionally considered the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews.</note>, remembering them, says among other things: *Others truly experienced mockery and beatings, and moreover chains and prisons; they were stoned, they were sawn asunder, they were tempted, they died by the edge of the sword. They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, distressed, afflicted, etc.* 

<margin>The voluntary affliction of some.</margin>
They were, therefore, like harpists playing on their harps, because while sounding the testimonies of truth, they were stretched out by many tribulations. But they also afflicted themselves by a voluntary stretching <note>Rupert compares the "stretching" of a harp string—necessary to produce a musical note—to the "stretching" of a martyr or ascetic through suffering or self-denial.</note>, so that they might deserve to receive the celestial grace of the blessed song, as we read concerning Daniel and his companions...

Thus they sang before the throne and before the four living creatures, that is, in preparation for the kingdom of God, in service to the Gospel of Christ, and for the instruction of those whose "venerable old age"—that is, their immaculate life—rules the Church of God. <margin>Firstfruits for God and the Lamb.</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 2</margin>
...they justify with all his same judgments, and they imitate the example of his charity even unto death, just as John says: "Because he laid down his life for us, we also ought to lay down our lives for our brothers." <note>original: "Quia ille pro nobis animam posuit, & nos debemus pro fratribus ponere," from 1 John 3:16</note> Likewise, this should not be overlooked: when he said, "These were bought from among men," he added, "firstfruits for God and the Lamb." <note>Revelation 14:4</note> For from this it is clear that the earlier saints are meant, of whom the holy mystical Law says: "If you offer a gift of the firstfruits of your crops to the Lord, from ears of grain still green, you shall roast them with fire and crush them in the manner of meal, and so you shall offer your firstfruits to the Lord, pouring oil over them and adding frankincense." <note>original: "Si obtuleris munus primitiarum frugum tuarum domino, de spicis adhuc virentibus, torres eas igni & cõfringes eas in morem farris..." from Leviticus 2:14-15</note> For the "ears of grain still green" were the holy men of the earlier ages of the world, from whom we then offer a gift to the Lord when we resolve to live well according to their example. Truly, in their actions some things are found that were permitted then, which now—in a more mature age—are cut away by the sickle of the Gospel; thus, it is said to the Son of Man sitting upon the cloud: "Put in your sharp sickle, for the hour to reap has come, because the harvest of the earth is ripe." <note>original: "Mitte falcem tuam acutam..." from Revelation 14:15. Rupert is contrasting the "green" or immature laws of the Old Testament with the "ripe" or "dry" harvest of the Gospel era.</note> Therefore, you "roast them with fire"—that is, through the holy spirit of discernment you immediately distinguish between the two eras. Those things which you have learned in the Gospel are not to be imitated, you will certainly not condemn, but neither will you imitate them; and so you will offer them with the addition of oil and frankincense—that is, you will imitate their good deeds with charity for the honor of God. Therefore, these were "bought from among men as firstfruits for God and the Lamb," which is the same as if he were to say: Christ, the Lamb of God, redeemed these from the mass of the human race, these who were proven by the testimony of faith in that earlier and still fresh age. Concerning which testimony of faith, it is further added:

*   **Revelation**: The uncovering of divine mysteries. <gloss>Apocalypse</gloss>

"...now," says the Spirit, "that they may rest from their labors, for their works follow them." <note>original: "iam dicit spiritus, ut requiescant a laboribus suis, Opera enim illorum sequuntur illos." This concludes Revelation 14:13, a blessing on those who die in the Lord.</note>

<margin>The humility of John speaking concerning himself.</margin>
After the song of the one Mount Zion, these four do not stand upon any single mountain or place, but fly through the midst of heaven, and with a loud, public voice, they preach to the whole world. The fourth is John himself, who, thinking more humbly of himself, did not say, "a fourth followed the three others flying through the midst of heaven," but rather, "I heard," he said, "a voice from heaven saying to me: Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord." Indeed, just as he had said: "I saw an angel flying through the midst of heaven," to preach the Gospel saying, "fear the Lord"; and "another followed him" saying, "fallen, fallen is Babylon"; and "a third followed them" saying, "if anyone shall worship the beast," etc.; so he could have said: "And a fourth—I myself—was about to follow them," saying, "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord." But he rightly preferred to speak this way, both to speak more humbly of himself and to express the reality of the matter. For now, through these who preach the Gospel—or who possess the **eternal Gospel**—among whom he places himself in the fourth position, the four Evangelists <note>The authors of the four Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.</note> are understood, of whom he is the fourth, because he wrote his Gospel last.

<margin>The Old Testament given to only one nation.</margin>
Meanwhile, it is necessary to remember what we said above: regarding the order of the **seven spirits** who are in the sight of the throne of God, we are preaching the specific works or gifts of the **Spirit of Knowledge** <term>spiritus scientiae: one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit listed in Isaiah 11</term> under the images of this present vision. Whatever of this grace had been given before the coming of Christ, whatever celestial knowledge was in the Law and the Prophets, it was celebrated on only one mountain, Zion, and in only one temple which was in Jerusalem; for only there were the holy people of that nation found.

<margin>The New Testament given to all nations.</margin>
But when Christ came, His Gospel immediately sounded through the public sphere of the whole world, with the Law and the Prophets joined to it, and then the knowledge of God was multiplied. This fulfilled what Daniel had foretold: "many shall pass through and knowledge shall be manifold." <note>A reference to Daniel 12:4, interpreted here as the expansion of Christian teaching across the globe.</note> Rightly, therefore, according to these visions, the song was first heard only on Mount Zion, but these...

# On Chapter 14 of the Apocalypse

...shall drink the undiluted wine in the cup of His wrath, and he shall be tormented with fire and sulfur in the sight of the holy angels and before the sight of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torments shall ascend forever and ever. Nor do they have rest day or night, those who have worshipped the beast and its image, and if anyone has received the mark of its name.

<margin>The third angel with the face of a man.</margin>
And this third angel speaks according to his face—that is, according to the face of a man. For it says that the third living creature <note>The "living creatures" (tetramorph) from Revelation 4:7—the lion, calf, man, and eagle—are here used by Rupert to categorize the sequence of angels and their specific messages.</note> had a face like that of a man. What indeed does he say? After the first angel, who had said, "Fear the Lord and worship Him," this one establishes the law and prescribes the sentence for those who have worshipped another besides the same God. For in the judging of those who have done this, the "face of a man" will appear to all <note>Rupert implies that Christ will judge in His human form, making the judgment visible and relatable to humanity.</note>. Concerning this beast and its image, its name, and even the number of its name and its mark—which anyone who does not have in that final persecution will be unable to sell or buy—these things were discussed above.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he also shall drink": he says this because the previous angel had said, "Babylon has fallen, has fallen," for her to fall is surely to drink the cup of damnation. 

<margin>The phrase "wine mixed with undiluted wine" is spoken ironically.</margin>
Moreover, this very punishment of damnation is called "wine" or "undiluted wine mixed" <note>original: "vinum aut merum mixtum"</note> with the gravest irony, for it would be more properly called the most bitter gall. In another sense, it truly is "undiluted wine" <note>original: "vinum merum"</note> because the judgment is just and irreproachable. In that place, judgment will be entirely without mercy. For who will show mercy where even the Lamb of mercies Himself will no longer be mindful of His own mercies? It should certainly be noted that when he had said, "and he shall be tormented with fire and sulfur," he added: "In the sight of the holy angels," and not content with that, he added further: "And in the sight of the Lamb." He called the judge himself "the Lamb" here, and yet he still added: "And the smoke of their torments shall ascend forever and ever, and they have no rest day or night," etc. It is a great and wonderful thing that He who judges or punishes is the Lamb Himself, and yet He is inflexible toward mercy forever and ever; and it is said: "Many things are judged here..."

->c<-

<summary>Rupert explains the third angel's warning in Revelation 14, identifying the angel with the 'face of a man' and interpreting the 'undiluted wine' of God's wrath as a metaphor for a final judgment that is perfectly just but entirely devoid of mercy.</summary>

<margin>The error of certain people.</margin>
...of His judgments is an abyss hidden from us. Many have borne their ignorance of this depth with impatience. They feel, without a doubt, that God is nonetheless merciful; they reckon instead that it is their own failing that they cannot penetrate the height of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, <margin>Romans 11</margin> nor comprehend His judgments, nor investigate His ways. They bear this same failing of theirs with great patience, <margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin> knowing that they "know in part" until that which is perfect comes. Whence it is immediately added:

<margin>The patience of the saints in the severity of judgment.</margin>
> Here is the patience of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.

*Here*, he says—that is, in the fact that [the wicked] are said to be tormented forever and ever in the sight of the Lamb, and in the fact that the Lamb <note>Rupert identifies the Lamb as the judge whose presence is a source of mercy for the saved but a source of "inflexible" torment for the damned.</note> shall be toward them for mercy forever and ever—is the inflexible patience of the saints. They do not murmur as if against excessive severity, those who keep the commandments of God, namely knowing that the judgment is to come; who keep the faith of Jesus, clearly not doubting that Jesus is faithful and true, who foretold and threatened such a terrible judgment. It follows:

The eagle is the symbol of John.</note> This is John, who hears and writes in the fourth place, because after the other Evangelists, having been petitioned by the churches and taught by revelations from heaven, he undertook...

...according to <note>The Latin text begins mid-word with "-tundum," likely the end of "secundum" (according to).</note> the face (as has already been said) of a flying eagle, beginning from the secret height of the eternal Beginning <note>A reference to the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word." <margin>Isaiah 19 <note>The original margin notes Isaiah 9, but the quote is from Isaiah 19:1.</note></margin>
The one whom he had designated above, saying: *And I saw, and behold he stood upon Mount Sion*, he now expresses having seen more clearly, calling him *like the Son of man*. This is because he who was previously figured in the Law through the unblemished lamb, has now spoken through himself in the Gospel, having become the Son of man, incarnate of the Virgin Mary. For that virginal flesh—immaculate flesh assumed without any stain of original sin <term>originalis peccati</term>—is signified here by the white cloud, according to the prophet saying: *Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a white cloud, and shall enter into Egypt* <note>original: "Ecce ascendet dominus supra nubē candidam, & ingredietur Ægyptum."</note>. That is, he shall take flesh from the Virgin and enter into this world <note>In medieval exegesis, "Egypt" often symbolizes the world or the state of sin which Christ enters to redeem.</note>. For just as the sun above a white cloud indeed creates daylight for us, but does not show its full brightness—it gives light, but withdraws its own form, nor does it put forth all its fires, and yet it adequately overcomes the cold of the past chilly night—so the most bright Divinity in the flesh illuminated us through miracles and the word of wisdom, but did not manifest itself just as it is. He spoke indeed and acted as God, yet he did not show the form of God, nor did he put forth his whole power, and yet he did enough to conquer the spiritual forces of wickedness. Therefore, the likeness of the Son of man sat upon a white cloud; or rather, that very thing upon which he seemed to sit was not a real cloud, but the likeness of a cloud. For he saw these things not corporally, but in the spirit. Although this sitting of the Son of man seems rightly to be understood as his second coming...

<summary>Rupert explains the vision of the Son of Man on a white cloud as a symbol of the Incarnation, where Christ's divinity is veiled by the "cloud" of his humanity, just as the sun is veiled by clouds.</summary>

<margin>Christ is king and priest, Ecclesiasticus 45.</margin> For a twofold reason, this Son of Man is said to have a golden crown on his head: both because he is a King, and because he is a Priest. For the wise man testifies that the honor of the priesthood possesses a crown, when he says regarding the priest Aaron in the *Praise of the Fathers*: *A golden crown upon his miter, engraved with the sign of holiness, the glory of honor and a work of power* <note>original: "Corona aurea super mitram eius..." quoted from Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 45:14.</note>. He says this, moreover, concerning the holy plate upon which was written the ineffable name of the Lord, the **tetragrammaton**, that is, the name of four letters <note>The Tetragrammaton (YHWH) was inscribed on a gold plate on the High Priest's turban.</note>. 

<margin>Psalm 8.</margin> For it signified the crown of this Son of Man, of whom the Psalmist said: *What is man that thou art mindful of him, or the son of man that thou visitest him? Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels,* and immediately added: *Thou hast crowned him with glory and honor.* <margin>Philippians 2.</margin> And his name is the one of which the Apostle says: *Because of which God also hath exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name.* Therefore, let him have on his head a **golden crown**, and in his hand, he says, a **sharp sickle**—it is understood, for the purpose of reaping. For there follows:

**And another angel came out of the temple, crying with a loud voice to him that sat upon the cloud: "Thrust in thy sharp sickle, for the hour is come to reap..."**

Furthermore, one thousand six hundred <term>stadia: a Greek unit of distance (furlongs), approximately 185 meters or 125 paces</term> are two hundred thousand paces. ### On Revelation, Chapter 15

<margin>The prophets and teachers of the Law are compared to narrow cups.</margin>
...there would be) no languages nor speeches where their voices were not heard <note>original: "non essent loquelae neque sermones, quorum non audirentur voces eorum"; a reference to Psalm 19:3, implying that the Gospel is now spoken in every tongue</note>; that is, so that all kinds of languages might be born in their mouths. On the other hand, the aforementioned singers—among whom the Law and the Prophets remained hidden within the Hebrew nation alone, and who sang or read those songs in only one language, namely Hebrew—are likened to <term>cups</term> <note>original: "cyathis"; Rupert is contrasting the narrow-mouthed *cyathus* (cup) of the Old Testament with the wide-mouthed *phiala* (vial/bowl) of the New Testament</note>. Thus he says: **And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvelous.** Indeed, after that sign where he had seen the Lamb standing upon Mount Sion with the 144,000 singing a new song, this sign is truly great and marvelous: namely, that while the Son of Man is harvesting the vintage of the earth, those seven angels have the seven last plagues, and in them the wrath of God is fulfilled.

<margin>The seven angels with the vials represent all the preachers of the Gospel.</margin>
For who are these seven angels, if not the universal preachers of the Gospel, the messengers of truth? Because the Holy Spirit—who gave them the <term>vials</term> <note>original: "phialas"; also translated as "bowls"</note> already mentioned and those to be mentioned later—is sevenfold <note>referring to the seven gifts of the Spirit</note>, they are rightly encompassed by the number seven, and through them all preachers are understood together. Furthermore, he calls these the "last plagues" in respect to the "first plagues," which we mentioned earlier when the seven angels sounded the trumpets. We must later explain in order how those were the first and these are the last. However, it should be briefly tasted here that those plagues are called "first" because they struck the bodies; but these are "last" because they reach even to the souls. From this, we should also note what he says: "because in them the wrath of God is fulfilled." For wrath begins with the killing of bodies, and after it has killed, it is fulfilled by sending souls into <term>Gehenna</term> <note>a place of spiritual punishment or hell</note>. It follows:

### And I saw those who had conquered the beast and its image standing over the sea of glass.

<margin>
Why that sea is called "glassy."

We rightly understand this to refer to all the saints of both the Old and the New Testaments. For surely both those who believed he *would* come, and these who believe that **CHRIST HAS COME**, conquer the beast and its image—that is, the devil and every wicked man who imitates him—through that same faith while they believe and are baptized. Ultimately, all crimes and all sins, both original and actual, which that beast and its image forced upon them through persuasion or example, are drowned in this sea. But they themselves stand *over* the sea; that is, they are survivors so that they may cross over to the true Promised Land. The "letter of the law" once hid that land while promising it, but now the "spirit of the gospel" reveals it. For this reason, it is beautifully called a **sea of glass**: because just as what is contained in glass shines through, so in this sacrament of the Gospel nothing is now hidden. Instead, what was first performed as a <term>figure</term> <note>original: "figura"; a prophetic symbol or "type" that points to a later reality</note> is now performed in reality, and everything is made manifest. But you also rightly understand why it is called a "glassy sea" so that you may know that...

<summary>Rupert explains that the saints of the Old Testament were not saved by their own rituals (like manna or the Red Sea crossing) but were "catechized" by them until Christ's passion provided true baptism. # Who will not fear you, Lord, and magnify your name?

<margin>
No one can resist God. John 9; Psalm 75 <note>original: "Ioan. ix. psal. lxxv." Rupert cites Job 9 rather than John 9, and Psalm 76 in modern numbering.</note>
</margin>
When they say, *Who will not fear*, it is to be understood: "and have peace?" For thus another Scripture says: *Who has resisted him, and had peace?* <note>Job 9:4</note>. Likewise, it is written elsewhere: *You are terrible, and who shall resist you?* <note>Psalm 76:7</note>; it is understood, of course: "No one." And immediately a very weighty reason is given why no one can resist: *From that time [comes] your wrath.* The meaning is this: From the moment a sinner sins—not by slipping through weakness or erring through ignorance, but by resisting you through pride—from that time your wrath comes, so that, evidently, you no longer ignore the sin or call back the one who has turned away, but strike and strongly break him. Therefore, *Who will not fear you, Lord, and magnify your name?* is the same as if he said: "Since your works are so great and wonderful, Lord, and your ways so just and true, where will the proud and ungrateful appear?"

<margin>
Isaiah 2.
</margin>
For he who does not fear now as one who is subject, will fear—or rather, will be thrown into confusion as one who is crushed—according to what is said through Isaiah in a prophetic invective against him: *Enter into the rock, hide in a pit in the ground from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he shall rise up to strike the earth.* <note>Isaiah 2:10</note>.

> After these things I looked, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened, and the seven angels, having the seven plagues, went out of the temple, clothed in clean, white stone, <note>original: "vestiti lapide mundo." This reflects a variant in some Latin Vulgate manuscripts of Revelation 15:6 which read "stone" rather than the "linen" found in most modern translations.</note> and girded about the breasts with golden girdles. And one of the four living creatures gave to the seven angels seven golden bowls <note>original: "phialas." While often translated as "vials," these were shallow, broad offering bowls.</note> full of the wrath of the living God forever and ever.

<margin>

</margin>
"After these things," he says, "I saw"—it is understood to be that which I had already begun to narrate above. <summary>Rupert explains that the fear of God is the only path to peace, as prideful resistance inevitably leads to divine wrath. This temple—that is, this Church—was enclosed within only one nation, Judea, where alone God was known <note>original: "in qua sola notus erat deus"; a reference to Psalm 76:1.</note>. Thus, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony was opened. Where? "In heaven," he says. "Heaven," or the "heavens," are all the holy ones in whom God dwells, and especially the apostles. For of them it is written: *The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.* <note>Psalm 19:1</note>. Therefore, it was opened "in heaven"—that is, in the hearts of the apostles—to whom, as was said above, he opened their minds so they might understand the scriptures. And so, with the temple thus opened:

->**"And there was made," it says, "a cruel and most grievous wound upon the men who have the mark of the beast, and those who worshipped its image."**<-

Likewise, the males, having left the natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males with males working filthiness, and receiving in themselves the reward that was due for their error <note>original: "mercedem quam oportuit erroris sui." For just as a swollen sea is churned within itself by reciprocal waves—being driven now by the tide coming in and now by the tide going out <note>original: "accessibus nunc recessibus," literally the coming and going of the tides.</note>, until at last, exhausted within itself, it is bridled and calmed—so Pharaoh or Egypt fluctuated while contending against God. This was like the ebbing and flowing of the sea, until finally they perished in the very element suited to their character: namely, they died in the middle of the sea.

For example, the Psalmist says of such people: "When he slew them, then they sought him, and they returned and came to him early in the morning. <margin>The second plague of the vial.</margin>
"At the second plague," he says, "a great mountain, burning with fire, was cast into the sea." <note>Rupert is quoting Revelation 8:8, the second trumpet, to draw a parallel with the second vial he is currently explaining.</note> The preaching of the Gospel brings no such thing upon the impious who are like them, but it terribly condemns them to the future judgment. And so, just as the sinking of the burning mountain followed the song of the angel <note>Rupert often refers to the sounding of the trumpets as "songs" or "canticles" of the angels.</note> in the first instance, so this pouring out of the vial into the sea is called the second among the latest plagues.

"And it became," he says, "blood like that of a dead man." <note>Revelation 16:3</note> That is, the damnation of such impious people will be like the damnation of the devil, who has truly been dead for a long time—that is, he is opposed to the life of God. For they shall be joined with him when the Judge says: *Depart into the eternal fire, which was prepared for the devil and his angels.* <note>Matthew 25:41</note> "And every living soul," he says, "died in the sea." This is because, clearly, it is not just a third part of the human race (of which the Egyptians were a part—for they themselves were born from one of the descendants of Ham, as has already been said), but every soul without distinction will be judged, whoever is in a sea of this kind, whether it be the soul of a Jew or a Greek. And rightly so: a soul that dies in this way is said to die "living" because whoever knowingly, and envying the good, works evil, is said to "live in sin"—just like Pharaoh, who persecuted the children of Israel not through ignorance, but through envy.

*And the third angel poured out his vial upon the rivers and upon the springs of waters, and they became blood.*
<margin>The rivers <gloss>per</gloss>secutors of the saints.</margin>
By the name of "rivers" in this place, we should understand those who have persecuted the saints with a physical sword <note>Rupert uses "material sword" to distinguish physical violence from spiritual or verbal conflict.</note> as well. Upon such rivers and springs of water, when the third angel sounded his trumpet, a great star burning like a torch fell from heaven <note>Revelation 8:10</note>, that is, the wrath of God which destroyed the seven nations at the entry of the children of Israel under the leadership of Joshua. For those nations held Israel in hatred
<margin>The hatred of Amalek and Edom against the children of Israel. <note>The margin cites Deuteronomy 32, though the text below quotes Exodus 15.</note> Deuteronomy 32</margin>
from the time it ascended from the land of Egypt, as you have it in the Song of Moses. For when he had said: "In your mercy you have been a leader to the people whom you redeemed, and in your strength you have carried them to your holy habitation," he immediately added: "The peoples ascended and were angry; sorrows took hold of all the inhabitants of Philistia," etc. <note>Exodus 15:13-14</note> For they had not yet passed through...

<summary>Rupert explains the second and third vials of wrath, interpreting the "sea" and "rivers" as symbols for those who persecute the faithful. He contrasts these final, total judgments with the earlier, partial judgments of the trumpets, linking the current suffering of the Church to the biblical history of Israel, Pharaoh, and the Canaanite nations.</summary>

...the sons of Israel, and they were already being tormented. This is a quote from the Song of Moses in Exodus 15:16, though the margin references the battle in Chapter 17.</note> Amalek was the first to attack them in war, whom Moses defeated by praying while the battle raged. From this, Balaam the son of Beor says: <margin>Numbers 24</margin> <note>The text cites Chapter 23, but the prophecy is in Numbers 24:20.</note> *Amalek is the first of nations, whose end shall be destruction.* I have chosen to remember these things now, lest you say that those who took up arms against Israel were all driven by zeal and necessity because of their land, which Israel might take away. Why then did Amalek come—who was descended from Edom, the brother of Jacob—and fight with Israel? Why did Edom himself come out armed to meet his brother?

<margin>The plague of the third [vial].</margin>
**And it became, he says, blood.**

Then [at the sounding of the trumpet] it did not happen this way; instead, a third part of the waters turned into wormwood, and many people died from the waters because they were made bitter. For many of the Canaanites—who belonged to that "third part" of humanity we have often mentioned <note>Rupert historically identifies the descendants of Ham (Canaanites/Egyptians) as the "third part" of the world's population in his symbolic scheme.</note>—survived at that time, and the children of Israel lived among them and <margin>Psalm 105</margin> <note>Psalm 106 in modern Bibles.</note> *learned their works, and served their idols, and it became a stumbling block to them.* This was surely the "turning of the waters into wormwood" for them; the waters became so bitter to those who drank that they incurred the wrath of their God because of it.

Furthermore, here where the third of the final plagues is poured out—that is, the third vial—it is not so. <margin>Water [becomes] blood.</margin> It is not a third part of the waters that becomes wormwood, but it universally becomes blood. For it is not only the descendants of Ham (who, as has often been said, was one of the three sons of Noah), but the whole universe of persecuting nations is condemned to eternal judgment through this third vial of God's wrath, so that there no longer remain any from among them who might be able to persecute or solicit His saints further. > And I heard the angel of the waters saying: You are just, you who are, and who were holy, who have judged these things; because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, you have also given them blood to drink, as they deserve. <note>original: "Et audiui angelū aquarū dicentē: Iustus es qui es, & qui eras sanctus..." This is Revelation 16:5-6.</note>

<margin>The angel of the waters, that is, of the faithful.</margin>
Who is this angel of the waters? Or rather, what kind of waters are these? Certainly, they are the faithful ones, of whom it is written in Isaiah: *His waters are faithful.* <margin>Isaiah 34</margin> <note>The text cites Chapter 34, but this passage is actually Isaiah 33:15-16. Rupert uses the word "faithful" (fideles) where the common Latin Bible uses "sure" (certae) to link the verse to the "faithful" believers.</note> *He who walks in justice and speaks the truth, who rejects greed born of oppression, and shakes his hands free from every bribe; who plugs his ear lest he hear of blood, and closes his eyes lest he see evil: he shall dwell on high, the heights of rocks shall be his stronghold, bread is given to him, and his waters are faithful.* Furthermore, these faithful waters are "living waters" which flow from the belly of the believer, just as the giver of those waters says: <margin>John 7</margin> *He who believes in me, as the scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.* <note>original: "flumina de vētre eius fluēt aquæ viuę."</note>

Therefore, this "angel of the waters" is the one to whom those waters belong, to whom they were given, and from whose belly they flow. Specifically, he represents every <term>scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven</term> <margin>Matthew 13. Malachi 2.</margin> <note>Rupert is referencing Matthew 13:52, where a "scribe" means a teacher of the faith.</note> and every faithful interpreter of the saints—or even the original authors of the scriptures. Because such a person’s "lips guard knowledge," he deserves in this passage to be called notably the "angel of the waters." This is not because he is only one man according to his person, but because according to faith, there is a single understanding among all. For indeed, among all who truly dwell within the "waters" of the holy scriptures, there is one spirit and one faith; and if you consult them rightly, they all speak in harmony and agree on this: that God is a just judge. Therefore, the angel of the waters says:

> You are just, you who are, and who were holy, who have judged these things; because they shed the blood of saints and prophets, you have also given them blood to drink, as they deserve.

This description of the eternal God has already been used frequently in this scripture: *Who was, and who is, and who is to come.* However, this third part—"and who is to come"—is not mentioned here. This is because this confession of God's justice belongs to that final time, after which He is no longer "to come" <note>Rupert argues that because the judgment is currently happening in the vision, the "future" aspect of God's arrival is fulfilled.</note>. Therefore: *You who are, and who were*—that is, you who now remain forever, and who were before all ages.

<summary>Rupert identifies the "Angel of the Waters" not as a literal celestial being, but as the collective voice of faithful teachers and biblical interpreters who recognize the justice of God's final judgment.</summary>

<meta>catchword: concerning the bowl</meta>

...of those killed for the word of God and for the testimony which they held, and they cried out with a loud voice saying: "How long, O holy and true Lord, do you not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" <note>original: "Vsquequo domine sanctus & verus..." Quoting Revelation 6:9-10.</note> But as for the phrase, "I heard the altar saying," and the meaning being, "I heard those who were under the altar saying," this is not an unusual way of speaking among Grammarians. It is a figure of speech <note>original: *pertropum*, from the Greek *tropos*</note> called <gloss>metonymy</gloss> <gloss>metonymia</gloss>, which signifies the thing contained by naming the thing that contains it. Therefore, "I heard the altar saying," means I heard those under the altar whom I had heard before—not now crying out and demanding judgment or vengeance for their blood, but now that the vengeance they required has been carried out, they are praising the justice of the one who judges and avenges, saying: "Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are your judgments." True indeed in word, just in action.

Psalm 89:36 (88:37 in the Vulgate).</note>—namely, the Church, concerning which or in which Christ is the <term>Sun of Justice</term> <note>Latin: *sol iustitiae*. This power was granted to this angel, namely to afflict carnal men—among whom, for example, there is jealousy and strife, which proves they are merely human—with a double evil: heat and fire. That is, with the power of judging in the present and in the future.
<margin>1 Corinthians 5</margin>

For example, the same Apostle says: "I indeed, absent in body but present in spirit, have already judged... to deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord." <note>1 Corinthians 5:3-5</note> To judge in such a way is certainly to afflict men with "heat."
<margin>Heat: excommunication by the prelates.</margin>
For they burn with a certain heat of shame when they are separated from the assembly of the Church, so that it is not permitted even to say "hail" <note>a greeting or blessing</note> to them, nor to take food with such a person.
<margin>2 John 1</margin>
But if, being scorched by such heat, they are not reformed, then finally it will be just that they be afflicted with fire in the future, so that by the judgment of those same authorities—since they remained rebellious and contemptuous—they may be delivered to the fire of Gehenna <term>Gehenna: a biblical name for a place of fiery punishment or hell</term>. ...of the beast, and his kingdom became dark. And they gnawed their tongues for pain, and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and wounds, and they did not repent of their works. <note>Rupert is quoting Revelation 16:10–11.</note>

When the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, the smoking pit of the abyss was opened to them; but here, where the fifth angel poured out his bowl, the seat of the beast grows dark. In the other instances, both in the sounding of the trumpets and the pouring of the bowls, the objects or parts of the world are mentioned by the same names: the earth, the sea, the rivers and springs, the sun, and the river Euphrates. Here, however, the naming varies, since the "seat of the beast" is written instead of the "pit of the abyss."

<margin>
The seat of the beast is a lie.
</margin>

<margin>
The fifth bowl is against heretics.
</margin>

What, I ask, is the seat of the beast, if not that upon which the beast rests? And what is that if not a lie <note>original: "mendacium"</note>? Indeed, just as the authority of God is nothing but the truth, so the support of the devil is nothing but a lie. Therefore, just as a lie is understood there in the pit of the abyss, so it is rightly understood here in the seat of the beast. Certainly, from the moment when the devil’s lie manifested itself through the tongues of heretics, the venerable order of the holy fathers rose up against it, convicted their treachery <note>original: "perfidiam"</note> with ready testimonies from the Scriptures, and furthermore condemned it with an eternal curse <term>anathema: a formal ecclesiastical curse that excommunicates a person or denounces a doctrine</term>. From that time, this angel poured out his bowl upon the seat of the beast. But what did the heretics do in response? Did they rest and obey the victorious truth? Not at all; on the contrary, they grew more insane, expanded their impiety further, and caused the whole world to suffer in their madness. It follows, then:

**And his kingdom became dark, and they gnawed their tongues for pain.**

For they themselves are, or were, the kingdom of the beast, since they are the ones in whom that seat of the beast—that is, falsehood—found a prepared place. Therefore, when the bowl was poured out, the kingdom of the beast became dark: because once the judicial sentences were passed upon the treachery of the heretics, they, smoking with fury and envy, were blinded even further. But how did these people gnaw their tongues?

<margin>Psalms 7 and 9</margin>
Truly, they think against themselves and speak against themselves, fighting against one another through the contradictions of their various sects. For while they fight against the Catholic Church with a common and, as it were, harmonious spirit of malice, they also clash discordantly with one another, having created many-sided heresies. Thus, by defending their own factions, contending and brawling, they "gnaw their tongues." <note>original: "linguas suas commanducant." This imagery comes from Revelation 16:10, describing the agony of the kingdom of the beast.</note> Why? "Because of the pain," it says—that is, because of envy <note>original: "invidia"</note>. For this "pain" is not to be understood in any other way than in that place where it is written: *Behold, he is in labor with injustice; he has conceived pain and brought forth iniquity.* <note>Quoting Psalm 7:14.</note> Likewise: *His mouth is full of cursing, and bitterness, and deceit; under his tongue are labor and pain.* <note>Quoting Psalm 10:7 (Psalm 9:28 in the Vulgate numbering).</note> Because of this kind of pain, they have gnawed their tongues; that is, because of the envy that leads them to create sects contrary to one another, they have infested themselves with their own tongues. It is further added:

->*And they blasphemed God because of their pains and their wounds.*<-

<margin>The blasphemy of Arius out of hatred.</margin>
A remarkable thing. "And they blasphemed God," it says. Why? "Because of their pains and their wounds"—that is, because of their private envies and hatreds, which are indeed wounds not of the body, but of the heart. This is astonishing, yet it is true. For example, as the records of the Church testify, it was because of his hatred for his bishop, Alexander, that the priest Arius <term>Arius: A 4th-century priest whose denial of Christ’s full divinity led to the Council of Nicaea and the first major split in Christianity.</term> broke out into blasphemy against God. To stir up a scandal against Alexander—because he hated and envied him—Arius began to teach dogmas about the Son of God that were contrary to the truth. Therefore, it is spoken truly and universally of all heretics: they blasphemed God because of their pains and wounds. Finally, it says:

->*And they did not repent of their works.*<-

<margin>Heretics sin against the Holy Spirit.</margin>
How could those who spoke words against the Holy Spirit perform penance <note>original: "pœnitentiam," meaning repentance or the act of penance.</note>? Indeed, as the authority of the earlier Church Fathers hands down to us, a person speaks a word against the Holy Spirit when they contradict the Holy Scriptures not out of ignorance, but out of envy—for these Scriptures are undoubtedly the voices of...

<summary>Rupert explains that the "gnawing of tongues" and "pains" mentioned in Revelation 16 symbolize the internal discord and envy among heretics. He specifically cites the historical conflict between Arius and Bishop Alexander as an example of how personal hatred leads to theological blasphemy and a refusal to repent.</summary>

**And the sixth angel poured out his bowl upon that great river Euphrates, and its waters were dried up, so that the way might be prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. <margin>The plague of the sixth trumpet upon bodies.</margin>
When the sixth angel sounded his trumpet, four angels were released who had been bound at the great river Euphrates, and the plague was one that seized the people of God through the four principal kingdoms of the world, under which the children of Israel or Judah were afflicted by the judgment of God. <note>Rupert is comparing the "Trumpets" of Revelation 9 with the "Bowls" of Revelation 16. <margin>The plague of the sixth bowl upon souls.</margin>
But truly, this bowl of the wrath of God is poured into the river—into that river, not so that such angels might be released, but so that its waters might be dried up, and the way prepared for the kings from the rising of the sun. Therefore, the bowl of God's wrath is poured into the water of the river, and for that reason, we must understand this "water" to be something to which the wrath of God is deservedly owed. Otherwise, since the sea, the rivers, and the springs of water have already been condemned to blood by the previous bowls, why is it that the river Euphrates deserves its own specific bowl? Is it not because, among the other evils committed under the sun, the water of this river signifies a particular evil? For there is an evil whose condemnation in...

...folly, by comparison with it <note>Referring to the divine wisdom mentioned on the previous page.</note>, it appeared to be foolish and dry, which until then seemed great and profound. **"And I saw three unclean spirits like frogs coming out of the mouth of the dragon, out of the mouth of the beast, and out of the mouth of the false prophet."**

<margin>The unclean spirits preside over magicians, poets, and philosophers.</margin>
By "unclean spirits," he means the "sects" <note>original: "sectas" — here referring to schools of thought or disciplines.</note> of a sort of wisdom and knowledge: the magical, the poetic, and the philosophical. These the unclean spirit of this world—who is the adversary of the Holy Spirit—has breathed out. For magicians especially have claimed unclean spirits as their patrons through I know not what unhappy pact. Poets, under honorable names, ask those same unclean spirits to breathe into them, calling them "gods" with sacrilegious presumption when they are actually demons. Furthermore, he who breathed his spirit into the philosophers was also undoubtedly unclean. 
<margin>Romans 1.</margin>
Does the Apostle <note>Saint Paul.</note> not say of them: *because claiming to be wise, they became fools, and vanished into their own thoughts*? And see how far into uncleanness they vanished—they who, serving the creature rather than the Creator, were for that reason already delivered up into shameful passions or into the desires of their hearts for uncleanness. Therefore they are rightly called "unclean spirits." Furthermore, by the name of the "dragon," the devil is meant; while by the name of the "beast," the beast-like kingdom of the devil is rightly understood to be designated in this place. For in the Book of Daniel, four principal kingdoms of the world are signified by four beasts—namely, the Babylonian, the Persian (or Median), the Macedonian, and the Roman. From the mouth of the dragon the first spirit <note>The spirit of Magic.</note> proceeded, because human curiosity learned the magic art from the storytelling of the devil. From the mouth of the beast the next spirit <note>The spirit of Poetry.</note> went out, because the ignobility of the human mind, by flattering the beast-like kingdom of this world, elevated earthly kings (who were but men) into gods through poetic fictions, and translated them into heaven and the spheres of the stars with fabulous nonsense...

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the "three unclean spirits like frogs" as the disciplines of magic, poetry, and philosophy, which he views as demonic corruptions of human thought. He links the "dragon" to the origin of magic and the "beast" to the poetic deification of secular rulers.</summary>

In the same way, other sorcerers, poets, and philosophers have gathered the kings of the whole earth—not necessarily into a single physical place, but into the same state of wicked intent—to do battle against the Lord. They did this so that the kings of the earth, biased by their high regard for these figures, might disdain or neglect the great miracles performed by the Lord’s servants, or fail to marvel at the wisdom they preached. This was because those worldly men were also accustomed to performing wonders and speaking with the magnificent eloquence of the wise. 

<margin>2 Timothy 3</margin>

...of his majesty, then not only kings, but also all nations will be gathered before him. This state is rightly designated by the name placed here: **Hermagedon**. <note>original: "Hermagedon" (Armageddon). Rupert uses medieval etymologies to explain the name.</note> For it is interpreted as "resurrection into former things," or "a rounded mountain." > **And the seventh poured out his bowl into the air,** 
> **And a great voice came out of the temple from the throne,**
> **saying: It is done.**

And just as when the seventh angel sounded the trumpet, great voices were made in heaven, saying: *The kingdom of this world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ.* <note>Referencing Revelation 11:15.</note> Therefore, here also when it is said, "it is done," the same thing must be understood: namely, the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ. This is understood, however, with a distinction: we should weigh more of the wrath of the living God in this seventh bowl than in that seventh trumpet. For these are the "last plagues," while those were the first. They are distinguished by the fact that those [the trumpets] are divisions and distinctions of visible evils, while these [the bowls] are of invisible ones. Therefore, in that seventh trumpet, we understand the visible conflagration of this whole world; in this seventh bowl, we rightly understand that fullness of damnation by which the demons are to be punished—those who now wander through this air, having been cast down from heaven. For this is what it says:

> **And the seventh poured out his bowl into the air.**

<margin>The pouring of the seventh bowl upon the demons.</margin>
That is, upon the aerial throngs or powers. The seventh bowl is rightly poured upon them because, clearly, whatever evils are punished in the preceding six bowls redound upon those who were the instigators of those very evils. Hence, they are the principalities and powers, and the rulers of this world, of darkness...

# On Revelation Chapter 16

in which only the <term>reprobate</term> <note>Those whom God has rejected or who have rejected God, contrasted with the "elect."</note> are assigned, it immediately adds concerning that city and says: **And great Babylon came into memory before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.** Therefore, both ought to be observed, and each one distinguished by its own probable meaning.

<margin>The whole world was one city before the coming of Christ.</margin>
That the whole world was not only one city, but even as it were one courtyard of one <term>strong man</term> <note>A reference to the devil, based on Jesus' parable in the Gospels.</note> before the coming of Christ, existing as a mixture of the elect and the reprobate, the authority of our Lord Jesus Christ teaches in this way:

<margin>Luke 11</margin>
**When a strong man armed guards his courtyard, all the things he possesses are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and overcomes him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted, and distributes his spoils.** Furthermore, because this city was to be divided into three parts at the preaching of the Gospel—by which, just as these <term>vials</term> <note>Also translated as "bowls" (Latin: *phialæ*), representing the outpouring of God's judgment.</note> signify by their own pouring out, the wrath of God is revealed—the Lord himself predicted it in this way:

<margin>Matthew 10</margin>
**Do not think that I have come to send peace on earth. For I did not come to send peace on earth, but a sword. For I have come to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law, and a man’s enemies will be those of his own household.** These are the three parts which Luke expressed even more distinctly with these words:

<margin>Luke 12</margin>
**Do you think that I have come to give peace on earth? I tell you no, but separation. For from now on there will be five in one house divided: three will be divided against two, and two against three. The father against the son, and the son against his father; the mother against the daughter, and the daughter against her mother; the mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.** It should be noted that there are two—namely, the father and the mother, that is, the husband and the wife—into whom the three are divided; however, these two, namely the husband and wife, are by no means divided against themselves on account of the Gospel. Nor for the cause of the Gospel—indeed for no cause, except for the cause of <term>fornication</term> <note>Rupert is emphasizing that while the Gospel divides families between believers and non-believers, it does not dissolve the marriage bond itself.</note> alone—

<margin>Matthew 5 and 19</margin>
is it permitted for a husband to depart from his wife, or a wife from her husband. Therefore, when the vials of God's wrath were poured out, the great city was made into three parts; that is, the wrath of God was revealed through the Gospel, with some fleeing to repentance, and others remaining in impenitence, while the common necessities of men <note>The text ends mid-sentence, suggesting the "three parts" involve the repentant, the unrepentant, and perhaps the shared earthly life they still inhabit together.</note>

<summary>Rupert interprets the "Great City" of Revelation as the world, which the Gospel divides into three spiritual factions. He uses Jesus' teachings on family division to explain how the "earthquake" of preaching separates the repentant from the unrepentant.</summary>
<keywords>Babylon, strong man armed, division of the city, three parts, marriage and divorce, Gospel preaching, repentance, Luke 11, Matthew 10</keywords>

relationships, which are naturally great: they are divided into three parts when they do not agree with one another in the way of the Lord, and the son departs from the father, the daughter from the mother, and the daughter-in-law from her mother-in-law. When these divisions are made, those who are converted become Jerusalem, the city of God, while the others remain as they were—Babylon, the city of the devil. Surely they become inexcusable, and then at last God remembers their sin, by which they persecute those who were once like them. Thus, as it is written:
<margin>Psalm 9</margin>
**For he who requires blood has remembered them; he has not forgotten the cry of the poor.** <note>original: "Quoniam requirens sanguinem, eorum recordatus est: non est oblitus clamorem pauperum."</note> It follows, therefore:
**And great Babylon came into memory before God, to give her the cup of the wine of the fury of his wrath.**
He calls the sentence of damnation a "cup of wine," adding "of the fury of his wrath" specifically to distinguish it from that good and excellent cup of which God speaks in the Psalm: 
<margin>
Two types of cups.
Psalm 9.
Psalm 23.
</margin>
**And my cup, how excellent and inebriating it is!** <note>original: "Et calix meus inebrians quam praeclarus est." This refers to Psalm 23:5. In medieval theology, "inebriation" often referred to spiritual ecstasy or being filled with the Holy Spirit.</note> In short, just as that cup of grace inebriates happily, so on the contrary this cup of wrath inebriates unhappily, so that the city of the devil is lulled to sleep by eternal foolishness, as Ecclesiastes says: 
<margin>Ecclesiastes 9</margin>
**Because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld where you are hastening.** He gives an even greater reason why that city came into such a memory before God. He says:
**And every island fled, and the mountains were not found.**
This is the same as if he were saying: "In this way, that city stirred up the memory of itself to its own misfortune: because the servants of God, fleeing the persecutions like waves of the sea, hid themselves in remote places." 
<margin>Hebrews 11</margin>
As Paul says with a groan regarding the ancient saints: **They went about in sheepskins and goatskins, being in want, distressed, and afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in solitudes, in mountains, and in caves and caverns of the earth.** Finally, it is common in the Scriptures for the "islands" to signify the churches, and the "mountains" to signify the more eminent saints. And did the preaching of the Gospel fall silent because of this flight of the saints? Not at all; on the contrary, it grew even stronger. It follows, therefore:

## And great hail like a talent descended from
## heaven upon men.

Such first were the Jews, of whom Luke speaks in the Acts of the Apostles: 

"When Silas and Timothy had come from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ. But when they contradicted and blasphemed, he shook his garments and said to them: 'Your blood be upon your own heads! I am clean; from now on I will go to the Gentiles.'" <note>Acts 18:5-6.</note>

### THE TENTH BOOK OF THE COMMENTARIES OF RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN THE APOSTLE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring a figure in a classical or biblical setting, possibly a prophet or saint, with architectural elements.</image-desc>

<margin>
Here the spirit of piety will be treated. 
2 Timothy 3.
</margin>
From here, through appropriate images and fitting words, the "spirit of piety" <note>original: "spiritus pietatis." In medieval theology, Piety is one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, representing a deep, filial love for God and compassion for others.</note> is demonstrated—specifically, what it works or is about to work toward the elect. For it is the work or office of the Holy Spirit—according to this very name, the Spirit of Piety—to console all the saints wandering as pilgrims in this world and suffering persecutions for living piously <note>Rupert alludes here to 2 Timothy 3:12: "All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution."</note>. He consoles them so that they are not fatigued by adversities, nor envious of the malignant, while those doing iniquity are lifted up and exalted in the glory of this world and enjoy the riches they desire. This, however, is dealt with in two ways in this part of the scripture which we are now entering...

For this is the sixth of the seven spirits from whom grace is sent to the churches at the beginning of this book <note>A reference to Revelation 1:4, where grace is given from the "seven spirits who are before his throne."</note>. <margin>Chapter 17</margin>
