> **And one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying: "Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great harlot, who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication, and those who inhabit the earth have been made drunk with the wine of her fornication."** <note>Revelation 17:1-2.</note>

This "one of the seven angels" who has the seven bowls signifies the one faith and the one Spirit who speaks through them. Indeed, all these angels—meaning all the writers or commentators of the Scriptures whom the Holy Church receives—say the same thing and think the same thing, and there are no schisms among them.

Furthermore, John—who says that this one angel came to him and spoke so many and such great words of consolation—represents in this place a model <note>original: "typum"; Rupert uses John as a "type" or symbolic representative for all faithful Christians.</note> of all the saints, whoever they may be, who while wandering as pilgrims in this world have deserved or do deserve to be comforted by a blessed hope through the consolation of the scriptures. For this same John, when he saw these things, had been made a sharer in their tribulation; indeed, he was living as an exile on the island of Patmos, sent there by the Emperor Domitian <note>Titus Flavius Domitianus, Roman Emperor (81–96 AD), who according to tradition exiled John the Apostle.</note> for the sake of the Gospel. Therefore, he deserved to experience their common consolations through his own vision.

->“Come,” he says, “I will show you the condemnation of the great whore.”<-

<margin>The City of the Devil</margin>
It is as if he were saying: "O you, whoever you are, seeker of the eternal city or fatherland whose one king is God who founded it, why do you look out with such sighs upon the hastening progress of the earthly fatherland, or the 'City of the Devil'? It hastens to reign while the kingdom of the one King, God, seems to delay for a little while—a city of many kings, like a hydra of many heads, and a whore of many lovers." Do not grieve or be weary in spirit, as if her current reigning and insulting of your exile were a sign of great happiness. Come, and I will show you the condemnation of her who seems so great to herself.

->“Because she sits upon many waters.”<-

For truly this whore sits upon many waters, because there are many nations over which lust <term>cupiditas</term> <note>original: "cupiditas"; in medieval theology, this refers to disordered desire, greed, or the love of worldly things over God.</note> reigns. Ultimately, in this place, the waters are the peoples or nations. For the angel explains this to John a little further down: "The waters," he says, "which you saw where the whore sits, are peoples, and nations, and tongues." Because this whore sits upon many waters—that is, because there are many peoples or nations over whom lust dominates—therefore, when he had said, "I will show you the condemnation of the whore," he added "the great." But certainly such greatness of hers is deceptive, because it does not stand. Nor was it in vain that it pleased the Spirit to signify the nations or peoples here through "waters." For nations flow through the generation of the flesh, and they flow away from their very beginning...

<sig>F</sig>

<summary>Rupert interprets John the Apostle as a representative of all suffering Christians and explains that the "Great Whore" represents the City of the Devil, which dominates the world through fleeting, disordered desire (lust).</summary>

...until the setting of death, and they never arrive at a certain place where they might be established and stand—that is, in God. She is a "great whore," however, not in true magnitude, but in her own estimation. He provides the reason why he called her a whore when he immediately adds:

<margin>
To fornicate: to depart from God for the sake of creatures. Psalm 72.
</margin>
**With whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication.**
For true and great fornication is for the rational creature—that is, man—to distance himself from God and to cling to the desire <term>cupiditati: Ruperti refers to "cupiditas" not just as greed for money, but as an disordered desire for worldly things over God.</term> of the world. For this reason the Psalmist, when he had said, "For behold, those who distance themselves from you shall perish," immediately added: "You have destroyed all who are unfaithful <note>original: "fornicantur"; Rupert uses the Latin Vulgate's phrasing from Psalm 72:27, where "fornication" is a metaphor for spiritual infidelity or idolatry.</note> to you." This the kings of the earth have done especially, whose desire for ruling no expanse of the earth could satisfy; indeed, for the sake of expanding their earthly lands, they perpetrated innumerable slaughters of men. Committing fornication in this way <note>original: "liter fornicãtes"</note>, they also fell into such madness that, having lost the dignity of reason, they worshipped demons through various forms of idols, and compelled the peoples subject to them to worship these things. Therefore, having well said "with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication," he immediately added:

**And those who inhabit the earth were intoxicated with the wine of her prostitution.**
<margin>
Intoxicated by desire.
</margin>
For by fornicating with the desire of this world they were intoxicated; that is, just as those who are drunk on wine lose the power of discernment and say and do all things without reason, so those people, bent entirely toward the earth through desire, could not look back toward the true Divinity dwelling in the heavens. Instead, they dreamed that power <note>original: "virtutem"</note> resided in their own idols of divinity. "Come, and I will show you the condemnation of this whore." When he says "Come," we should understand the chosen soul being called, as it were, inward, so that she herself does not wander outside after 

<margin>1 John 2</margin>
the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes, but rather collects herself within for the secret of contemplation. There, she may diligently weigh those things that are and those things that are to come, within herself, by the judgment of reason. For this is what follows:

**And he carried me away into the desert in the spirit.**
For the "desert," because of its own solitude, signifies...

Following the previous page’s discussion on the "Great Whore" as the embodiment of worldly desire (cupiditas), Rupert now interprets the "wilderness" as a state of spiritual withdrawal and identifies the "seven heads" of the scarlet beast as historical kingdoms that have persecuted the faithful from the time of Abraham to the future Antichrist.</meta>

<page-num>451</page-num>

-> ### On the Apocalypse, Chapter 17 <-

[This] place [signifies] the withdrawal of a solitary mind, when it removes itself from the tumults of cares for the sake of searching out God's truth. Wherefore, after he had rightly said, "And he carried me away into the wilderness," he added **in the spirit**, because truly whoever seeks such solitude is led not by the flesh but by the spirit. It follows:
**And I saw a woman sitting upon a scarlet beast, full of names of blasphemy, having seven heads and ten horns.**

<margin>The Whore, desire</margin>
A little before, the one who was speaking said that the whore sat upon many waters; here, however, he says that she sits upon a scarlet beast. Therefore, that very multitude of waters—that is, of peoples or nations—is the beast. This is truly the case, because the woman who sits upon such a multitude of waters is the "whore," which is <term>cupiditas: a technical term in medieval theology for disordered desire or greed for worldly things</term>, which drives her to live in a beastly manner. This is called a "scarlet" beast, which is the color of fire, because clearly for those whom desire commands, the whole multitude is burning for slaughter and for lust. What or who these seven heads and ten horns of the beast are or were has already been stated above, where the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, and where this beast was seen ascending from the sea. But also regarding the names of blasphemy with which the beast is said to be full, that has also been discussed there. Nevertheless, a brief knowledge of these heads,

<margin>Seven heads: seven kingdoms of the world against the people of God.</margin>
horns, and names of blasphemy must be brought forward. There are indeed seven heads, seven kingdoms of the world, which from the time of the promise by which Christ, the seed of blessing, was promised to our father Abraham, have fought against the faith of his offspring and striven to extinguish it by attacking the faithful people: namely, the kingdom of the Egyptians, the kingdom of the carnal Israelites <note>Rupert uses the term "carnal Israelites" to distinguish between the physical nation of Israel and what he considers the "spiritual Israel" or the Church.</note>, the kingdom of the Babylonians, the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, the kingdom of the Macedonians, the kingdom of the Romans, and the kingdom of the Antichrist, which shall be the last. These seven kingdoms of the world are the seven heads of the beast. Furthermore, the ten horns of the seven heads are understood to be ten kings of those same seven kingdoms. For one

<margin>Ten horns, ten [kings]</margin>
of those kingdoms—namely, the kingdom of the Macedonians—while Alexander the Great was living, had only one horn, that is, [one] king...

<summary>Rupert interprets the scarlet beast's seven heads as seven historical and future kingdoms—ranging from ancient Egypt to the Antichrist—that have persecuted the faithful since the age of Abraham. He identifies the "whore" as the personification of worldly desire that drives these nations toward violence and lust.</summary>

Following the previous page’s discussion on the "scarlet beast" and the woman as "cupiditas" (disordered desire), Rupert now addresses the historical interpretation of the beast's horns through the lens of Alexander the Great’s empire and the moral failings of the "City of the Devil."</meta>

<page-num>352</page-num>
<header>352 Commentary of Rupert, Book [XIV]</header>

<margin>Kings in seven parts of the kingdoms.</margin>
The one and the same Alexander <note>original: "Alexandrum"; referring to Alexander the Great</note>, after his death, was divided into the four winds of heaven, and one kingdom began to have four kings, and in this way the ten horns are made—that is, ten kings. Truly, the **names of blasphemy** were names of usurped divinity: because, clearly, by flattering their kings while governing the kingdoms of the world, they wished them to be held as gods, and they especially exalted the deceased to heaven with false praises. "Upon such a beast I saw," he said, "a woman sitting," that is, **desire** <note>original: "cupiditatem"</note> and the corruption of all vices reigning.

> **And the woman was arrayed in purple and scarlet color, and decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, having a golden cup in her hand full of abominations and filthiness of her fornication, and upon her forehead was a name written: Mystery, Babylon the Great, the mother of fornications and abominations of the earth. And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.**

<margin>Two causes of damnation against this whore.</margin>
About to see the damnation of the woman or the whore according to the response of the speaking angel: 
> **Come; I will show unto thee the judgment of the great whore that sitteth upon many waters,**

he first testifies that he has seen the causes of that same damnation. The first of these is that she took up a public profession of the fornications and abominations of the earth. For it is said: 
> **And on her forehead a name was written, a mystery: Babylon the Great, the mother of fornications and abominations.**

Clearly, he accuses her of public profession; namely, that the **City of the Devil** <note>A common medieval trope, derived from St. Augustine, contrasting the 'City of God' with the 'City of Man/Devil'</note> does not only sin or commit "fornication," but even glories in those very sins and fornications of hers. The second cause of her damnation is that she shed the blood of the saints who did not consent to her. For this is what he says when reporting his vision: "And I saw," he said, "the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus." Therefore, let us look more diligently at these two causes of her damnation prescribed here.

<summary>Rupert interprets the beast's horns as the fragmented empire of Alexander the Great and identifies the "Whore of Babylon" as the City of the Devil, characterized by its public pride in sin and its persecution of Christian martyrs.</summary>

He continues here by interpreting her clothing and ornaments as symbols of royal pride and the violent history of earthly empires.</meta>

<page-num>453</page-num>
<header>On Apocalypse Chapter 17</header>
<sig>F iii</sig>

### And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet.

<margin>The greed of kings.</margin>
Purple is the garment of royalty, and it signifies all the courtly power or pride of the kingdoms and kings of this world. Furthermore, who does not know that murderous cruelty has almost always accompanied royal power? Books are full—indeed, the theaters of the world are already satiated—with the tragedies of kings who, out of a greed for ruling, not only took up arms against foreigners, but even drove the cruel sword into their own kinsmen, brothers, or even parents, because they would not endure partners or rivals in their kingdom. Therefore, scarlet <note>original: "coccinum"; often associated with blood or fire</note> is rightly joined with purple by saying: *And the woman was clothed in purple and scarlet*, because indeed the fiery cruelty of murders has always accompanied the purple of kingdoms. It is beautifully stated that she was "clothed" in purple, for by this saying he reminds the watchful listener how much vanity exists in the royal dress of the proud. For on the outside they can be colored with beautiful appearances—of which royal purple seems the finest—but inside, or beneath that same purple, their mortal bodies are no less wretched and decaying than those of peasants, not only because of the ulcers of overflowing lust, but also through various types of accidental diseases.

### And gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls.

<margin>False and borrowed beauty in gold and gems.</margin>
All these are the riches of the woman; all these are the fruits of human greed <note>original: "cupiditatis"</note>, which is false and deceptive. For human presumption seeks a beauty outside itself and affects a borrowed brilliance as if it were its own; since it is unable to change its own nature—for she herself is but mud—she surrounds herself with shimmering gold, precious stones, and pearls. Thus, even while sometimes foul with sores or pale with leprosy, she may shine most proudly from above with such trappings that do not truly belong to her. Moreover, in this regard, she is always a great burden to the rational intentions of the elect <note>the "electi" or those chosen by God</note>, and she wearies their minds with manifold temptation. It follows:

### Having a golden cup in her hand, full of abominations

<summary>Rupert of Deutz interprets the Whore of Babylon’s purple and scarlet clothing as symbols of royal pride and the bloodstained history of earthly power. He contrasts the external splendor of gold and jewels with the internal corruption and mortality common to all people.</summary>

Here, he interprets the contents of her cup as the spiritual "poison" of idolatry and misplaced desire.</meta>

<header>Commentary of Rupert, Book [XII]</header>

...of the abominations and the impurity of her fornication.
<margin>Her drink: error and oblivion</margin>
For what purpose is she said to have a cup in her hand, if not to serve and offer her drink to all who pass by? And what is her drink, except error and oblivion, by which the human senses—soaked in the allurements of vices—withdraw from God? Therefore, the woman is said to have in her hand a cup full of the abominations and the impurity of her fornication, by which surely the entire fruit or effect of greed <note>original: "cupiditas"; Rupert uses this term to mean a disordered, grasping desire for power or material things</note> is to subvert the rational man and to utterly overwhelm his senses. Thus, he commits fornication in mind and body away from the living and true God, handed over in his soul to idolatry and subjected in his body to every impurity and all shameful passions. And one must note the persistence of her wicked intention: to better entice and more quickly deceive, she is said to have in her hand not a wooden or bronze cup, but a golden one. Surely this woman seized such a cup when, to more easily seduce the greedy and ambitious eyes of men, the kings of the world established idols that were not only stone or wood, but even golden; to worship these was indeed the height of abominations and the beginning of all impurity and fornication.
<margin>1 Kings 12: The golden calves of Jeroboam.</margin>
For example: when Jeroboam made golden calves—not wooden or stone ones—placing one in Bethel and the other in Dan <note>Jeroboam was the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel; he set up these idols to prevent his people from traveling to the Temple in Jerusalem</note>, then surely the woman had a golden cup in her hand, full of the abominations and the impurity of her fornication. This was because the greed for ruling, which sat so heavily upon that man, deceived the eyes of the common people through the beauty of the gold, so that they drank the fornication of the one saying: *These are your gods, O Israel, who led you out of Egypt*, so that they might commit fornication away from their God, and withdraw from the house of David and from the temple of the Lord which was in Jerusalem. This was especially effective because among such gods they were permitted to eat and commit fornication, to pollute and be polluted, and to afflict their own bodies with every abomination and impurity. The Gentiles practiced such outrages not even in secret, but—what is worse—they frequented them boastfully, publicly, and everywhere. From which also...

there should be no doubt, nor can carnal Judaism be excused <note>Rupert argues that Judaism, when focused only on physical rituals ("carnal") rather than spiritual truth, becomes part of the world’s opposition to God.</note>, from being a primary or even the principal portion of that great city Babylon—nay, rather, as it is written here, of the **great harlot**, whose first foundations were laid by **Cain**, who slew his righteous brother. <margin>John wonders here in the person of the imperfect.</margin>

This wonder belongs to an imperfect heart. For a perfect heart does not much admire or highly value the purple and scarlet, the gold, precious stones, and pearls of the harlot. Thus, this John also testifies that he "wondered with great admiration" in the person of those who, having weak hearts, looked upon the brilliance of the great harlot while they themselves were being troubled; for truly, in his own right, he would never deign to wonder at such things. Furthermore, for any of God's elect who wonder (or have wondered) at that harlot through weakness, the consolation of the Holy Spirit has not been—and cannot be—lacking. # Rupert’s Commentary on Revelation
### On Revelation Chapter 17, Page 461

And the inhabitants of the earth, he says, whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, shall wonder.

<margin>Those written in the book of life from the foundation of the world.</margin>
What will they wonder at? Surely at that which I do not want you to wonder at, as I rebuke you and ask: "Why do you wonder?" Let those wonder who do not look to heaven, but inhabit the earth in both body and mind. These are the ones whose names are not written in the book of life—that is, those whom God did not predestine <term>predestine: the theological concept that God has ordained from the beginning who will achieve eternal life</term> for life from the foundation of the world. By "foundation," he refers to when God established the world and the human race, when He blessed the first created humans and said: *Increase and multiply.* Those whom God did not write in His book at that time—whom He did not command to be born through that specific blessing, or who do not belong to that blessing of the Creator—they are the ones who will wonder, just as they have always wondered at a beast of this kind. In this, those admirers are already convicted of folly, for it is said: *which was and is not.* By contrast, you should wonder at and proclaim as wonderful Him *who was, and who is, and who is to come.* <note>Rupert contrasts the temporary nature of the worldly "beast" with the eternal nature of God.</note>

# Rupert’s Commentary, Book 10
### Page 462

<margin>
The tribulations of the righteous from the seven heads of the beast.
Exodus 1:5

Why the kingdoms are called seven mountains.
</margin>

... [throughout] time, as the sacred scriptures testify, stood against the kingdom of God, and oppressed its citizens—who are travelers <note>original: "peregrinantes," implying those on a spiritual pilgrimage or journey through the world</note> in this world—with various tribulations. For first, the kingdom of the **Egyptians** afflicted the sons of Israel. Second, the kingdom of the **Israelites** <note>Referring to the northern Kingdom of Israel during its periods of apostasy</note> killed the righteous men and the prophets of the Lord, beginning with Jezebel. Third, the kingdom of the **Babylonians** burned Jerusalem with fire, took its people captive, and cast the three youths into the fiery furnace. Fourth, the kingdom of the **Persians and Medes**, at the instigation of the most arrogant Haman, nearly destroyed the entire race of the Jews because of Mordecai. Fifth, the kingdom of the **Macedonians** <note>The Greek empire following Alexander the Great</note>, through Antiochus Epiphanes, cruelly afflicted that same people; it was under him that the Maccabean brothers were crowned with a wondrous martyrdom. Sixth, the kingdom of the **Romans** filled the whole circle of the earth with the blood of Christians. Seventh, the kingdom of the **Antichrist** will afflict the faithful with such great tribulation that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error.

These are the **seven mountains**, which is to say, the seven kingdoms. Ultimately, he called these kingdoms "mountains" because of their pride, by which they swelled up <note>original: "tumuerunt," meaning to swell with pride or tumor-like arrogance</note> on high against God. Hence, when he had said, "the seven heads are seven mountains," explaining what he meant, he added: *and they are seven kings.* For he used "kings" as an equivalent for "kingdoms"—indeed, more precisely so, because it is not so much the kingdoms or the stretches of land that are in a state of sin <note>original: "in crimine sunt"</note>, but rather the kings themselves, so that they may be called and truly be the "heads" of the beast. And although many have reigned in each kingdom through succession, he beautifully set down as many kings as there are kingdoms; for the current cause demands the counting not so much of individual persons reigning, but of the royal powers themselves. Therefore, it follows:

**Five have fallen, one is, and the other has not yet come.**

# In the Book of Revelation Chapter 17

Five had fallen; they had been buried in hell. It should certainly be noted that such heavenly judgments were carried out upon each of these individuals that, if you consider the outcome of each one, you would not hesitate to admit it was rightly said that they "fell." For instance, the **Egyptian king** <note>Pharaoh</note> fell into the sea with his chariots and horsemen; dogs licked the blood of **Ahab**, and they devoured **Jezebel**; **Nebuchadnezzar** was cast out from his kingdom and ate grass like an ox; **Haman** was hanged on a gallows; and **Antiochus**, rotting away, ended his impious life with a miserable death. Therefore, five had already fallen, and "one is," he says. Who is that "one"? Without a doubt, it is the Roman king or emperor, who existed at that time and was raging against Christians when these words were spoken. To be sure, **Nero** had already perished in a shameful and disgraceful manner, but the persecution which he was the first to decree against Christians was still flourishing in the Roman state at that time. Although there were many princes of that same empire who were persecutors of Christians, nevertheless, as a single kingdom, the whole sum of them is counted as "one king."

"And the other," he says, "has not yet come."
This is clearly the one who will be the **Antichrist**. That "one" who he said existed then, and the "other" whom he asserts has not yet come, are added to those five who fell, making seven in total. When he had said, "and the other has not yet come," he immediately added:

**And when he comes, he must remain for a short time.**

<margin>Matthew 24</margin>
Why must he remain for a short time and not a long time? Clearly, it is for the sake of the elect. For the Lord says, "In those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation which God created until now, nor ever shall be. And unless the Lord had shortened the days, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect whom He chose, He shortened the days." Therefore, when he comes, he must indeed remain, but only for a short time. Here, because we are proud and weak, the mercy of the Lord, joined with His truth, both terrifies us with the magnitude of the adversity and restores us by the brevity of the time. It follows:

**And the beast that was and is not, even he is the eighth,**

### Page 464 Rupert’s Commentary. Book 10.

> and he is of the seven, and goes into destruction. <note>original: "et de septem est, et in interitum vadet." Revelation 17:11</note>

In this passage, the beast must be understood as one specific head of the beast, which is clearly the **Antichrist**. This beast, he says, is both the eighth and is of the seven. This is the same as saying that the Antichrist is one and the same head of the beast, being both the eighth and the seventh. This, of course, could not stand or be understood unless it were established that in one and the same Antichrist there are two aspects existing together. For that <term>son of perdition</term> <note>A biblical title for the Antichrist, implying one destined for waste and ruin.</note> is simultaneously both man and devil. Therefore, if you only attend to what is seen outwardly in the Antichrist, he is "of the seven," because he is of the same kind or nature as the other kings or impious men. If, however, you look at what lies hidden within, he is the eighth head, because he is the devil, who—before he entered the dwelling of that lost man—raised himself up against God in heaven and even now remains invisibly proud. Nevertheless, he says, "he goes into destruction," because it is as easy for God to send both man and devil together into destruction as it is to send a simple or lone man, so that it may be truly said of both that "he was and is not," while God always is. It follows:

> And the ten horns which you saw are ten kings, who have not yet received a kingdom, but they will receive power as kings for one hour after the beast. <note>Revelation 17:12</note>

<margin>
The Antichrist as a man is the seventh beast; as the devil, he is the eighth.
</margin>
This has already been discussed above: there are indeed seven very well-known kingdoms in the series of the Holy Scriptures which exercised enmity against the saints of the Most High. However, there are ten kings of those same kingdoms because one of them—the **kingdom of the Macedonians**—was divided among the four successors of **Alexander the Great** through the "four winds of heaven" after his death. Each of these successors placed crowns upon themselves, and in this way, ten kings were created. For this reason, he said earlier "and there are seven kings," but now says "there are ten kings." This is because three of those successors of Alexander are recorded as having done nothing against the people of God; only that fourth one, who held **Syria** <note>Reference to the Seleucid Empire, specifically Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a famous persecutor of the Jews.</note>, was an enemy. Therefore, they are ten in number, but in terms of [their actions...]

<summary>Rupert explains that the Antichrist is the seventh king by his human nature and the eighth by his demonic possession. He further reconciles the "seven kingdoms" with the "ten horns" by referencing the historical division of Alexander the Great's empire.</summary>

# On Revelation, Chapter 17

465

G

...in action pertaining to the present cause—that is, for the persecution of martyrs—there are only seven. However, since he said a little while ago, "five have fallen, and one is," <note>original: "quinque ceciderunt, & unus est"</note> why does he now say, "who have not yet received a kingdom"? <note>original: "qui regnum nondum acceperunt"</note> Clearly, he says this with a wonderful irony, as if to say: they indeed seemed to reign, and they usurped the rank and the name of "kingdom" for themselves, but in truth they never reigned. For their kingdom is not truly a kingdom; the kingdom belongs to the Lord alone. 

This refers to what he said earlier in his rebuke: "Why do you wonder?" <note>original: "Quare miraris?"</note> For truly, kings of this sort are not to be wondered at, but are to be judged as miserable; they committed so many homicides in order to reign, yet they have fallen and are dead, and they "have not yet received a kingdom." But what then? "They will receive power," he says, "as if they were kings, for one hour after the beast." <note>original: "post bestiam." Note: Standard biblical versions usually say "with the beast" (cum bestia), but Rupert's text reads "after" or "following."</note> They do not receive a true kingdom, but they will receive a certain power "as kings," and this for "one hour after the beast," as if he were saying: You should not think that their voices or their power ought to be called a "kingdom" anymore. For the word "kingdom" implies a long duration of power. But they have received, or will receive, power not for a long duration, but for "one hour." 

Now, he said "they will receive" in the future tense because when the Antichrist comes, he will restore the strengths or the kingdoms of those same kings who have already fallen for the purpose of persecuting the saints. Furthermore, he briefly hints at what kind of power they will receive when he says, "after the beast." For it is the same as if he were saying: "for the shedding of the blood of the saints," because the power of the beast is not truly for reigning, but for raging—for the shedding of blood. Therefore, it was beautifully and truly said, "that they have not yet received a kingdom." It follows:

> These have one purpose, and they will hand over their strength and power to the beast. These will fight with the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, because he is the Lord of lords and King of kings, and those who are with him are called, and chosen, and faithful.

"These," he says, "have one purpose": it is understood that when the Antichrist comes and remains for a short time, all <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the next page.</note>

### Commentary of Rupert, Book [X]

466

...for they will conspire to the consensus of that **son of perdition** <note>original: "filij perditionis." A title for the Antichrist drawn from 2 Thessalonians 2:3.</note>. What of those kings who existed before the coming of that same Antichrist? Did they not already share one plan with the one who is to come? Did they not have the same intention? Did they not have the same will? For by whatever plan, intention, and will he will persecute the saints when he comes, with that same will the King of Egypt and the others—about whom we have already spoken—afflicted the people of God in each of their own times. Their goal was that no one would remain mindful of the one true God; and in them and through them, the devil worked to make void the faith of the promise—specifically the promise of the "seed," which is Christ, whom God promised to our fathers. <margin>The ancient plan of the serpent.</margin> This was the ancient plan of that serpent from the moment he first deceived man: namely, that no human should be saved. With this same plan, he armed all those we have often mentioned: the Egyptians, the carnal Israelites, the Babylonians, the Persians or Medes, the Macedonians, the kings named Antiochus, the Roman Caesars, and finally, he will raise up the head of this same plan in that often-mentioned **man of sin**, the Antichrist. Truly, therefore, they share one plan.

**And they will hand over their strength, he says, and their power to the beast.** <note>original: "Et virtutẽ... & ptãtem suã bestiæ tradẽt." Revelation 17:13.</note> 
This is as if he were to say: "What they intended, they were not or will not be able to fulfill, but the devil whom they serve will make his own man, the Antichrist, the heir of their strength and power." It is as if the devil hopes that what he could not accomplish through the others, he might at least be able to achieve through this "illustrious" <term>egregium</term> <note>Rupert uses this term ironically to describe the Antichrist as a "distinguished" or "preeminent" vessel of evil.</note> successor. And it is a beautiful thing that, although he could have said, "these will fight with Christ, and Christ will overcome them," he preferred to say: "These will fight with the lamb, and the lamb will overcome them." For truly, that first enemy—the Egyptian king—was conquered through the sacrifice of the lamb <margin>Exodus 12.</margin> so that he might release the children of Israel; and when he pursued them, he was overwhelmed <note>original: "rumensus" likely a variant or error for "submersus" (drowned/submerged).</note> in the sea. Therefore, although he speaks of the future, saying, "These will fight with the lamb, and the lamb will overcome them," nevertheless also...

### On Revelation, Chapter 17

467

It must be understood regarding the time before this John, that they fought with the Lamb, and the Lamb conquered them. For John here bears the likeness <note>original: "typum gerit." In medieval theology, a 'type' is a historical person or event that foreshadows a spiritual reality.</note> of all those who, from of old since the people of God began to be afflicted under the aforementioned kingdoms, earned divine consolation. This is wonderful, indeed praiseworthy and true, because before this Lamb had come into this world, these [kings] fought with the Lamb, and he himself conquered them. Whence quite elegantly in the prophet it is commanded that his name be called: <margin>Isaiah 8</margin> "Strip the spoils quickly, plunder fast" <note>original: "velociter spolia detrahe, cito prędare." This refers to the prophetic name 'Maher-shalal-hash-baz' in Isaiah 8:1–4, symbolizing the rapid defeat of Israel's enemies.</note> or, "Hasten to take the spoils, hurry to plunder." Why? Because, he says, before the child knows how to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians. This is the same as if he were to say: This child who is the Savior, before he comes into this world by birth, knowing or having experienced his mother, the Virgin, and Joseph, his adoptive father, he himself will deliver Israel from the hand of its enemies. <margin>Christ conquered those kings before he was born.</margin> A wonderful acceleration, a marvelous haste, that a child not yet born should himself deliver the people who hold or expect the promise of his birth. This, however, is so true that he who does not believe it is not a believer. For it is necessary to believe that before this child was born of his mother, he was God Almighty with the Father. Whence, when it had been said: "And the Lamb will conquer them," it immediately followed:

->**For he is the Lord of lords and King of kings.**<-

Did he not, before he was born, conquer the Babylonians as well, and the Persians or Medes, and the Macedonians, who fought against him—that is, against his own people who held faith in his coming—and held them captive? For what else was being demonstrated to King Nebuchadnezzar or to the prophet Daniel when the stone cut without hands <margin>Daniel 2</margin> struck the great statue, and the gold, silver, bronze, and iron were crushed together? <note>Referring to the vision in Daniel 2:31-45, where a stone (Christ) destroys a statue representing successive worldly empires.</note> What, I say, did it mean except that Christ, who is (as is said here) the Lamb, was hastening to conquer with wonderful haste (as has been said) before he was born, and did not allow his chosen ones, held captive under those kingdoms, to be tempted beyond what they were able to bear?

<summary>Rupert argues that Christ, the eternal "Lamb," defeated historical pagan empires like Babylon and Persia even before his physical birth. He links this to the prophetic "stone" in Daniel and the rapid victory promised in Isaiah, emphasizing Christ's eternal divinity.</summary>

### Rupert’s Commentary, Book 10

470

A strange assertion, a strange and violent loathing of the ungodly! How can the kings, who are represented by the horns, be said to hate their own harlot <note>The "harlot" here is a metaphor for the enticing but corrupting glory and greed of the material world.</note> with whom they themselves commit fornication? For they are the very same kings, and no others, of whom it was said above: *Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits upon many waters*, to which was added: *with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication.* Therefore, the very ones who fornicate with her are said to hate her, and to make her desolate and naked, and to eat her flesh, and to burn her with fire. This is strange, yet it is true. For who does not know how much the kings of the world have always been restless with hatred? And against whom have they been hostile in their restlessness, if not against that very greed or worldly glory with which they surely committed fornication by preferring it to their Creator? The instruments of their fornication were the beauties of cities and the wealthy multitudes of the nations over whom they ruled, and all other such things in the world that provoke the "lust of the eyes." Yet they never permitted these things to flourish in peace; they desolated everything with wars, slaughtered crowds of men with the sword, and burned cities and fortresses with fire. Nor did they do these things in a hostile manner only against each other—kings against kings, or kingdoms against kingdoms—but individual kings very often brought these evils upon their own people and their own cities.

<margin>Nero’s hatred toward the Roman realm.</margin>
For to say nothing of the others, who ever existed as a more cruel or wicked enemy to the Roman city, its people, and its Senate than its own emperor, Nero? He made the city desolate; he, by killing the people and the Senate, in a certain sense "ate her flesh." He also burned the city with physical fire, solely so that he might delight in the beauty of the flame, watching in that likeness how Troy had once burned; and sitting in the highest tower of Maecenas, dancing at such a spectacle, he sang the *Iliad* aloud.

<margin>Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book 2, Poem 6.</margin>
Someone, remembering and mourning such great cruelty, sang thus:

> We know how much ruin he wrought,
> With the city in flames and the senators slain,
> That cruel man who, having murdered his brother,
> Was drenched in his mother’s spilled blood.
> Alas, a heavy fate! etc. <note>original: "Novimus quantas dederit ruinas... Heu gravem sortem." Rupert quotes Boethius to illustrate the self-destructive nature of tyrants who destroy the very "harlot" (the world/state) they desire to possess.</note>

It is true, therefore, that the kings of the earth, who abandoned God to commit fornication with the beauty of worldly creation, hated their harlot; and what kind of violent hatreds they threatened...

<summary>Rupert explains the paradox of Revelation 17:16, where the kings of the earth destroy the Harlot they once loved. He uses the Emperor Nero as a historical example of a ruler destroying his own kingdom and people out of perverse desire and cruelty.</summary>
<keywords>Nero, Boethius, Harlot of Babylon, worldly greed, Roman history, Revelation 17, destruction of cities, tyranny</keywords>

<margin>Isaiah 57. The wretched condition of temporal kingdoms.</margin>
...they offered the price of their fornication, and they have returned it to him. <note>original: "strabāt pręciū suę fornicationis, illi reddiderūt." Rupert is likely referring to the cyclic nature of worldly greed.</note> "There is no peace for the wicked," says the Lord. <note>A reference to Isaiah 48:22 or 57:21.</note> O, therefore, how wretched is the condition of Babylon, the earthly city, which commits fornication away from God with her lovers! For she does not even merely fornicate with lovers, but with enemies; and if there is any love among them, it is mixed with such bitterness of gall that they hostilly tear apart the very one with whom they fornicate. The cause or inciter of these evils is the devil. Therefore, the Scripture did not only say, "and the ten horns which you saw, these shall hate the harlot," but it says, "and the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these shall hate their harlot," etc. He immediately adds:
**For God has put it into their hearts to do what is pleasing to him, to give their kingdom to the beast until the words of God are fulfilled.**

"To do," he says, "what is pleasing to him." To whom? This seems to refer to God, because it was phrased this way: "God gave it into their hearts." And so it is understood that they do what is pleasing to *him*—meaning to God. However, because he had previously stated, "And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these shall hate the harlot," and then, after saying "to do what is pleasing to him," he added "to give their kingdom to the beast," it is more correctly referred to the same beast. That is, so that they may do what is pleasing to *it*—meaning the beast—and then give their kingdom to the beast. This means they expend the strength of their whole kingdom upon the devil by doing his will, which is always opposed to God's good purpose.

<margin>Doing evil does not please God. Psalm 5. Isaiah 45.</margin>
For what do they do but evil? Now, evil does not please God; indeed, He himself hates those who work evil, as Scripture bears witness, saying: "You have hated all who work iniquity." <note>Psalm 5:5.</note> Likewise: "For you are not a God who wills iniquity." <note>Psalm 5:4.</note> But on the other hand, the Scripture says: "Making peace, and creating evil." <note>Isaiah 45:7.</note> Between these statements, according to the logic of truth and according to the truthful authority of the orthodox <term>Fathers</term> <note>The early Christian theologians and bishops who established church doctrine.</note>, it must be said and held that that "evil"—

which is affliction or war, the opposite of the "peace" of which it was said "making peace"—God sometimes creates for the sake of correction. But "evil" in the sense of iniquity or sin, He neither creates, nor is it pleasing to Him. And it is indeed of His will that war or some other such affliction, when...

<summary>Rupert explains that while the wicked kings serve the Beast (the Devil) out of their own malice, God paradoxically uses their actions to fulfill His divine judgment. ### Rupert of Deutz: Commentary on Revelation, Book 10

472

...should come upon those who, because of their preceding sins, deserve to suffer, they cannot escape; however, it was never, nor is it now, pleasing to Him that men should do evil or that they should become evil. 

The question is therefore asked: If the evil they do, or the very fact that they are evil, is not pleasing to God, how is it stated here previously: "For God has put it into their hearts"? <note>Rupert is quoting Revelation 17:17: "For God has put it into their hearts to accomplish his purpose."</note> While this is being asked, one must simultaneously or consequently ask about what the Psalmist says:
<margin>Psalm 103</margin>
> He turned their heart so that they hated his people, and dealt deceitfully with his servants. <note>original: "conuertit cor eorum vt odirent populum eius, & dolum facerent in seruos eius." This is Psalm 105:25 in modern numbering (104 in the Vulgate).</note>

However, that must be understood in such a way that no suspicion ever finds a place in the heart of man as if God were ever the author of hatred or deceit; to even suspect such a thing is the height of madness and impiety. For God neither hardened Pharaoh, nor did He turn the heart of the Egyptians toward hatred by desiring their hardness or hatred, but only by doing good things for the children of Israel, multiplying them in that land just as He had promised to Abraham, saying:
<margin>Genesis 22</margin>
> I will bless you, and I will multiply your seed. <note>original: "Benedicā tibi, & multiplicabo semen tuum."</note>

<margin>How God hardened Pharaoh’s heart.</margin>
But Pharaoh and the Egyptians were as proud as they were envious; and according to the custom of the envious, the more or greater divine benefits they saw bestowed upon those whom they envied, the more they raged against them with greater hatred. 
<margin>Exodus 7</margin>
Foreseeing this, God said to Moses:
> I will harden Pharaoh's heart. <note>original: "Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis."</note>

This is the same as if He were to say: "I indeed will perform signs and wonders for the children of Israel before Pharaoh and his servants; but because they are envious, this will serve for nothing else for them except that they will be hardened with greater hatred against them." Father Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), the influential theologian whose works Rupert frequently cites to support his interpretations.</note> explains the aforementioned verse in this sense. Therefore, what is said here—"For God has put it into their hearts"—must be understood in this way: we should by no means suspect that God put anything into the hearts of any of those kings so that they would do something evil, or that they themselves would become evil. Rather, God performed the good things He willed for each kingdom in its own time, but the kings of the world were as proud as they were envious, and they were envious of each other's prosperity. 

For example: God made the affairs of Babylon prosperous, so that they might be stronger than the other nations. And lest there be any doubt that this [was given] to them by God...

<summary>Rupert explains that God does not "create" evil in human hearts; rather, the wicked (like Pharaoh) react to God's blessings with envy and pride, which "hardens" them. He applies this logic to Revelation, arguing that God's "putting it into the hearts" of kings refers to His providential governance that the wicked misuse.</summary>

<margin>Jeremiah 27</margin>

God did not resist them, but rather permitted it because of the sins of Babylon. In the same way, the prosperity <note>original: *felicitas*</note> of the Persians and Medes later incited the Macedonians <note>The Macedonian Empire under Alexander the Great.</note>; this prosperity was certainly not brought about by chance, but by the ordination of God. Therefore, the scripture says, "God put it into their hearts to do what is pleasing to them, to give their kingdom to the beast." This means that the success granted to one nation by the gift of God incited the envious hearts of others toward hatred. In this way, they were stirred up against one another through envy, so that they might spend all the power of their kingdoms in a competitive service to diabolical malice. For how long?

"Until," he says, "the words of God are fulfilled."

<margin>All the deeds of kingdoms were previously foreknown by God.</margin>

For what was going to happen to them that the Word of God had not already sufficiently predicted to mankind? Or what did the Word of God predict about them, except that which ought to have justly happened to them? Finally, it was to happen, and it was just that it should happen, that after the Egyptians had oppressed the children of Israel, they themselves would pay the penalties for their iniquity; God Himself foretold this to Abraham long before. For He said: *Know for certain that your descendants shall be strangers in a land not their own, and they shall subject them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years. But nevertheless, I will judge the nation to which they shall be enslaved, and afterward they shall go out with great substance.* <note>Rupert quotes Genesis 15:13–14.</note> Likewise, it was to be that the kings of Israel and Judah, on account of the abominations they committed and the innocent blood they shed, would receive what they deservedly earned. Eventually, both Israel and Judah would be led away as captives to the Assyrians and Chaldeans <note>The Chaldeans are the Neo-Babylonians.</note>; God foretold this more than once through the prophets. The books of the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel are full of—

# 478 Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

...spirits, he repeated this by saying, "and the prison of every unclean spirit." For indeed, demons are unclean spirits. And for what reason did he repeat this? Evidently because the damned angels—who are demons or malignant spirits—will suffer punishment for a twofold reason. One reason is because they grew proud against the Creator in heaven. The other is because they polluted the human race with every filth of vice, having first deceived it through the serpent’s initial transgression. On account of the first reason they are called **demons**—that is, "knowing ones" <note>Rupert relies on a common medieval etymology, derived from the Greek *daimon*, which scholars of the time linked to the word for "knowing" or "wise," suggesting they possessed knowledge but lacked charity</note>—because they raised themselves up against the knowledge of God. On account of the second reason they are called **unclean spirits**, because they are most filthy; for, as has already been said, they have afflicted the human race through their suggestions with many kinds of passions of uncleanness and shame. Furthermore, "unclean and hateful birds" are rightly understood as all the proud, both demons and humans. For flight signifies the rush toward profit, and the levity and vanity of the proud. Nor are they compared to just any birds, but to unclean ones. For example, owls or hoopoes <note>original: "noctuas siue upupis"</note>, which delight in sitting upon human dung, and for that reason are rightly held to be unclean and hateful. 

Babylon has become a prison for such birds; and as was said through Isaiah, <margin>Isaiah 8</margin> they will not be able to fly away from their distress <note>original: "non poterit auolare de angustia"</note>. The cause or reasoning which follows is again manifest and was partly explained above:

> Because all nations have drunk of the wine of the wrath of
> her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed
> fornication with her, and the merchants of the earth 
> have become rich through the abundance of her luxuries.

Three things are stated here: that all nations drank of the wrath of her fornication; that the kings of the earth committed fornication with her; and that the merchants of the earth were made rich by her luxuries. In summary, the whole reproach of fornication is imputed to the kings, <margin>The chief blame lies with the kings.</margin> and they are more frequently noted in this reading as guilty of the crime of this same fornication. And deservedly so: because they not only accepted what that harlot taught, but they even reinforced it by the decree of their empire and by the strength of the sword. Furthermore, the nations who were subject to the kings—whether because of the kings' command or of their own accord—worshiped monsters instead of God; rightly, he says, they drank of the wrath of the same fornication...

<summary>Rupert explains that demons are punished for both their pride against God and their corruption of humanity, comparing the proud to "unclean birds" trapped in Babylon. He emphasizes that the kings of the earth bear the greatest guilt for state-sanctioned idolatry and vice.</summary>

# On Revelation Chapter 18

...drank. <note>The transcription begins mid-sentence with "runt," the ending of "biberunt" (they have drunk), referring to the nations drinking the wine of Babylon's wrath.</note> Yet he does not say they drank of her fornication, but of the **wrath of her fornication**. This is because the wrath of God immediately followed that fornication—in which they worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator—
<margin>Romans 1</margin>
so that He might abandon them and hand them over to shameful passions, handing them over to the desires of their hearts unto uncleanness, and to a depraved mind, to do those things which are not fitting. <note>Rupert is paraphrasing Romans 1:24-28 to explain that God's punishment for idolatry is often allowing the sinner to become enslaved to their own vices.</note> But does he not state as a testimony that 
<margin>The merchants of the earth were made rich. 1 Timothy 6</margin>
**the merchants of the earth were made rich** from the power of her luxuries? And are those very merchants not blamed for having judged so falsely? After all, it is not Babylon herself—that is, greed <note>original: *cupiditas*</note>, the root of all evils—nor those who preside over greed (the malignant demons and perverse men who deceive the world, the sum of whom is here called "Babylon" and the "mother of fornications") who created these goods. It was not the perversity of such beings, I say, but the goodness of the one God that created and gave even those good things by which the merchants of the earth were enriched. They, however, judged the matter quite differently.

<margin>Hosea 2</margin>
Hence God rightly says of such people through the prophet:
> "And I will not have mercy on her children, for they are children of fornications, because their mother has played the harlot. She who conceived them is confounded, because she said: 'I will go after my lovers who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.' And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain and the wine and the oil, and I multiplied for her the silver and gold which they used for Baal." <note>Hosea 2:4-8. Rupert uses this to show that people often credit their own "lovers" (idols or greed) for the blessings God actually provided.</note>

Moreover, the fact that he did not speak merely of her luxuries, but said they were made rich by the **power** <note>original: *virtute*, which can mean power, strength, or moral virtue</note> of her luxuries, denotes the foolishness of those for whom poverty is held as a reproach and is despised as a monstrous vice. To them, an abundance of riches is considered "virtue." This is despite the fact that even a pagan says:
<margin>Horace</margin>
> "Silver is worth less than gold, gold than virtues." <note>Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.52. Rupert contrasts the spiritual "virtue" of the classics with the material "power/virtue" of the merchants.</note>

It should be noted, however, that he was not content to say "Babylon has fallen" just once; rather, with the word for "fall" or "ruin" doubled, he said: **"Fallen, fallen is Babylon."** Truly, repetition is an affirmation. But beyond this, it must be known that this Babylon fell on both sides—as that angel cried out the aforementioned cry—which is to say, as Christ suffered for the salvation of all.

<summary>Rupert explains that Babylon represents the "root of all evil" (greed), arguing that while wealth comes from God's goodness, merchants sin by attributing their prosperity to their own vices or false gods. He highlights the moral inversion where wealth is mistaken for virtue and notes that Babylon's fall is doubled to emphasize its certainty and completeness through Christ's passion.</summary>

Rightly, then, is the word doubled <note>Rupert refers to the phrase "Fallen, fallen is Babylon" (Rev 18:2), interpreted as a dual victory over death and over idolatry</note>, because both the power of death there, and the worship of demons here, has fallen.

<margin>Acts 2</margin>

# On Revelation, Chapter 18

...her sins. For he says, **"her sins have reached even to heaven"** <note>original: *peruenerunt peccata eius vsque ad coelum*</note>. That is, because by her fornication and by intoxicating herself with the blood of the saints, she went so far as to kill the very King and Lord of heaven. And for this reason, he says, **"the Lord has remembered her iniquities"** <note>original: *recordatus est dominus iniquitatum eius*</note>. That is, He has appointed the day of universal judgment in which her iniquities may be punished. From this it follows: **"Render to her as she herself has rendered to you, and double the double according to her works. In the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double. As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give to her torment and mourning."**

<margin>
Matthew 19

Render to her double

Luke 12

Two causes of her damnation.
</margin>

Who are these who are commanded to render to her as she rendered to them, and to double the double according to her works, if not those who will sit with the Lord as He sits to judge on the throne of His majesty? They themselves will sit on judicial seats—namely, the saints and the martyrs of Jesus, with whose blood this harlot was shown above to be drunk. **"Render, therefore,"** he says, **"to her as she herself rendered to you."** That is: condemn her just as she condemned your innocent blood. It was not enough to have said, "as she herself rendered to you," unless he had immediately added, **"and double the double according to her works."** 

For it is clear that while this woman <note>representing Babylon or the worldly power</note> persecuted the saints and martyrs of Jesus, she killed only the body, and after this she has nothing more she can do; but they themselves, in judgment with the same Lord Jesus, have this power: to cast both body and soul into Gehenna <note>the place of final punishment; original: *gehennam*</note>. Well, then, does he say: **"double the double according to her works."** And likewise: **"and in the cup in which she mixed, mix for her double."** And he immediately says: **"As much as she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so much give to her torment and mourning."** For the pride with which she exalted herself, give her mourning; for the luxuries she used inordinately, give her torment. These are the two causes of her damnation: one, because she returned evil to the saints and martyrs of Jesus when she shed their blood; the other, because she overflowed in her luxuries and fornications—which causes were indeed written above and are repeated here in reverse order.

482 Rupert’s Commentary, Book <note>The header indicates page 482 of Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on the Apocalypse.</note>

The sum of her guilt is noted, so that the punishment for her sin may be unending: her pride <note>original: *superbia*</note>. For she does not merely sin or commit fornication in any ordinary way, but she glories or glorifies herself in her sins and fornications. Whence it is further added:
**"Because she says in her heart: I sit as a queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall see no mourning. Therefore her plagues shall come in one day: death, and mourning, and famine, and she shall be burned with fire, because God is strong, who has judged her."**
Regarding how and why she says in her heart, "I sit as a queen," etc.

<margin>
Isaiah 47. Babylon, ironically a virgin.
</margin>

Truth <note>a common medieval title for Christ or the Holy Spirit as the source of Scripture</note> long ago confirmed the prophecy that she must therefore endure these plagues. For in the prophet Isaiah it is said to her among other things: **"Come down, sit in the dust, O most heavy virgin daughter of Babylon, sit on the ground, O virgin."** <note>original: *Descende sede in puluere virgo grauissima...*</note> "Most heavy" is said there with irony; for here she is truly pronounced a harlot <note>original: *meretrix*</note>.
Immediately after it is said to her: **"You said: I shall be a lady forever. You did not lay these things to your heart, nor did you remember your end. And now hear these things, you who are delicate and dwell confidently, who say in your heart: I am, and besides me there is no other. I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know barrenness. These two things shall come to you suddenly in one day: barrenness and widowhood, etc."** <note>Rupert is quoting Isaiah 47:7-9 to show the continuity of God's judgment against worldly pride.</note>
Therefore, on account of pride—because this harlot does not just sin in any fashion, but sins by being proud, and in sinning she is proud and exults—she does not consider herself a widow like the City of God <note>referring to the Church, which "mourns" while waiting for Christ</note>, which lives as a pilgrim in this world. Instead, being a harlot, many kings commit fornication with her, as if this were the legitimate marriage of a blessed, powerful, and dominant queen. Because of this, I say, the judgment is just and irreproachable, that these plagues should come upon her: death, mourning, and famine, and that she should be burned with eternal fire. Nor is the sentence doubtful; rather, it must have a certain effect, because **"strong,"** he says, **"is the God who has judged her,"** and once the sentence is brought forth by voice or writing, He is not powerless to fulfill it.

**"And the kings of the earth, who have committed fornication with her and lived in luxury, shall weep and bewail themselves over her, when they see the smoke of her burning, standing afar off..."**

<meta>This page continues Rupert of Deutz’s commentary on Revelation 18, moving from the internal pride of Babylon to the external reaction of the world to its sudden downfall. He draws a sophisticated parallel between the "woes" cried out by the kings and merchants and the prophetic scroll described in the Book of Ezekiel.</meta>

### On Apocalypse Chapter 18

...[they will stand] far off for fear of her torment, and they shall say: "Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city, for in one hour your judgment has come."

<margin>The rolled-up book in which there was a song and woe. Ezekiel 2.</margin>
At this point, it is helpful to recall that writing or scroll of which it is written in the prophet Ezekiel: **"And I saw, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled-up book, and he spread it before me; it was written within and without: and there were written in it lamentations, and a song, and woe."** <note>Ezekiel 2:9-10. Rupert uses this Old Testament image to explain the structure of divine judgment.</note> For that book is the whole of divinely inspired Scripture, which is spread out before the prophet because it is made intelligible to a faithful man through the opening grace of Christ.

<margin>A song is for the blessed, woe for the damned, lamentation for the penitent.</margin>
In that book are written lamentations, and a song, and woe. Of these three, "song" and "woe" are opposites, while "lamentations" hold a middle place. For the Holy Scriptures promise an eternal song <note>original: *carmen*</note> to the saints and the elect in the world to come. "Woe," however, is for all the impious, such as are denoted in this passage: the kings of the earth who committed fornication with the harlot and lived in luxuries, and the merchants of the earth who became rich from the power of her delights. Furthermore, "lamentations" belong to the penitent, who in the present life lament their sins for a time, so that they might not come to that eternal woe.

This present passage of Scripture demonstrates all these things—namely lamentations, song, and woe—gathered together for those who read studiously. For when it is said: **"Go out from her, my people, so that you do not participate in her crimes, and that you do not receive her plagues,"** repentance is preached to all nations (as has already been said), which is certainly a form of lamenting. 

But "Woe" is expressed here more clearly (as it is their specific lot), when they themselves say: **"Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city, for in one hour your judgment has come."** And again: **"Woe, woe, that great city which was clothed in fine linen, and purple, and scarlet, and was gilded with gold, and precious stones, and pearls, for in one hour such great riches have been brought to nothing."** And likewise a third time: **"Woe, woe, great city, in which all who have ships in the sea became rich from her prices: for..."**

<summary>Rupert explains the "threefold woe" of Babylon's fall by linking it to Ezekiel’s prophetic scroll, categorizing divine messages into songs for the saved, lamentations for the penitent, and woes for the damned.</summary>
<keywords>Babylon, Ezekiel, Apocalypse, Lamentations, Song, Woe, Judgment, Repentance, Kings of the Earth, Merchants of the Earth</keywords>

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

...in one hour she is made desolate. A third time "woe" is doubled, and thus "woe" is spoken six times in total. And one and the same cause for saying "woe, woe" is given everywhere, though with a few words changed: "for in one hour your judgment has come," "for in one hour such great riches are stripped away," "for in one hour she is made desolate." For the crimes of all the ages of the world, which are six in number, shall now be avenged upon them all at once; for these people, there is no seventh age, that is, no Sabbath <note>Rupert refers to the common medieval theology of the "Six Ages of the World" corresponding to the six days of creation. The "seventh age" or Sabbath represents eternal rest in God, which the wicked will never reach.</note>. 

And this will be a marvelous and most wretched thing for those to behold who so greatly love this wicked world: because the evil works of so many days or times, and so many ages of the world, shall be judged, and their joys shall perish—replaced by an unending magnitude of torments—in one hour of judgment, one hour of deprivation, and one hour of desolation. Then all those things shall perish at once, in

<margin>All the world’s concupiscence <note>original: *concupiscẽtia*, or intense worldly desire</note> shall perish.</margin>

which the fornicators and lovers of the world lived in luxury with the oft-mentioned harlot. Gold and silver, and precious stones, and pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood <note>original: *lignum tinum*; an aromatic wood used for costly furniture</note>, and every vessel of ivory, and every vessel of precious stone, and of brass, and of iron, and of marble—all of which pertain to the **fornication of the eyes**. 

Next are cinnamon and amomum <note>an ancient spice plant</note>, and other kinds of incense and perfumes, which are surely referred here to the **fornicating sense of smell**. Next are the types of ointment, which look toward luxury <note>The sense of touch or general excess</note>. Then, he says, wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, which (or things similar to them) are referred to the **sense of taste**. 

After many things, there is also brought in the voice of harpers, and musicians, and pipe-players. And the trumpet shall be heard in you no more; these look toward the fifth sense of the body, that is, **hearing**. Therefore, all the instruments of fornication that entice through the five senses of the body are damned; for it is through these senses that every adultery of the soul—which fornicates by turning away from God—is committed. 

The service of beasts of burden and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves <note>original: *mancipiorum*</note>, and the souls of men, are also numbered among the perishing furniture of the world. Even the fruits <note>original: *poma*</note> are expressed by their own name, because they too must perish for their role in inordinate desire...

### On the Apocalypse, Chapter 18

...they should, by saying: "And the fruit of your soul’s desire has departed from you." <note>original: *poma tua desideriũ aīæ*; a reference to Revelation 18:14</note> Nevertheless, among these things are included whatever are the enticements of gluttony or the delicacies of the kitchen, when it is added: "and all things fat and bright have perished from you." Almost all the instruments of pleasure, however many or great they may be, which are drawn in through the five senses of the body—and through which the more noble part of man <note>The "noble part" refers to the soul, which in medieval theology is "imprisoned" or "sickened" by excessive sensory indulgence.</note> grows faint and is taken captive—are expressed by their own names as being about to perish, through the marvelous diligence of the one seeing and writing <note>The "one seeing and writing" refers to St. John the Apostle, the traditional author of Revelation.</note>.

<margin>A wretched spectacle in the final fire of the world.</margin>
Because, evidently, in that hour when this world begins to be consumed by the final fire, it provides a wretched spectacle to all its lovers, where they will see everything they possessed with excessive love perish, not without great sorrow. Therefore, to suggest that the intensity of the pain will be no small thing, he describes the inconsolable misery of those weeping and mourning once, twice, and a third time:

> And the kings of the earth shall weep and mourn over her.
> And again: And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her, for no one buys their merchandise anymore.
> And thereafter: And every shipmaster, and everyone who sails to a place, and sailors, and those who work the seas, stood afar off and cried out, seeing the place of her burning, saying: "What city is like this great city?"
> And they cast, he says, dust upon their heads.

<margin>Not a true repentance of those mourning.</margin>
Dust upon the head signifies the sadness of repentance <note>original: *pœnitudo*; a sorrow for sin or a change of mind</note>. But that repentance is no longer useful or fruitful, because it is far too late. At the same time, it must be known that there is now no reason or wisdom in those repenting. For what kind of repentance, or how rational a manner of it, is there when those weeping and mourning cry out and say: "What city is like this great city?" Even now, they imagine the phantom <note>original: *phantasiām*</note> of transitory glory which they had seen to have been a "great city." Therefore, they do not grieve so much that they allowed themselves harmful pleasures, as they do that these same pleasures are perishing from them beyond recovery. And indeed, if they could [keep] all these perishing fuels of greed, which are here expressed by name alongside their torment...

### Commentary of Rupert, Book 10

...[they desire] to rescue her from the fire and keep her for themselves. But without a doubt they will not be able to; while things are perishing, the help of those who are likewise perishing will be far away. Hence, as a significant sign of their helplessness, it is said here once, twice, and a third time that "they stood afar off."

> "When," he says, "the kings of the earth see the smoke of her burning, standing afar off for fear of her torments, they shall say: 'Woe, woe!'" <note>original: *væ væ*; Revelation 18:9–10</note>

> Likewise: "And the merchants of these things, who were made rich by her, shall stand afar off for fear of her torments, weeping and mourning, and saying: 'Woe, woe!'" And a little after: "And every shipmaster and all the sailors stood afar off, and cried out, weeping and mourning, and saying: 'Woe, woe!'" <note>Revelation 18:15, 17–18</note>

All of them—kings as well as sailors or shipmasters, sailors as well as merchants—will "stand afar off," not so much in physical distance as by a failing of the heart and a weakened spirit. For it is evident that at that time the kings will have neither weapons nor armies to fight with, the sailors no oars for rowing, and the merchants no stalls <note>original: *institias*; referring to the places or structures used for trade and packing</note> to gather their bundles. For even the support of pack animals, horses, and carriages will be lacking. 

<margin>A distinction between the simple life and worldly greed.</margin>
Meanwhile, it should be noted that shepherds or countryfolk are not written of as having this weeping and mourning. This is because their duties belong to a simple life, and they serve necessary use rather than superfluous greed. Sailors, however, are rightly not excluded from this sort of weeping and mourning. For they themselves laugh and boast not a little while they row and are carried on a prosperous course through the seas. Anyone who has ever seen ships <note>The original OCR reads *auium* (birds), but the context of *velificantium* (sailing) indicates it should be *nauium* (ships).</note> sailing along favorably, or has heard the <term>celeuma</term> (which is a sailor's song) <note>A rhythmic chant used by ancient and medieval rowers to coordinate their strokes.</note> of wanton sailors, undoubtedly perceives that this is so. 

Nor can these sailors be seen as excusable like the countryfolk or shepherds—with some of whom God spoke from the beginning <note>A reference to the patriarchs and prophets of the Bible, such as Abel, Abraham, or David, who were shepherds and were considered "closer to God" for their simple lifestyle.</note>—for by the strength of the sailors' arms, not only merchant ships but even warships have been driven along, and they have very often stained the sea's waves with the blood of war.

Matthew 25.
</margin>
who shall be on his left hand: "Depart, you cursed, into everlasting fire, which is prepared for the devil and his angels." <note>original: "Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum..." — Matthew 25:41. Rupert links the fall of Babylon directly to the Final Judgment.</note> For then, in truth, the entire city of the devil will be cast with great violence into the deep; and just as a great stone cast into the sea does not float or leap back out again, so once she has been cast down, she shall never emerge from hell again. And he fittingly spoke not of just any stone, but one "like a millstone" <term>millstone (lapis molaris): a heavy stone used to grind grain, here symbolizing both the weight of sin and the repetitive, "circular" nature of worldly error</term> to express the comparison: namely, because this Babylon is both heavy with the weight of sin and unstable with the agitation of error. A millstone aptly suggests both of these qualities, as it is heavy in weight and always goes around in its duty of grinding. And there follows immediately:

> "And the voice of harpers, and of musicians, and of those playing flutes, and of trumpets shall be heard in you no more." <note>Revelation 18:22</note>

<margin>
The music of the harlot is condemned, but not the song of the saints.
</margin>
Now, we anticipated this point earlier to keep together the pleasures of each of the bodily senses. The other things lamented in that place serve the other luxuriating senses; however, by these—that is, by musical instruments—the sense of hearing is soothed. Nor is all the music of such a great harlot <note>The "harlot" represents the corrupt worldly system of Babylon.</note> condemned without reason: for undoubtedly the things she sings are playful and lascivious—even shameful—and are also the phantoms of demons. The harlot abuses the sweetness of these sounds especially to incite lusts. Otherwise, in the true praises of the true God, the reasonable service of the beautiful art of music is laudably accepted; and for those who sing lawfully and play the psalms wisely, the reward or prize will be an eternal song. Regarding this, a little later, this scripture—reporting good news—will magnificently console the patience of the saints.

> "And every craftsman and every art shall not be found..." <note>Revelation 18:22b</note>

...in you any more. And the voice of a millstone shall not be heard in you any more. And the light of a lamp shall not shine in you any more.
